findings.requirement_type: No Commercial Auto Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. ... Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.B, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.11, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided in the program submission. The Hanover Package (ZB4 H221415 05) is a Property + GL + Equipment Breakdown + Data Breach package and does not include Commercial Auto coverage. Hanover GL form 421-2915 does not endorse Hired/Non-Owned Auto onto the GL.
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento County ($1M CSL) and Maricopa County ($2M CSL) contractually require Commercial Auto Liability covering owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles. There is no Commercial Auto policy in the program. Run-Test transports ballots, election technology, mail, and high-value equipment between facilities and county election offices, and operates owned and/or hired vehicles in the course of those operations. Without an Auto policy, every line of the Commercial Auto RMF (AI / Waiver of Subrogation / Primary & Non-Contributory / Hired-Non-Owned / Symbols 1 vs 7 / Mobile Equipment / Mental Anguish / Fellow Employee / Notice & Knowledge / UM-UIM / Drive Other Car / Lease Gap) is unaddressed and any third-party auto loss arising from operations is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: You are contractually required to carry Auto Liability for Sacramento, Maricopa, and likely every other county you serve — but there is no Auto policy in the program. If a Run-Test driver, a hired truck, or even an employee using their personal car on company business causes a serious crash while transporting ballots or election equipment, there is nothing in your program to defend or pay the claim. This is also a contract breach with every county.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Auto policy immediately covering Symbol 1 (Any Auto) for owned vehicles plus Hired & Non-Owned. Limits: minimum $2M CSL to satisfy Maricopa; pair with the umbrella for any higher-county requirements. Add blanket AI, blanket Waiver of Subrogation, Primary & Non-Contributory, Mental Anguish in BI, deletion of Fellow Employee Exclusion, Drive Other Car for executive officers, Hired Auto Physical Damage, and Notice & Knowledge endorsement. Verify Symbol 1 vs 8/9 against actual ownership and add CA 9933 / CA 2054 if employees use personal vehicles for company business.
discoveryQuestions: How are Run-Test ballots, election equipment, and mail being moved between your facility and the 31 states / 90+ million voters you serve — is that on owned trucks, hired carriers, or employees' personal vehicles?
If a Run-Test driver had a serious accident tomorrow while delivering ballots to a county election office, who do you believe would defend and pay the claim?
Have any of the counties you contract with ever asked you for an Auto certificate, and what did you provide?
When employees pick up supplies, drive to vendor sites, or run errands in their own cars on company business, is that exposure something you have ever insured?

findings.requirement_type: No Workers' Compensation Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance. ... Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes having jurisdiction of Contractor's employees engaged in the performance of the work or services under this contract; and Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.C / §III.C–D, Page 1–2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.12, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation / Employers Liability policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has 50–200 employees in AZ and a stated working footprint across 31 states. AZ is a non-monopolistic NCCI state requiring statutory WC coverage. Sacramento contractually requires California statutory WC coverage (or Other States Coverage extending to CA in Item 3.A). Maricopa requires statutory WC plus EL $1M/$1M/$1M. There is no WC policy in the program. Every WC RMF item — All States Endorsement (Item 3.A vs 3.C), Alternate Employer for staffing, EL limits supporting umbrella, Experience Mod management, classification codes, Waiver of Subrogation (WC 04 03 06 in CA), USL&H/MEL/DBA — is unaddressed.
findings.plain_english: You have employees in Arizona and you do work in 31 states including California. Workers' Comp is required by statute in every NCCI state and is required by every county contract. There is no WC policy in your program. If an employee gets hurt today, the entire claim — medical, lost wages, employer liability, defense — falls on the company directly, plus AZ statutory penalties for non-coverage and material breach of every county contract.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Workers' Compensation policy immediately. Required structure: AZ as Item 3.A primary state; Item 3.C 'All States' (or specifically schedule every state where you have payroll exposure including CA, the District of Columbia, and the 31 states served); EL limits $1M/$1M/$1M minimum to satisfy Maricopa and support umbrella attachment; blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CA-specific WC 04 03 06 form for Sacramento work); Alternate Employer endorsement if you use staffing or temp labor; review Owner exclusions; verify classification codes against actual operations (printing/mailing/election technology installation/clerical).
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through how Run-Test currently handles a workplace injury — if a press operator hurt their back loading a pallet of ballots tomorrow, what happens?
When you take on a CA county contract, who confirms that your WC will respond for an employee who travels to California to support that contract?
Are you using any temp or staffing agency labor on the printing or mail-processing floor? If so, whose WC covers them?
When was the last time anyone reviewed the experience mod or class codes against what your employees actually do?

findings.requirement_type: No Professional Liability / E&O Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement... B. Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions / Tech E&O policy was provided in the program submission. Hanover GL endorsement 421-2915 §1.c.(5) excludes professional services from Additional Insured coverage. Hanover GL is occurrence-based and contains no professional services giveback for election technology operations.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no policy located; AI carve-out at Page 194
findings.gap_description: Run-Test designs, prints, processes, and provides technology platforms for ballots and elections — squarely 'professional services' as the term is used in standard policy forms. Sacramento contractually requires $1M/$1M E&O on a continuous-retro basis with Sacramento expressly stating Umbrella may NOT satisfy the PL minimum (§II.E). The Hanover GL contains a professional services carve-out within the AI provision and an absolute Cyber Incident Exclusion (421-5286) — meaning a claim alleging an error in ballot design, election software, mail-piece processing, or election data handling has no coverage anywhere in the program.
findings.plain_english: Election services is a professional/technology service. If a county sues you because a ballot was misprinted, scanned incorrectly, mailed late, or the technology platform failed during an election, the GL will deny coverage citing the professional services and cyber exclusions, and there is no E&O policy to pick up the loss. This is the single biggest exposure facing this company and it is currently 100% uninsured. It is also a contract breach with Sacramento (and likely every other county).
findings.recommendation: Bind a Technology / Professional Liability / Election-Services E&O policy immediately. Negotiate the definition of 'Professional Services' to expressly include ballot design, ballot printing, election mail processing, ballot scanning/sorting, voter list services, election technology software/SaaS, and emergency election support. Limits $5M+ given the scale of operations (90M voter records, 31 states); continuous retro back to inception of operations or earliest contract performance date; minimum 1-year ERP per Sacramento §V.B-C and 2-year ERP per Maricopa §8.2.3; duty-to-defend; broad consent-to-settle (no hammer or capped hammer); cyber/privacy carve-back or — preferably — combined Tech E&O + Cyber form to eliminate inter-policy gaps.
discoveryQuestions: If a county claimed that 50,000 ballots were misprinted or processed incorrectly and they incurred $2M of remediation costs, where would that claim go in your insurance program?
How would you respond if Sacramento or Maricopa asked you tomorrow for proof of $1M Professional Liability with a retroactive date going back to your earliest county relationship?
Have any vendor or county contracts ever rejected your COI because there was no E&O listed?
When you bid on new county work, is the absence of E&O a competitive disadvantage you've heard about — and what would the right policy let you say 'yes' to that you currently have to say 'no' to?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Effectively No Real Cyber Coverage in Program
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information), crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Data Breach Coverage Form 411-0669 01 15: '$10,000 aggregate / $10,000 sublimit for breach expenses / $1,000 deductible / 24-hour cyber BI waiting period.' §B.1.d excludes 'any fees, costs, settlements, judgments, or liability of any kind arising in the course of, or as a result of a claim for damages, lawsuit, administrative proceedings...' (i.e., third-party liability is not covered). §B.1.c excludes 'fines, penalties, fees or assessments.' §B.1.g excludes 'legal obligations arising by reason of assumption of liability in a contract or agreement.' §E.4 anti-stacking. GL forms CG 00 69, CG 21 06, and 421-5286 contain three overlapping absolute exclusions for any cyber, data privacy, or confidential-information disclosure claims.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $5M dedicated Cyber/Network Security/Privacy Liability with an itemized list of inclusions including third-party liability, regulatory defense plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer, third-party fidelity, and broad social engineering. The program contains: (1) a $10,000 aggregate first-party-only Data Breach token endorsement that excludes third-party liability, contractually-assumed liability, and fines/penalties; (2) GL forms with three stacked absolute exclusions for cyber and data privacy claims. For a contractor handling 90M+ voter records across 31 states and the District of Columbia, with nation-state cyber actors targeting US election infrastructure, this is the single most critical exposure in the audit.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test handles voter data for over 90 million Americans. The contract requires $5M of real cyber coverage. What you have is a $10,000 token endorsement that only handles first-party breach notification — it does not cover lawsuits from voters, counties, or state attorneys general; it does not cover regulatory fines from CCPA/state breach laws; it does not cover ransomware extortion at any meaningful limit; and the GL has three separate exclusions blocking any cyber-related liability claim. A single nation-state attack, ransomware event, or data exfiltration claim would be effectively uninsured and could bankrupt the company.
findings.recommendation: Bind a stand-alone Cyber Liability policy at $10M+ aggregate (above Maricopa's $5M minimum given 90M voter records, election-sector criticality, PE-backed status). Coverage must include: third-party privacy liability, regulatory defense PLUS fines and penalties (where insurable by law), cyber extortion / ransomware (no sublimit or sublimit ≥ $5M), social engineering / fraudulent instruction at full limit, computer fraud / funds transfer fraud, network business interruption, dependent BI (cloud/SaaS/processing-vendor failures), data restoration, breach response, PCI/HIPAA/CCPA regulatory, war/cyber-war carve-back via Lloyd's-style affirmative coverage. Retro date back to inception of operations. Continuous retro requirement per Maricopa §8.2.3 (must precede contract effective date with 2-year ERP).
discoveryQuestions: If voter data for one of your county clients was exfiltrated tomorrow, walk me through who pays for forensics, notification to 1+ million people, regulatory defense, and the inevitable AG investigation.
Has Run-Test ever modeled what a ransomware attack during election week — say October — would cost in business interruption alone?
Election infrastructure is designated critical infrastructure by CISA. Has any insurer ever asked about your nation-state threat posture, MFA, EDR coverage, or backup segmentation?
When Maricopa or any county asks for a $5M cyber COI today, what do you send them?

findings.requirement_type: No Umbrella / Excess Liability Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements... If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.9, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella or Excess Liability policy was provided in the program submission.
findings.gap_description: There is no umbrella in the program. This means: (a) the underlying GL ($1M occurrence / $2M aggregate with $2M total cap) cannot be augmented to meet Maricopa's $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate requirement (§8.2.10); (b) any Auto policy would have to be written at full $2M CSL standalone; (c) every umbrella RMF item — defense inside vs outside limits, follow-form, drop-down, AI follow-form, WoS follow-form, primary/non-contributory other-insurance condition, maintenance of underlying, punitive damages, right and duty when underlying exhausted, professional liability follow-form — is unaddressed. For a PE-backed manufacturer/technology firm with multi-state government contracts, $1M primary limits are dramatically inadequate.
findings.plain_english: There is no umbrella protecting this company. A serious lawsuit — auto crash, products liability claim from a printing chemical, premises injury at the Phoenix facility, a personal injury claim from someone affected by an election error — easily exceeds the $1M GL limit. PE-backed sponsors typically demand $10M–$25M of total liability protection as a baseline. You have $1M.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Umbrella at $10M minimum (recommend $25M given PE sponsorship, government-contract footprint, and election-sector liability profile). Follow-form across all underlying liability lines (GL, Auto once bound, Employers Liability once WC bound). Specifically negotiate: defense costs outside limits where possible, drop-down for exhausted underlying aggregates, AI and WoS follow-form, punitive damages 'where insurable,' right and duty to defend if underlying is exhausted, schedule of underlying that lists every required underlying policy and limit. Confirm the umbrella will satisfy Maricopa §8.2.9 program-level umbrella permission and Sacramento §II.E follow-form requirement (Sacramento expressly excludes umbrella from satisfying the Professional Liability minimum).
discoveryQuestions: What does your PE sponsor expect for total liability limits across the program — and how does $1M of GL match up against that expectation?
If a claim from a Sacramento or Maricopa contract exceeded $1M, where would the extra dollars come from?
Has a county ever asked for a $5M or $10M umbrella COI and you've had to negotiate down?
When is the last time you compared the cost of buying $10M of umbrella against the cost of a single uninsured judgment exceeding your primary limit?

findings.requirement_type: No EPLI Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: (Industry standard for 50–200 employee companies; not a specific contract requirement, but a critical RMF gap given Hanover GL employment-practices exclusion.)
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL CG 21 47 12 07 Employment-Related Practices Exclusion: 'Excludes BI and Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of refusal to employ, termination, or employment-related practices (coercion, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, malicious prosecution).' No EPLI policy located in program. EBL form CG 04 35 12 07 expressly excludes 'employment-related practices' (EBL is administrative E&O only).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has 50–200 employees including printing/manufacturing floor workers and salaried staff. EEOC, wrongful termination, harassment, retaliation, and wage-and-hour claims are statistically frequent for companies of this size. The GL excludes all employment-related practices, the EBL is administrative-only, and there is no EPLI policy in the program. The next harassment, discrimination, or wrongful-termination suit is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: If an employee files a harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or wrongful-termination claim, you pay every dollar of defense and settlement out of pocket. Companies your size average a 3-year EPL claim probability above 15%. Defense alone on a typical EEOC matter runs $75k–$250k.
findings.recommendation: Bind an EPLI policy with $1M–$3M limit. Required components: third-party EPLI (claims by non-employees — counties, vendors, voters), Wage & Hour defense sublimit (minimum $250k–$500k), broad definition of 'Employee' to include temps/seasonal/contractors, duty to defend, hammer clause review (prefer 80/20 or no hammer), prior acts coverage. Pay attention to PE-backed exclusion language and consider standalone vs Management Liability bundle.
discoveryQuestions: How many employees has Run-Test parted ways with in the last 24 months — and how do you currently handle the legal risk on each separation?
If a former employee filed an EEOC charge tomorrow, who defends and pays?
Have any of your county clients ever made a third-party harassment or discrimination claim — say a temp worker or vendor employee?
Are you using any seasonal or temp labor on the printing/mail floor, and have they been trained on your harassment policy?

findings.requirement_type: No D&O / Management Liability Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: (PE-backed entity baseline — not contract-specific. PE sponsors and lenders virtually always require D&O. Government-contracts and election-sector regulatory exposure heighten exposure.)
findings.policy_quote: No D&O / Side A / Management Liability policy located in program submission.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is PE-backed, holds government contracts, and operates in a heavily politicized industry (election services). D&O exposures include: PE-sponsor demands, securities-style claims on a future exit, regulatory investigations (DOJ, state AGs, EAC, CISA, congressional inquiries), shareholder/investor disputes, M&A litigation, fiduciary claims, and politically motivated litigation against directors. There is no D&O policy. Individual directors and officers — including PE-appointed board members — have no defense or indemnity protection.
findings.plain_english: Your directors and officers — including PE-appointed board members — are personally on the hook for any lawsuit, regulatory investigation, or political/election-related claim that names them as individuals. This is unusual for a PE-backed company; most PE sponsors require it as a condition of investment. A single politically-motivated investigation could exhaust personal assets in defense costs alone.
findings.recommendation: Bind D&O / Management Liability with: $5M–$10M minimum aggregate; Side A (non-indemnifiable claims), Side B (corporate reimbursement), Side C (entity securities) coverage; broad definition of 'Claim' including regulatory and government investigations; broad definition of 'Wrongful Act'; Insured-vs-Insured carve-backs for whistleblower and regulatory; prior/pending litigation date; bump-up coverage for change-of-control. Coordinate with PE sponsor's portfolio program if available. Often packaged with EPLI + Fiduciary + Crime in a Management Liability program.
discoveryQuestions: What does your PE sponsor's portfolio insurance program look like — are you supposed to be on a master D&O tower, or is each portfolio company on its own?
Given how politicized election services has become, has any director ever expressed concern about personal exposure from a politically-motivated lawsuit or congressional inquiry?
If the DOJ or a state AG opened an investigation tomorrow, who pays the directors' personal counsel?
When the next exit or recapitalization happens, do you have run-off coverage for the current board secured?

findings.requirement_type: No Stand-Alone Crime / Fidelity Policy
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa cyber spec includes 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured' — components typically delivered via stand-alone Crime.)
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Property package contains crime sublimits via 411-0793 02 23 Gold Property Broadening: Employee Theft $250,000; Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud $50,000; Forgery or Alteration $100,000; Money & Securities $50,000. Social engineering scope is narrow per §III.A.12 — only 'fraudulent instruction received from a computer software contractor' carve-back. No stand-alone Crime/Fidelity policy in program.
findings.gap_description: Crime exposures are addressed only by sublimits within the Property form. Limits are token relative to the company's profile: $250K Employee Theft for a $5M–$25M revenue PE-backed company is low; $50K Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud is severely below a one-event social-engineering loss; social engineering is not affirmatively endorsed in a meaningful way; third-party fidelity (handling clients' money/property) is not addressed. Anti-stacking provision §E.4 caps total crime recovery at the highest single applicable form limit. Maricopa cyber spec calls for these as components, which the cyber program (currently a $10K Data Breach token) cannot deliver.
findings.plain_english: Your only protection against employee theft, wire fraud, and social engineering is buried inside the property policy with very low caps. A typical wire-fraud event today is $250K–$2M; you have $50K. Employee theft schemes commonly run six figures and you have $250K. For a PE-backed manufacturer with vendor payments, payroll, and county receipts moving through bank accounts, this is well below baseline.
findings.recommendation: Bind a stand-alone Commercial Crime policy at $1M–$2M minimum: Employee Theft, Forgery & Alteration, Computer Fraud, Funds Transfer Fraud, Social Engineering / Fraudulent Instruction at full limit (NOT sublimit), Money & Securities In/Out, Client Coverage (third-party fidelity for client/county property in your possession), No-arrest-and-conviction wording. Coordinate with cyber so social-engineering coverage is consistent. Ensure ERISA fidelity for any 401(k) plan is at statutory level.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partial — Hanover Property crime sublimits (411-0793) and $10K Data Breach (411-0669)
discoveryQuestions: If a fraudulent wire-transfer email tricked your AP team into wiring $500K to a bad actor next week, what would be recoverable from insurance?
How often does Run-Test process payments from counties or to vendors, and what are typical wire amounts?
Have any of your peers in election services had social engineering or vendor-impersonation losses?
Does your 401(k) administrator carry the required ERISA fidelity, and is your own employee theft cap aligned with PE-sponsor expectations?

findings.requirement_type: GL Limits — Below Maricopa Minimum + Aggregate Cap Defeats Per-Project Benefit
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Common Declarations: 'Each Occurrence $1,000,000; General Aggregate $2,000,000; Products/Completed Ops Aggregate Included in General Aggregate.' Form 421-3635 07 16 Aggregate Limits per Project and Per Location With Cap: 'capped at $2,000,000 Policy Aggregate. Does NOT apply to products-completed operations hazard.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M occurrence / $4M Products-Comp/Op aggregate / $4M General aggregate. Hanover GL provides $1M occurrence / $2M general aggregate, with NO separate Products/Completed Ops aggregate (it is included in the General Aggregate). On top of that, the per-project aggregate endorsement is capped at $2M Policy Aggregate, which neutralizes the per-project benefit Maricopa would otherwise demand. Without an umbrella in the program, the Maricopa minimum is failed on three separate axes: occurrence limit, general aggregate, and absence of a separate Products/Completed Ops aggregate. Sacramento's $1M/$2M minimum is met technically, but Sacramento also requires a separate $2M Products-Comp/Op aggregate which is also failed.
findings.plain_english: The Maricopa contract requires $2M-per-occurrence, $4M general aggregate, and a separate $4M Products/Completed Operations aggregate. You currently carry $1M occurrence, $2M total aggregate, and the products aggregate is shared with the general aggregate (so a couple of products claims could exhaust it for everything). Sacramento requires a separate $2M products aggregate and that's also missing. Without an umbrella to bridge to $2M occurrence, you are out of compliance on the limit specs of every county contract reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Two-prong fix: (1) endorse Hanover GL to provide a separate Products/Completed Operations Aggregate at minimum $2M (Sacramento) / $4M (Maricopa) — this typically requires repricing; alternatively, raise primary GL aggregate. (2) Bind a $10M–$25M Umbrella to satisfy the $2M occurrence at the Maricopa level. Note the per-project aggregate (421-3635) carries a $2M Policy Aggregate cap that defeats most of its value — request the cap be removed or significantly raised on renewal.
discoveryQuestions: When you submitted the COI to Maricopa, did anyone reconcile the $2M / $4M / $4M requirement against your $1M / $2M / shared-aggregate policy?
If a single bad print run triggered three separate county claims of $700K each, how would your aggregate hold up?
Have you ever had a county come back after the fact and require you to top up your limits or face contract termination?

When you renew next April, what would it cost to restructure to a $2M/$4M/$4M GL with separate products aggregate plus a $10M umbrella, versus the cost of a single contract being terminated for non-compliance?

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured — Completed Operations Gap
findings.contract_quote: ADDITIONAL INSURED STATUS: The COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, and volunteers are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR; premises owned, occupied or used by the CONTRACTOR; or automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR. The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY...
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VII.A, Page 3 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.7, Page 5 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Hanover form 421-2915 06 15 Commercial General Liability Broadening Endorsement — Additional Insured by Contract/Agreement/Permit: 'when required by written contract — ongoing ops your work for the additional insured, premises owned/rented/leased/occupied, equipment leased to you.' Per analysis: 'Does not extend to completed operations.'
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.A expressly requires AI status for 'products and completed operations' — Hanover's blanket AI endorsement (421-2915) covers ongoing operations only. There is no CG 20 37 (or equivalent) products/completed operations AI on the policy. Election services produce a deliverable product (printed ballots, processed mail, deployed technology). After the contract is performed, completed-operations exposure persists for the duration of the products/completed-operations aggregate period. A claim from a county or third party arising months or years after delivery would not trigger AI coverage to the county.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's contract demands you name them as Additional Insured for both 'ongoing' work AND 'completed operations' (claims after the work is done). Your blanket AI endorsement only covers ongoing work. If a county sues a year later because a ballot defect caused harm, the county is NOT an additional insured on a completed-operations basis, and they will treat that as a contract breach.
findings.recommendation: Add CG 20 37 (Additional Insured – Owners, Lessees or Contractors – Completed Operations) on a blanket-by-contract basis, OR confirm with Hanover that the broadening endorsement language can be amended to expressly include 'products-completed operations hazard' in the scope of AI coverage. Verify the AI form does not contain an exclusion for damages arising solely from the AI's negligence (consistent with Sacramento §VII.B Civil Code §2782 carve-out). Confirm the form edition matches or exceeds the latest ISO edition (current is CG 20 37 04 13).
discoveryQuestions: When ballots from a county election cycle finish and you've delivered the work, does anyone at the county still hold any of your records, software, or equipment for which a delayed claim could arise?
If a voter sued Sacramento County two years after an election claiming a ballot-design problem, and the County tendered to you for AI defense, would your COI hold up?
Has any county audit ever flagged the lack of CG 20 37 on your AI endorsement?
How long after a county contract ends would a claim still affect Run-Test's reputation or contractual obligations?

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured — Professional Services Carve-Out (CG 421-2915 §1.c.(5))
findings.contract_quote: The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, or volunteers.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover form 421-2915 06 15 — AI provision §1.c.(5) excludes professional services. Per per-policy analysis: 'CRITICAL: AI provision §1.c.(5) excludes professional services — election technology operations may implicate this carve-out.'
findings.gap_description: Sacramento expressly prohibits ANY endorsed limitations on the scope of AI protection. Hanover's blanket AI form contains a carve-out for 'professional services' — and Run-Test's core operations (ballot design, election software, ballot processing, technology platform) sit at the outer edge of what carriers would call 'professional services.' If a county tenders an AI claim that the carrier characterizes as arising from professional services, AI coverage may be denied. This is both a substantive coverage issue and a literal contract violation of Sacramento's 'no limitations' clause.
findings.plain_english: Your AI endorsement has a carve-out for 'professional services' — but a lot of what Run-Test does could be called professional services. If a county tenders a claim and the carrier says 'sorry, that's a professional services act, AI excluded,' the county is left exposed and you're left in breach of contract. Sacramento's contract forbids exactly this kind of carve-out.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate with Hanover to: (a) delete §1.c.(5) of 421-2915 for AI extensions to county/government clients; or (b) endorse a giveback affirming AI coverage for professional services to the extent contractually required; or (c) move to a manuscripted broader AI endorsement. Combined with binding a Tech E&O policy with AI endorsement (Finding 003), close this gap from both directions.
discoveryQuestions: How would Sacramento react if they reviewed the actual AI endorsement language and saw the professional-services carve-out?
When a county claim alleges that election software or ballot design caused a problem, do you think the carrier defends or denies?
Has any prior county tender ever resulted in a coverage dispute or partial denial?
What would it be worth to take the carve-out off the table before a claim happens, rather than litigating it after?

findings.requirement_type: GL Cyber/Data Privacy — Triple Absolute Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: (Sacramento and Maricopa contracts both rely on the GL to defend operational claims; Maricopa cyber spec assumes a separate Cyber policy carries the data-privacy load. With no real cyber program, the GL exclusions become the operative coverage decision.)
findings.policy_quote: (1) 421-5286 01 25 Exclusion — Cyber Incident — Cyber Content (Page 208): absolute exclusion for any BI/PD/PI&AI 'caused by, arising out of or as a consequence of' unauthorized access, malicious code, denial of service, IP infringement, plagiarism, defamation arising from electronic content. (2) CG 00 69 12 23 Exclusion — Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy (Page 226): excludes BI/PD/PAI 'arising out of violation of any law addressing data privacy — including BIPA, CCPA, GDPR.' (3) CG 21 06 12 23 Exclusion — Access Or Disclosure Of Confidential Or Personal Material Or Information (Page 236): excludes any BI/PD or P&AI from data access/disclosure plus notification, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, data restoration, extortion costs.
findings.gap_description: Three overlapping absolute exclusions sweep ALL cyber, data privacy, and confidential-information disclosure claims out of the GL. For Run-Test, which handles 90M+ voter records and is in the election-technology critical-infrastructure sector, this is the heart of the operational risk profile. With only a $10K Data Breach token and no stand-alone Cyber policy, every cyber exposure — voter data breach, ransomware, extortion, regulatory fines, third-party privacy class action — has zero coverage.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has three separate, absolute exclusions that block every cyber, voter-data, or privacy-related claim. The data breach endorsement is a $10,000 token. There is no real cyber policy. This is the exposure that defines Run-Test's risk profile — and it is currently uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Resolve via Finding 004 (bind real Cyber policy at $10M+). Do NOT attempt to remove the GL cyber exclusions — these are now standard market and underwriters will not delete them. The correct response is to backstop the GL with a robust stand-alone Cyber policy that affirmatively grants what the GL excludes.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone ever explain that your GL has THREE separate exclusions for cyber and voter-data claims?
What's your CCPA / state-breach-notification compliance posture — and have you measured the cost of a 1M-record breach with no cyber policy to respond?
If a voter sued in a class action saying their data was mishandled, where in your program does that get defended?
Election infrastructure is a federally designated critical sector; have any of your contracts or RFPs started asking for cyber insurance as a hard requirement?

findings.requirement_type: GL Pollution Exclusion — Conflicting Forms (CG 21 49 vs CG 21 55) + No CPL in Program
findings.contract_quote: (Industry baseline; no specific contract clause. Relevant because Run-Test runs printing/manufacturing operations involving inks, toners, solvents, plastics.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 49 09 99 Total Pollution Exclusion Endorsement (Page 240): 'Absolute pollution exclusion — no hostile fire exception.' AND CG 21 55 09 99 Total Pollution Exclusion With A Hostile Fire Exception (Page 242): both attached. 'CONFLICT: CG 21 49 also attached (with hostile fire exception) — verify which controls.'
findings.gap_description: Two pollution exclusion endorsements are attached to the same policy with materially different scopes. Default carrier interpretation in a coverage dispute is that the broader (more restrictive) exclusion controls (CG 21 49 — no hostile fire exception). Run-Test's printing/mailing operations involve inks, toners, solvents, and chemicals; a pollution-related loss (release at facility, transit spill, fire-fighting runoff) could result in coverage denial. There is no Contractors Pollution Liability or Premises Pollution Liability policy in the program to backstop.
findings.plain_english: Two contradictory pollution exclusions are attached. If a chemical spill or printing-ink release occurs, the carrier will probably apply the broader exclusion and deny coverage. There is no separate pollution policy to fall back on. For a printing/manufacturing facility this is a real-world exposure.
findings.recommendation: Two actions: (1) Get written carrier confirmation as to which form controls — request that CG 21 49 (the broader form) be removed and only CG 21 55 (with hostile-fire exception) remain. (2) Evaluate a Premises Pollution Liability or Contractors Pollution Liability policy ($1M–$5M limit) given printing chemistry and transit exposures. Coordinate with PFAS/Phthalates exclusions (Findings 014, 015).
discoveryQuestions: What inks, toners, solvents, and chemicals are stored at the Phoenix facility on a typical day?
If a tank, drum, or solvent line ruptured tomorrow, where would cleanup costs come from?
Have you ever had an EPA, ADEQ, or fire-marshal incident at the printing operation?
When ballots and supplies are in transit, what happens if a vehicle leaks fluids onto a county lot or roadway?

findings.requirement_type: GL PFAS Exclusion (CG 40 32) — Industry-Wide Tightening
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — printing inks and paper coatings historically contained PFAS.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 40 32 05 23 Exclusion — Perfluoroalkyl And Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS): 'Absolute PFAS exclusion — excludes BI/PD/PAI arising from any inhalation, ingestion, absorption, contact with, or presence of perfluoroalkyl/polyfluoroalkyl substances. Broad definition covering PFAA, PFOA, PFOS, PFPE, fluorotelomer substances, side-chain fluorinated polymers, and any product containing these.'
findings.gap_description: Some printing inks, paper coatings (water/grease-resistant), toners, and de-greasing chemicals historically contained PFAS. This is now a standard market exclusion industry-wide. If a future toxic-tort or product liability claim alleges PFAS exposure from ballot materials or printing operations, no GL coverage. No CPL or Products Pollution policy in program to address this.
findings.plain_english: PFAS — 'forever chemicals' — are now totally excluded on your GL. Ballot paper, ink coatings, and certain printing chemistry historically contained PFAS. If a class action alleges PFAS in your products or facility, the GL pays nothing.
findings.recommendation: (a) Audit ink, paper, and chemical suppliers to confirm whether any current or historical materials contain PFAS. (b) Obtain supplier representations and indemnities for PFAS-free materials. (c) Document the audit for underwriting purposes. (d) Consider whether a Products Pollution Liability or Premises Pollution Liability policy with PFAS carve-back can be obtained — increasingly difficult in current market but worth pricing. (e) Strengthen contractual indemnity from raw-material suppliers.
discoveryQuestions: Do you have written supplier confirmations that your inks, paper coatings, and toners are PFAS-free?
If a state AG or class action alleged PFAS in ballot materials, where in your contracts does the indemnity flow back to the supplier?
Have any of your peers or suppliers received PFAS-related notices or testing requests?
What would it cost to switch to certified PFAS-free chemistry vs. the cost of one PFAS class action?

findings.requirement_type: GL Phthalates Exclusion — Manufacturing Relevance
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — ballot envelopes, sleeves, plastic components may contain phthalates.)
findings.policy_quote: 421-5203 07 23 Exclusion — Phthalates: 'Absolute exclusion for BI/PD/PI&AI arising from exposure to or presence of phthalates (DBP, DIBP, BBP, DEHP, DnOP, DINP, DIDP, DEP, MEHP, etc.) — applies to CGL and Products/Completed Operations Liability Coverage Parts.'
findings.gap_description: Plastics and vinyl materials commonly used in ballot envelopes, sleeves, mailing wraps, and equipment housings can contain phthalates. Absolute exclusion eliminates GL response to any phthalate-related toxic-tort or products claim.
findings.plain_english: Phthalates — chemicals in many plastics — are now totally excluded. Ballot envelopes, sleeves, plastic packaging, and equipment housings may contain them. A future class action would be uninsured.
findings.recommendation: (a) Supply-chain audit similar to PFAS — get supplier reps that ballot-related plastic and vinyl components are phthalate-free. (b) Update purchase orders / supplier agreements with phthalate indemnification. (c) Document for underwriting. (d) Consider Products Pollution / Toxic Tort coverage if available.
discoveryQuestions: What plastic and vinyl components do you use in ballot envelopes, sleeves, and packaging?
Do your suppliers confirm phthalate-free formulations in writing?
Have any state consumer-protection laws started restricting phthalates in mail or packaging materials in the states you serve?
If a class action alleged phthalate exposure from ballot envelopes, who indemnifies whom in your supply contracts?

findings.requirement_type: Notice of Cancellation — Sacramento County Not on Designated Entity Schedule
findings.contract_quote: MAINTENANCE OF INSURANCE COVERAGE: ... Contractor is required by this Agreement to immediately notify County if they receive a communication from their insurance carrier or agent that any required insurance is to be canceled, non-renewed, reduced in scope or limits or otherwise materially changed.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover form 401-1235 Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): designated entities listed are 'The New York State Office Of General Services; Procurement Services; Amazon.com Services LLC; ARC Airport 2800, LLC; Banterra Bank.' 30-day NOC. NOC for non-payment is NOT triggered.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's contractual notice obligation is technically on the Contractor — but in practice the broker target and best practice is to schedule each governmental contract counterparty on the carrier's Designated Entity NOC endorsement so the carrier directly notifies the county. Sacramento County is NOT on the schedule; current scheduled entities are NY OGS, Amazon, the landlord, and the lender.
findings.plain_english: Best-practice insurance language puts the County on the carrier's direct-notification list so they hear from the insurer if your policy is canceled. Sacramento isn't on that list. If anything happens to your policy mid-term, Sacramento finds out too late and treats it as a material breach.
findings.recommendation: Endorse 401-1235 to add Sacramento County (Risk Manager address), Maricopa County, Los Angeles County (if applicable), and any other governmental contract counterparties to the Designated Entity NOC schedule. Push for a 60- or 90-day NOC if available; minimum 30-day per Maricopa §8.2.15. Verify NOC also triggers for material changes, not just cancellation/non-renewal.
discoveryQuestions: How does Sacramento currently learn if your insurance changes mid-term?
Would you rather rely on yourself remembering to notify them, or have the carrier do it directly?
Has a county ever flagged that your COI lacks proper cancellation notice language?
Which other counties should be added to the same schedule?

findings.requirement_type: Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa County Not on Designated Entity Schedule + Material-Change Trigger Missing
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover form 401-1235 NOC to Designated Entity(s): 30-day NOC. Maricopa County is NOT listed on the schedule. The endorsement covers 'cancellation/non-renewal' but does not appear to expressly cover 'material change.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 requires 30-day notice for cancellation, suspension, expiration, OR material change — broader than typical NOC endorsement language which usually covers only cancellation/non-renewal. Maricopa is not on the Designated Entity NOC schedule. Failure to have appropriate NOC = direct contract breach. The standard ACORD COI cancellation disclaimer (the 'will endeavor to' language) does NOT satisfy Maricopa's requirement.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract specifically requires 30-day notice not just for cancellation but for any 'material change' — and they want it to come from the insurer, not just from you. Maricopa isn't on the carrier's notification list and the form doesn't cover 'material change.' This is a direct contract breach today.
findings.recommendation: (1) Endorse 401-1235 to add Maricopa County (c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003) to the Designated Entity NOC schedule. (2) Confirm with Hanover whether 401-1235 trigger language can be amended to include 'material change' language. If not, supplement with CG 02 24 (Notice of Cancellation Provided By Us) or a manuscript endorsement. (3) Apply same fix to every other governmental contract counterparty.
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa ever audited your COI for the 30-day-NOC-with-material-change requirement?
If your carrier reduced limits or added an exclusion mid-term, would Maricopa hear about it from anyone?
What happens if Maricopa flags a NOC deficiency during a renewal review — can you afford to lose that contract?
Are there other counties you serve with similar material-change NOC requirements?

findings.requirement_type: Notice of Cancellation — 90-Day Broker Target Not Met Generally
findings.contract_quote: (Broker best-practice baseline — 90-day NOC where available; minimum 60-day for material risks.)
findings.policy_quote: IL 02 58 04 21 Arizona Changes - Cancellation And Nonrenewal: '10 days nonpayment / 45 days other reasons / 45 days nonrenewal.' 401-1235 Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): 30 days.
findings.gap_description: AZ amendatory provides 45-day other-reason notice direct-to-named-insured. Designated entities receive only 30 days. Broker best-practice target is 90 days where the market will allow it for governmental and PE-backed accounts. Run-Test could likely negotiate a longer NOC schedule on renewal given multi-state government footprint and PE-sponsored balance sheet.
findings.plain_english: Brokers typically target 90 days of cancellation notice for sophisticated buyers. You have 30–45 days. That doesn't violate any specific contract today, but it leaves limited time to remarket if the carrier non-renews — particularly if it happens close to election season when you can't afford a coverage gap.
findings.recommendation: On renewal, request 90-day NOC for all-reasons cancellation/non-renewal as a designated-entity protection, scheduled for the Named Insured plus all governmental contract counterparties. Some carriers will agree on PE-sponsored placements; if Hanover refuses, consider this a market-test issue.
discoveryQuestions: If Hanover non-renewed in March of an election year with 45 days notice, could you remarket and still be in force by April 1 across every contract you hold?
Has your PE sponsor ever asked for 90-day NOC as a portfolio standard?
What's the cost of even a 24-hour coverage gap during the October peak?

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project Aggregate — $2M Cap Defeats the Endorsement Benefit
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).
findings.policy_quote: Form 421-3635 07 16 Aggregate Limits of Insurance Per Project and Per Location With Cap: 'Per-project and per-location aggregate applies, but capped at $2,000,000 Policy Aggregate. Does NOT apply to products-completed operations hazard.'
findings.gap_description: Hanover form 421-3635 nominally provides per-project / per-location aggregate but caps the total at $2M Policy Aggregate. This effectively defeats the benefit — you can have multiple projects, but total non-products GL aggregate cannot exceed $2M regardless of how many separate projects/locations are insured. Sacramento §III.A only triggers if Run-Test is engaged in 'construction' per the contract — likely not implicated for printing/mailing/election-tech operations. But for Maricopa-style multi-county operations, the cap meaningfully reduces total available aggregate.
findings.plain_english: Your per-project aggregate sounds like protection but it has a $2M total cap — meaning even if you have ten county contracts running simultaneously, your total non-products GL limit across all of them is still $2M. Lose two big claims and the aggregate is exhausted across every other county.
findings.recommendation: On renewal: request the $2M Policy Aggregate cap on 421-3635 be removed or significantly raised (target $4M or higher). Couple with a $10M+ umbrella to provide drop-down for exhausted aggregates. If Sacramento construction trigger is implicated by any current scope, replace with ISO CG 25 03 form (no cap).
discoveryQuestions: How many county contracts are active simultaneously at any given moment in election season?
If you had two GL claims of $1M each from different counties, would you have any aggregate left for the other 28 counties you serve?
Is your scope ever 'construction' (installing tabulation equipment, retrofitting election rooms) within the Sacramento definition?
What would a true per-project aggregate without a cap cost on renewal?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Equipment in Transit Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: 411-0793 02 23 Gold Property Broadening Endorsement provides 'BPP In Transit $100,000.' No standalone Inland Marine policy in program. 'Worldwide BPP Off Premises $75,000.' Property-form transit coverage is sublimited and limited to traditional perils.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports high-value election technology (ballot scanners, sorters, printers, tabulation hardware) across 31 states and to/from county election offices. The total BPP schedule is $16.28M; the in-transit sublimit is $100K. A single rolling load of a high-end ballot sorter or scanner can easily exceed $100K. There is no standalone Inland Marine policy with proper transit, exhibition/installation, or contractor's tools coverage. Sacramento §IX requires Inland Marine WoS if Run-Test maintains IM — currently moot only because no IM is maintained.
findings.plain_english: You move multi-million-dollar election equipment across the country. Your only in-transit coverage is a $100K sublimit on the property policy — orders of magnitude below the value of a single piece of equipment. A truck rollover, theft, or fire could destroy a $1M sorter and you'd recover $100K.
findings.recommendation: Bind a stand-alone Inland Marine / Transit policy with limits aligned to actual maximum load values (recommend $2M+ per conveyance, $5M+ in catastrophic limit). Coverage components: contractor's equipment, equipment in transit, exhibition / installation, tools and equipment, leased/rented equipment, accounts receivable, valuable papers/records (election records, voter data backup tapes). Add blanket WoS to satisfy Sacramento §IX. Coordinate with cyber for data-on-equipment exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partial — Hanover Property $100K BPP-in-transit and $75K worldwide-off-premises sublimits
discoveryQuestions: What's the highest-value piece of equipment you've ever shipped — and how was it insured?
How many shipments of election equipment cross state lines in October each year, and what's the typical truckload value?
If a truck carrying $1M of ballot sorters rolled over tomorrow, where do you recover that value?
Have any counties ever required proof of inland-marine transit coverage and you couldn't produce it?

findings.requirement_type: Equipment Breakdown — Excludes Programming/Virus/Data Loss + Direct Deductible $100K
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — election technology equipment failure during election week is a critical event.)
findings.policy_quote: 451-0038 11 16 Equipment Breakdown: 'An accident under EB does NOT include defect, programming error, programming limitation, computer virus, malicious code, loss of data, loss of access, loss of use, loss of functionality. Also excludes misalignment, miscalibration, tripping off-line, or any condition correctable by reset/cleaning/maintenance.' Direct deductible $100,000; Indirect 1× ADV; Spoilage $10K.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's equipment is heavily software/firmware-driven (scanners, sorters, mail-piece processing, voter registration tech). EB excludes all software/programming/virus/data-driven failures — the most likely cause of operational disruption during an election cycle. $100K direct deductible is high relative to typical equipment failures. ECI extension excludes incompatibility with software updates installed within prior 30 days — so the very moment when a software patch is most likely to cause a failure is excluded.
findings.plain_english: Your equipment breakdown coverage doesn't pay if a ballot scanner fails because of a software bug, virus, or compatibility issue with a recent update — which is exactly how election technology actually breaks down. The deductible is $100K. And if you patch software and it causes an issue within 30 days, that's also excluded.
findings.recommendation: (a) Negotiate lower direct deductible ($25K target). (b) Negotiate broader ECI / Electronic Circuitry Impairment language with shorter exclusion windows. (c) Address software/programming failures via Tech E&O / Cyber policy that affirmatively covers software defect first-party loss and dependent business interruption from software/cloud failures. (d) Confirm contracts with election-technology vendors include indemnification and warranty for firmware/software defects.
discoveryQuestions: When a ballot scanner or sorter fails during election week, what's the typical cause — mechanical, electrical, or software?
If a software update bricked your tabulation hardware on Election Day, what coverage would respond?
Have you ever had a $100K-or-less equipment failure that you ate yourself rather than running through insurance because of the deductible?
Who indemnifies you if a vendor's firmware update causes downtime?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Valuable Papers / Electronic Data Sublimit Inadequate for Election Records
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — Run-Test maintains voter rolls, ballot designs, election records, and processed mail data.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10 10 12 Building and Personal Property Coverage Form: 'Cost to replace/restore information on valuable papers and records (deeds, manuscripts, books of account, abstracts, drawings, card index systems) excluded from Covered Property. Limited Coverage Extension provides only $2,500 per premises unless higher limit shown.' Electronic data: '$2,500 default sublimit.'
findings.gap_description: Property form excludes valuable papers/records and electronic data with only $2,500 default sublimits. Run-Test's records — election records, voter data, ballot designs, processed mail manifests — are core operational assets. A fire, water event, or sprinkler discharge that destroys physical or electronic records would be effectively uninsured. No Inland Marine 'Valuable Papers' policy in program, and the Cyber Data Breach form (411-0669) doesn't cover first-party data restoration in any meaningful amount either.
findings.plain_english: If a fire or water event destroyed your voter rolls, ballot designs, or election records, your property policy pays $2,500 — total. Election records are arguably your most valuable asset and they're effectively uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Increase Valuable Papers and Electronic Data limits via property endorsement (target $500K–$1M each). Or — better — bind stand-alone Inland Marine with Valuable Papers and Electronic Data Restoration coverage, plus Cyber with first-party data restoration coverage at $1M+. Document data backup/redundancy procedures for underwriting.
discoveryQuestions: What's your offsite backup posture for voter data, ballot designs, and election records?
If the Phoenix server room flooded tomorrow and you lost local storage, what's the recovery cost?
How much of your work-product is paper vs. digital today?
Have you ever quantified the value of your election-records archive?

findings.requirement_type: Recording And Distribution Of Material Or Information In Violation Of Law (TCPA/CAN-SPAM/FCRA)
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — Run-Test handles voter contact data and distributes mail at scale.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Coverage A para 2.q and Coverage B para 2.p: 'Absolute exclusion for BI/PD and Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of violations of TCPA, CAN-SPAM, FCRA/FACTA.'
findings.gap_description: Run-Test mails ballots, election notices, and voter information at massive scale across 31 states. TCPA/CAN-SPAM/FCRA class actions arise when contact data or messaging is sent without proper consent or opt-out — high-frequency, high-severity claim type. GL excludes absolutely. Cyber would need to affirmatively grant 'media liability' or 'unlawful collection / distribution' coverage to address.
findings.plain_english: You mail and contact tens of millions of voters. Class actions for technical violations of TCPA, CAN-SPAM, or FCRA can run into the tens of millions on statutory damages alone. Your GL excludes them completely. There's no media or privacy policy in your program to backstop.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Cyber/Media Liability coverage (Finding 004) affirmatively includes 'wrongful collection or distribution of personal information' and TCPA/CAN-SPAM/FCRA defense. Add Media Liability sublimit if needed. Review consent/opt-out workflows with privacy counsel. Document data-sharing agreements with counties to confirm Run-Test acts within county-authorized scope.
discoveryQuestions: Roughly how many voter contacts/mailings does Run-Test process per election cycle?
Who confirms that the data you mail to was lawfully collected and consent-cleared by the county?
Have any TCPA / FCRA class-action plaintiffs' firms ever sent you a demand letter?
Does your contract with each county allocate liability for opt-out and consent compliance?

findings.requirement_type: Broad Form Named Insured — LLC / Partnership / JV Carve-Out (421-2916 §4.b)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF General — Item 3 Named Insureds. Verify all entities consistently insured across program.)
findings.policy_quote: 421-2916 06 15 Commercial General Liability Enhancement Endorsement §4.b Broad Form Named Insured: 'Item 4.b explicitly excludes partnerships, joint ventures, and limited liability companies from automatic Named Insured extension: That is not a partnership, joint venture or limited liability company.'
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broad Form NI extension covers majority-owned organizations BUT expressly excludes any entity that is an LLC, partnership, or JV. Runbeck Investments LLC is named on the Dec page directly so it's covered, but any other affiliated LLC, partnership, or JV (real-estate holding LLCs, election-technology JVs, regional service LLCs) would NOT be automatically a Named Insured. Common gap pattern post-acquisition or after entity restructuring.
findings.plain_english: Your policy covers 'subsidiaries' automatically — but only if they're corporations. Any LLC, partnership, or joint venture you own or form has to be specifically scheduled. PE-backed companies routinely create LLCs for new operations or ventures. Any of those that aren't explicitly listed have no GL coverage.
findings.recommendation: (1) Run an entity-chart review against the policy Dec page. Schedule every affiliated LLC, partnership, and JV by endorsement. (2) Negotiate on renewal to delete §4.b carve-out so the Broad Form NI extension covers LLCs/partnerships. (3) Implement a procedure: anytime a new entity is formed, broker is notified and entity is added by endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your entity chart — are there any LLCs, partnerships, or JVs that aren't on the policy declarations page?
If you formed a new LLC tomorrow for a regional contract, who at Run-Test would notify the broker?
Have you ever discovered an entity wasn't insured during a claim?
What does the PE sponsor's structure require in terms of named insured coverage for portfolio entities?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody, and Control — Standard Exclusion, No Giveback
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL — Item 2. Run-Test handles county-owned ballot equipment, software, and election records.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Section I Coverage A 2.j(4): standard exclusion for 'Personal property in the care, custody or control of the insured.' No giveback or carve-back endorsement located in submission.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test routinely has county property in its care/custody/control: ballots prior to mailing, county-owned equipment being serviced, election records, voter data, processed mail. The standard ISO CCC exclusion bars GL coverage for damage to such property. No giveback endorsement is included. Inland Marine could address third-party property in care, custody, control via Bailee Coverage — but no IM in program.
findings.plain_english: When county property — ballots, election equipment, voter records — is sitting in your facility or on your trucks, your GL has a standard exclusion that says any damage to that property is your problem, not the carrier's. There is no inland-marine policy backstopping it.
findings.recommendation: (a) Endorse a Care, Custody, Control giveback to GL up to a meaningful sublimit ($100K–$500K). (b) More effective: bind a stand-alone Inland Marine policy with Bailee Coverage / Property of Others at full value. Coordinate with Finding 020 (transit/inland marine).
discoveryQuestions: On any given day, how much county-owned property sits in your facility or on your trucks?
If a fire damaged a county's ballot equipment in your care tomorrow, how would the loss be paid?
Have any county contracts allocated who insures county property while in Run-Test possession?
What's your typical peak inventory of third-party property during election season?

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Exclusion — Not Deleted (CGL)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL — Item 20. Standard ISO fellow-employee exclusion bars GL response to employee-vs-employee claims.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Section II 2.a.(1) excludes 'Bodily injury or personal and advertising injury to a co-employee.' No giveback endorsement located in submission.
findings.gap_description: Standard fellow-employee exclusion stands. If one employee tortiously injures another in the course of employment, neither GL nor the (currently absent) WC has a path to defend the at-fault employee against a co-worker civil claim. Common giveback (CG 04 24 or carrier proprietary) was not endorsed.
findings.plain_english: If one of your employees injures another at work — say, a manager hits a press operator with a forklift — your GL won't defend the at-fault employee. WC pays the injured worker, but the at-fault employee is exposed personally. A simple endorsement deletes this exclusion at minimal cost.
findings.recommendation: Endorse Fellow Employee Exclusion deletion at GL renewal — typically minimal premium impact. Also delete on Auto policy when bound (Finding 001). Inform leadership that the gap is closed on the next renewal cycle.
discoveryQuestions: Has any employee ever filed a personal-injury claim against another employee following a workplace incident?
Would your senior managers be surprised to learn they're not personally protected by the GL if a workplace accident is alleged to be their fault?
What's your safety/training program look like, and does it document supervision standards?

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability for Personal & Advertising Injury — Not Endorsed Back
findings.contract_quote: (RMF CGL — Item 7. Standard CG 00 01 limits contractual liability under Coverage B to 'an Insured Contract' definition that may not capture all assumed P&AI risks.)
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Coverage B 2.e: 'Personal and Advertising Injury arising out of a contract or agreement, except for liability for damages that the insured would have in the absence of the contract or agreement.' No CG 22 74 or equivalent contractual liability for P&AI giveback located.
findings.gap_description: Coverage B Personal & Advertising Injury contractual liability is excluded by default. Sacramento and Maricopa county indemnification clauses are broad ('indemnify, defend, and hold harmless... arising out of...'). If a claim under those indemnifications involves P&AI (defamation, copyright, advertising) the GL may decline based on the contractual liability exclusion. Endorsing this back is uncommon but available in some markets.
findings.plain_english: If a county tendered a defamation, advertising-injury, or media-related claim to you under their broad indemnification, the GL has a default exclusion for contractually-assumed personal-and-advertising-injury liability. You're contractually obligated to defend; the policy may not respond.
findings.recommendation: Request CG 22 74 or carrier-equivalent endorsement to give back contractual liability for P&AI to the extent assumed under written contract. Often available, sometimes nominal-premium. Coordinate with Cyber/Media Liability for content-related exposures.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test produce any voter outreach materials, advertising, or content that could give rise to defamation or advertising-injury claims?
When a county includes a broad indemnification clause, do you understand whether your GL will respond if the indemnified claim is for advertising injury?
Has a county ever tendered a defamation or media-style claim to you?

findings.requirement_type: TCPA / Action-Over Limitation Check — Maricopa §8.2.10 'No Third-Party Action-Over Limitation'
findings.contract_quote: The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage, and shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.policy_quote: No specific Action-Over exclusion located in the endorsement schedule. CG 00 01 default does not contain an action-over limitation. However, certain absolute exclusions (Cyber, PFAS, Phthalates, Pollution) could indirectly limit action-over response on covered theories.
findings.policy_page: N/A — review of full endorsement schedule needed
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.10 prohibits any provision limiting third-party action-over claims (e.g., NY Labor Law-style action-over claims by an injured employee against the principal who then tenders to the employer). Hanover schedule does not appear to contain a specific action-over exclusion. Confirm with carrier in writing that no carrier-proprietary action-over limitation is buried in package endorsements.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa specifically forbids any policy provision that limits 'action-over' claims — claims where an injured worker sues a third party who then turns around and tenders to you. The policy doesn't appear to have one, but confirmation in writing from Hanover is the safe play.
findings.recommendation: Request written confirmation from Hanover that no action-over limitation is contained in the GL coverage part. Document for Maricopa file. Re-confirm at every renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Protective Safeguards — Sprinkler Maintenance Warranty
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — sprinkler-warranty endorsement creates a coverage trigger that can deny fire claims.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 04 11 09 17 Protective Safeguards: 'Schedule lists Premises 1, Building 1, Symbol P-1 (Automatic Sprinkler System). Insured must maintain sprinkler system in working order and notify carrier of any suspension/impairment (>48 hours). Failure to comply triggers fire exclusion.'
findings.gap_description: Protective Safeguards endorsement creates a coverage condition: if the sprinkler system is offline for more than 48 hours and the insured fails to notify the carrier, fire coverage is excluded. Common compliance gap when sprinkler maintenance is performed without insurance-team notification, or when a controller failure goes unreported.
findings.plain_english: If your sprinkler system is offline for more than 48 hours without telling the carrier, fire coverage is gone. A typical maintenance shutdown that runs over by a day, or a controller failure no one noticed, can void the entire fire claim.
findings.recommendation: (1) Document a sprinkler-impairment protocol: any maintenance, controller failure, or impairment >48 hours triggers immediate broker/carrier notification. (2) Train facilities staff. (3) Maintain logs. (4) Verify monthly that Symbol P-1 reflects the actual system installed (sprinkler, fire pump, fire alarm, watch service, gas system, etc.) — incorrect symbol can also trigger denial.
discoveryQuestions: Who at the Phoenix facility is responsible for notifying you (or the broker) when the sprinkler system is shut down for any reason?
When was the last time the sprinkler system was tested, serviced, or impaired, and did anyone notify the carrier?
Is there a written impairment protocol?
What's the value of the building and contents that depend on this sprinkler functioning?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Virus or Bacteria Exclusion (Pandemic BI Gap)
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 01 40 07 06 Exclusion of Loss Due to Virus or Bacteria: 'Pandemic/virus exclusion on Property. Excludes loss/damage caused by virus, bacterium, or other microorganism. Applies to ALL coverage including BI/EE/Civil Authority.'
findings.gap_description: Standard post-COVID exclusion eliminates pandemic / communicable-disease BI/CA. For an election services contractor with peaks tied to October-November windows, a pandemic-driven shutdown or supply-chain disruption is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: If a pandemic or communicable-disease event disrupts operations — facility quarantine, employee outbreak, supplier shutdown — the property policy pays nothing for the lost income. Industry standard exclusion now, but worth knowing as part of business-continuity planning.
findings.recommendation: Pandemic risk transfer is largely uninsurable in commercial market today. Build operational redundancy: backup facilities, remote-work continuity for office functions, redundant suppliers. Consider parametric pandemic products if available and priced reasonably.
discoveryQuestions: What did COVID-19 cost Run-Test in 2020 in business interruption, supply-chain disruption, and lost contracts?
Does your continuity plan assume a pandemic-driven facility shutdown is covered? It isn't.
What's your backup-facility / remote-work posture for the office and design functions?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Earthquake / Flood Exclusions (AZ Phoenix Exposure)
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — Phoenix HQ at 2800 S 36th St.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 10 30 09 17 §B.1.b Earth Movement: 'Excludes earthquake, landslide, mine subsidence, soil sinking/rising/shifting, volcanic eruption.' §B.1.g Water/Flood: 'Excludes flood, surface water, tides, mudslide, sewer backup, groundwater seepage.' Hanover Gold endorsement has $50K Underground Water Seepage carve-back; sewer/drain backup is included.
findings.gap_description: Phoenix has limited earthquake exposure but real flood/microburst exposure. No DIC or stand-alone earthquake/flood policy noted in program. Coverage gap depends on actual Phoenix flood-zone classification of 2800 S 36th St and on the adequacy of $50K Underground Water carve-back vs. actual flood-event severity.
findings.plain_english: Phoenix has flood and microburst exposures even though earthquake is mostly off the table. Your property policy excludes flood and earth movement; sewer backup is covered up to a sublimit. Verify the address isn't in a FEMA flood zone and right-size the flood/DIC coverage accordingly.
findings.recommendation: (1) Pull the FEMA flood-zone map for 2800 S 36th St, Phoenix, AZ 85034. (2) If Zone X-shaded or higher, evaluate stand-alone Flood policy ($1M+ building/contents, $1M+ BI). (3) Consider DIC policy for catastrophic earth-movement/flood combination. (4) Review sewer/drain backup sublimit (should be $250K+ for a manufacturing operation).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Blanket Waiver of Subrogation
findings.contract_quote: Waiver of subrogation - does the policy have the correct wording and is it blanket? / The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.contract_page: RMF General Item 5 / Maricopa §8.2.8 / Sacramento §VIII (WC) and §IX (Property/IM)
findings.policy_quote: CG 24 04 05 09 Waiver Of Transfer Of Rights Of Recovery Against Others To Us: 'BLANKET Waiver of Subrogation — Blanket where required by written contract. Applies to CGL and Products/Completed Operations Liability for both ongoing operations and your work under products-completed operations hazard.'
findings.gap_description: Hanover GL has blanket Waiver of Subrogation by written contract — best-practice form, satisfies Sacramento, Maricopa, and broker target. Applies to both ongoing and products/completed-operations hazards.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has a 'blanket' Waiver of Subrogation — meaning automatically waives subrogation against any party where required by written contract, without separately scheduling each one. This is exactly what counties want.
findings.recommendation: No action — confirm same blanket language is replicated on every other policy in the program once Auto, WC, Cyber, and Umbrella are bound. WC will need a state-specific waiver form (CA WC 04 03 06 for Sacramento work).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Primary & Non-Contributory by Written Contract
findings.contract_quote: PRIMARY INSURANCE: For any claims related to this Agreement, the CONTRACTOR's insurance coverage shall be endorsed to be primary insurance as respects the COUNTY... and shall not contribute with it.
findings.policy_quote: 421-0452 12 14 Additional Insured — Primary and Non-Contributory: 'Provides primary & non-contributory only when required by written contract/agreement/permit.' Backed up by 421-2915 §AI provision.
findings.gap_description: Two endorsements provide P&NC on a blanket-by-contract basis: stand-alone 421-0452 plus 421-2915 broadening. Belt-and-suspenders structure is best practice.
findings.plain_english: When a county contract requires it, your insurance automatically goes 'primary' (pays first) and 'non-contributory' (does not split the bill with their coverage). Two endorsements both confirm this — strong structure.
findings.recommendation: No action. Replicate identical language on Auto, Cyber, and Umbrella once bound.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Severability of Interest / Separation of Insureds
findings.contract_quote: SEVERABILITY OF INTEREST: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Section IV.7 Separation of Insureds (severability) included as standard form provision.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CG 00 01 includes Separation of Insureds as a standard provision. Sacramento §VII.D is satisfied automatically.
findings.plain_english: Your policy treats each insured (you and any additional insureds) separately when claims are made. Sacramento's Severability of Interest requirement is automatically met.
findings.recommendation: No action.
