findings.requirement_type: GL — Contractual Liability via CG 00 01 (Insured Contract Definition Unmodified)
findings.contract_quote: Contractual Liability - Part 1 Does the policy have the proper wording for an Insured contract... blanket contractual coverage / The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 standard form 'Insured Contract' definition unmodified — provides blanket contractual liability for assumed tort liability of another party. No 'Amendment of Insured Contract Definition' (CG 24 26) exclusion attached.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CG 00 01 'Insured Contract' definition is intact — provides blanket contractual liability for assumed tort liability under written contracts. No common amendment-of-insured-contract carve-back attached. Maricopa §8.2.10 'blanket contractual' requirement is met.
findings.plain_english: The contractual liability section of your GL is in its full standard form — meaning the indemnification obligations you assume in county contracts are insured to the extent the contracts qualify as 'insured contracts.' This is the right starting position.
findings.recommendation: No action — but verify on every renewal that Hanover does not add the 'Amendment of Insured Contract' restrictive endorsement (CG 24 26) which dramatically narrows this coverage.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Duty to Defend
findings.contract_quote: Duty to Defend - Do all policies include the duty to defend clause...
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Section I, Coverage A, 1.a: 'We will have the right and duty to defend the insured against any suit seeking those damages.' Standard ISO form provision.
findings.gap_description: Hanover GL retains standard duty-to-defend language. No reimbursement-style modification.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has standard 'duty-to-defend' coverage — meaning the carrier hires and pays the lawyer, not you waiting for reimbursement. Important for cash-flow management on long-running suits.
findings.recommendation: No action. Verify same language on every other liability policy bound (Auto, Cyber, E&O, Umbrella).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Mental Anguish in BI Definition
findings.contract_quote: Mental Anguish - Is it included in the definition of Bodily Injury?
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 Commercial General Liability Broadening Endorsement: '(4) Bodily Injury redefined to include mental anguish/mental injury.'
findings.gap_description: BI definition broadened to include mental anguish/mental injury — covers stand-alone emotional-distress claims, not solely those connected to physical bodily injury. Strong RMF compliance.
findings.plain_english: Standalone emotional-distress claims (a county employee alleging trauma from a Run-Test interaction, for example) are covered under the BI definition. Many policies don't include this — yours does.
findings.recommendation: No action — verify Auto policy (when bound) includes equivalent Mental Anguish in BI definition (Mental Anguish is a separate Auto-RMF item).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Knowledge of Occurrence (Notice & Knowledge) Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: Notice and Knowledge - Is the policy wording endorsed so notice of an occurrence is only considered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, and/or the risk manager is notified?
findings.contract_page: RMF General Item 4 / RMF CGL Item 25
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15: '(6) Knowledge of Occurrence' included in broadening endorsement. Limits 'knowledge' to the person responsible for insurance / officer / risk manager.
findings.gap_description: GL includes Knowledge of Occurrence officer-limited endorsement — knowledge of an occurrence by a low-level employee is not imputed to the entity for notice purposes. Strong RMF compliance for GL. Note this is a CGL-specific finding; Auto, WC, Cyber when bound need their own equivalent endorsements.
findings.plain_english: If a press operator sees an incident and forgets to report it, that's not automatically your problem — the carrier's notice clock starts when an officer, risk manager, or insurance person finds out. This protects you from late-notice denials based on unreported employee-level incidents.
findings.recommendation: No action on GL. When Auto, WC, Cyber, and Umbrella are bound, request equivalent officer-limited Notice & Knowledge endorsement on each.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Unintentional Failure to Disclose / Notify (Unintentional E&O Giveback)
findings.contract_quote: Does the policy include an Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback...
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15: '(12) Unintentional Failure to Disclose Hazards; (13) Unintentional Failure to Notify.'
findings.gap_description: Standard Unintentional E&O giveback embedded in broadening form. Protects against coverage denial for inadvertent failure to report a location, vehicle, operation, or claim.
findings.plain_english: If you accidentally forgot to tell the carrier about a new location or operation, the policy says that won't void your coverage — provided it was unintentional.
findings.recommendation: No action on GL. Add equivalent givebacks on every other policy bound.

findings.requirement_type: GL — ISO CG 0001 04 13 Occurrence Form (Sacramento Compliant)
findings.contract_quote: Form must be ISO CG 0001 occurrence — claims-made GL is NOT acceptable. No added exclusions/limitations without Risk Manager approval.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Commercial General Liability Coverage Form (ISO occurrence form) — primary GL form on the policy.
findings.gap_description: GL is written on ISO CG 00 01 04 13 occurrence form — satisfies Sacramento's specific form requirement. The 'no added exclusions/limitations' aspect of Sacramento §III.A is NOT met (multiple problematic exclusions covered in separate findings) but the form-type requirement is satisfied.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires ISO CG 0001 occurrence-based GL — you have it. (Separate findings address exclusions added to the form.)
findings.recommendation: No action on form-type. Address added exclusions per other findings.

findings.requirement_type: Carrier AM Best Rating — Citizens / Hanover Group
findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. ... an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Citizens Insurance Company of America (The Hanover Insurance Group). Hanover group is consistently rated A or higher by AM Best with size category XV.
findings.gap_description: Citizens / Hanover meets both Sacramento's A-VII threshold and Maricopa's B++ threshold comfortably. Verify current rating annually at renewal.
findings.plain_english: Hanover/Citizens is a strong, well-rated admitted carrier. Meets both county minimums easily.
findings.recommendation: No action. Verify current AM Best rating at every renewal. When other policies (Auto, WC, E&O, Cyber, Umbrella) are bound, confirm each carrier meets A-VII for Sacramento.

findings.requirement_type: EBL Coverage — $1M/$1M Claims-Made with 04/08/2017 Retro
findings.contract_quote: Employer Benefit Liability (EBL) Coverage - Does the insured have EBL coverage?
findings.policy_quote: CG 04 35 12 07 Employee Benefits Liability Coverage (Claims-Made): 'Limits: $1M each employee / $1M aggregate. Deductible: $1,000. Retroactive Date: 04/08/2017. Premium: $275.' Five-year ERP available.
findings.gap_description: EBL is in place at $1M/$1M with a long retro date. Covers administrative E&O for benefits administration (eligibility, enrollment, plan information). Note: EBL is NOT ERISA fiduciary liability — see Finding 057 for that gap.
findings.plain_english: If your benefits administration team makes a clerical error — wrong eligibility, missed enrollment, mis-quoted plan info — EBL covers it. The retro date goes back to 2017 so historical errors are also covered if claims emerge later.
findings.recommendation: No action — EBL is properly in place. Note ERISA fiduciary exposure is a separate gap (Finding 057). Maintain continuous retro date at every renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Damage to Premises Rented to You — $1M Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Damage to premises - You must calculate the prospect's exposure versus the policy sub-limit.
findings.policy_quote: Common Declarations: 'damage_to_premises_rented: $1,000,000.' Boosted by 421-2916 06 15 Property Damage Legal Liability Broad Form to $1M.
findings.gap_description: $1M Damage to Premises sublimit is appropriate for a manufacturing/printing operation in leased space (vs. the standard $100K). Reflects realistic fire-damage exposure to leased structures.
findings.plain_english: If a fire at your facility damages the leased building, you have $1M of liability coverage for that — five times the typical default amount.
findings.recommendation: No action. Verify renewal maintains the $1M sublimit (don't let it slide back to $100K default).

findings.requirement_type: TRIA — Terrorism Coverage Accepted (with Form Conflict)
findings.contract_quote: Tria - Does the insured buy terrorism and has it been explained thoroughly.
findings.policy_quote: 401-1374 Disclosure Pursuant To Terrorism Risk Insurance Act: 'TRIA disclosure — terrorism coverage accepted, $468 premium charged.' AND CG 21 73 01 15 Exclusion Of Certified Acts Of Terrorism: 'Excludes any injury or damage arising out of a certified act of terrorism as defined under TRIA.' Per analysis: 'TRIA acceptance overrides this; verify.'
findings.gap_description: Two forms appear contradictory — TRIA was accepted with premium charged, but the certified-acts exclusion is also attached. Standard practice: TRIA acceptance overrides the exclusion for the GL coverage part. But CG 21 73 sometimes operates as a backup exclusion if TRIA expires (federal program reauthorization). Election infrastructure is a designated CISA critical-infrastructure sector and is realistically a terrorism target.
findings.plain_english: Terrorism coverage was bought and paid for — but there's also a terrorism exclusion endorsement attached. Standard rule says the acceptance wins, but it's worth getting it in writing from Hanover. Election infrastructure is a designated terrorism target and worth special attention.
findings.recommendation: (1) Get Hanover written confirmation that TRIA acceptance controls and CG 21 73 is inoperative for the GL coverage part. (2) Evaluate stand-alone Terrorism policy (T3/T4 market) for non-certified events and broader perils — particularly election-day threats which may not meet TRIA 'certified act' threshold. (3) Coordinate with property terrorism (CG 21 73 also applies to certain coverage parts per 401-1501).

findings.requirement_type: Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out — Compliant by Default
findings.contract_quote: CIVIL CODE PROVISION: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level acknowledgement; no specific policy endorsement required. Standard ISO CG 00 01 and 421-2915 do not affirmatively cover indemnification for AI's sole/active negligence — California public-policy carve-out is preserved by default.)
findings.gap_description: California public-policy limit on indemnification of an AI's own active negligence is satisfied by default policy structure — no special endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: California law forbids you from indemnifying the County for the County's own active negligence. Your policy structure already respects this — you're compliant by default.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Coverage Territory — US/CAN/Territories Standard
findings.contract_quote: Coverage Territory - Is the insured's product sold outside the USA or Canada or 'could' their product end up outside the US territories/possessions, or Canada?
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Section V definition of 'Coverage Territory': USA (including territories/possessions), Puerto Rico, Canada — plus international travel for short business visits and internet exposure carve-back. Election services served: '31 states and the District of Columbia.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO territory definition. Run-Test serves 31 states + DC — squarely within US/territories. Verify whether any operations involve overseas military or DoD voting (UOCAVA — Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act) — if Run-Test handles overseas voter ballots, mail crosses international borders, which may implicate territory definition.
findings.plain_english: Your coverage area is the US, territories, and Canada — fine for domestic election services. If you handle UOCAVA overseas-voter ballots that physically travel to/from foreign countries, that could create a territory question worth confirming.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with operations whether any UOCAVA or military overseas voting work is performed. If so, verify carrier endorses 'worldwide' coverage for that scope or add a Foreign General Liability or DBA-style endorsement as needed.

findings.requirement_type: Hired & Non-Owned Auto on CGL — Not Endorsed; No Auto Policy
findings.contract_quote: Hired and Non-owned Coverage - is this included on the CGL as needed, when the insured does not have an auto policy.
findings.policy_quote: No HNOA endorsement on Hanover GL identified in submission. No stand-alone Commercial Auto policy in program (Finding 001).
findings.gap_description: Hired & Non-Owned Auto exposure exists in any operation where employees use personal vehicles for company business or where the company hires/rents vehicles. Run-Test almost certainly has this exposure (delivering ballots, errands, vendor pickups, employee travel). Without either an Auto policy or HNOA endorsement on the GL, this exposure is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Even if Run-Test owns no vehicles, every time an employee uses their car for company business or you rent a vehicle, there is a Hired & Non-Owned Auto exposure. With no Auto policy AND no HNOA endorsement on the GL, this is uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Auto policy (Finding 001) including blanket Hired & Non-Owned coverage. Until then, request an interim HNOA endorsement on the GL as a stop-gap. Verify employee-use-of-personal-vehicle policies and require employees to maintain personal auto with adequate limits.
discoveryQuestions: How often do employees use their own cars to run errands, deliver materials, or visit vendors / counties?
Do you require employees to carry personal auto with minimum limits when using their cars for work?
When Run-Test rents a U-Haul or other vehicle for a peak-season delivery, who is on the rental contract and whose insurance responds?
Has anyone modeled the lawsuit exposure if an employee crashes their personal car on a company errand?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Increased Cost of Construction Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — manufacturing/printing facility may face code-mandated rebuild costs after a loss.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10 10 12: 'Only $10,000 or 5% of building Limit (whichever less) for ICC. Does NOT apply to ordinance/law triggered by pollution, fungus, wet/dry rot, or bacteria.'
findings.gap_description: $10K / 5% Increased Cost of Construction sublimit is severely inadequate for a $21M building. Phoenix and AZ jurisdictions update commercial codes regularly; rebuild after a fire or major loss may require code upgrades costing 10-20% of the original building. Without proper Ordinance & Law Coverage A/B/C, the insured eats the difference.
findings.plain_english: If your building burns and you have to rebuild to current code, the policy gives you $10,000 for code upgrades. On a $21M building, that's nothing. Real rebuild-to-code costs run hundreds of thousands.
findings.recommendation: Endorse Ordinance & Law Coverage A (undamaged portion), B (demolition cost), and C (increased cost of construction) at meaningful limits — recommend $2M–$5M aggregate. Standard CP 04 05 ISO endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: When was the building at 2800 S 36th St last code-evaluated by a structural engineer?
What's the rough age of the building and what code era is it built to?
If a fire forced a rebuild, do you have liquidity to absorb $1M–$3M of code-upgrade costs out of pocket?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber/Data Breach — War and Cyber-War Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — election infrastructure is a state-sponsored attack target.)
findings.policy_quote: 411-0669 01 15 §B.1.s: 'Standard war/cyber-war exclusion. Given heightened nation-state cyber attack risk against US election infrastructure, this is a meaningful concern for an election services contractor. State-sponsored attacks could be argued under warlike action by a military force or usurped power.'
findings.gap_description: War/cyber-war exclusion in the Data Breach form, combined with the broader 2022-2024 industry-wide tightening of cyber-war exclusions (NotPetya / Merck precedent), creates real risk of denial when a state-sponsored actor attacks election infrastructure. The token Data Breach limit ($10K) makes this academic for now, but on a real Cyber policy this is a critical negotiation.
findings.plain_english: If a nation-state attacker hits Run-Test (which is exactly the threat model for election infrastructure), the carrier may invoke the war exclusion to deny the claim. This is a hot-button issue across the cyber market right now.
findings.recommendation: When binding stand-alone Cyber (Finding 004), require Lloyd's-style affirmative cyber-war carve-back wording (LMA 5564 or LMA 5565). Negotiate exclusion to require formal attribution and government action — not insurer's unilateral assertion. Document this as a non-negotiable underwriting position.
discoveryQuestions: Has CISA, FBI, or state intelligence ever briefed Run-Test on nation-state threat indicators?
If a Russia / China / Iran-attributed attack hit your environment, do you understand how the carrier might frame the war exclusion?
What's your incident-response runbook for an attack with potential nation-state attribution?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber/Data Breach — Contractually Assumed Liability Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa, Sacramento, and county contracts contain broad indemnification obligations that may be barred by the cyber form's contractual-liability exclusion.)
findings.policy_quote: 411-0669 01 15 §B.1.g: 'legal obligations arising by reason of assumption of liability in a contract or agreement.' Exclusion covers contractual indemnity assumed in writing.
findings.gap_description: The token Data Breach form excludes contractually-assumed liability — meaning indemnification of counties for breach-related losses may not be covered. Combined with the form's first-party-only scope and $10K aggregate, the form is effectively useless for satisfying any county cyber requirement.
findings.plain_english: Your data breach endorsement won't cover what you've promised counties in your contracts. So even the $10K of nominal coverage doesn't apply where you most need it.
findings.recommendation: Resolved by Finding 004 (bind real Cyber policy). Negotiated cyber forms typically include a contractual-liability carve-back for breach-of-confidentiality / privacy-related obligations.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever counted up the cumulative breach-indemnification obligations across all your county contracts?
If a single breach triggered indemnity obligations to 30 counties, where would that money come from?
Does any county contract you sign limit the dollar amount of breach-related indemnity?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber/Data Breach — Fines and Penalties Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties
findings.policy_quote: 411-0669 01 15 §B.1.c: 'Excludes fines, penalties, fees or assessments... including but not limited to fees or surcharges from financial institutions.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa expressly requires fines AND penalties coverage. Data Breach form excludes them. Confirms Finding 004 — Maricopa's specification cannot be satisfied without a real Cyber policy with affirmative regulatory fines/penalties grant.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires you to carry coverage for both regulatory defense AND fines/penalties — and this Data Breach form excludes the fines/penalties piece. Yet another reason the current $10K endorsement does not satisfy Maricopa.
findings.recommendation: Resolved by Finding 004 — stand-alone Cyber must affirmatively grant Regulatory Fines and Penalties coverage 'where insurable by law' at a meaningful sublimit ($1M+ recommended).
discoveryQuestions: What state breach-notification laws apply across your 31-state footprint, and what's the maximum fine on each?
Has Run-Test ever been subject to an AG investigation, FTC inquiry, or state regulatory action?
If the California AG opened a CCPA enforcement action tomorrow, who pays for the fine?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud + Social Engineering Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft
findings.policy_quote: 411-0793 02 23 §III.A.12: 'Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud coverage at $50K excludes acts in collusion, indirect/consequential loss, virtual/crypto currency, authorized-access fraudulent entries... SOCIAL ENGINEERING coverage is NARROW — only the fraudulent instruction received from a computer software contractor carve-back.'
findings.gap_description: Property-form Crime sublimits at $50K Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud and narrow social engineering scope are inadequate against (a) Maricopa's contract requirement and (b) industry baseline for a $5M-25M revenue PE-backed company. Real-world social-engineering losses (BEC, vendor impersonation) routinely run $500K-$2M.
findings.plain_english: If a fraudulent vendor email tricks AP into wiring $750K to a bad actor — the most common business loss in the country today — you recover $50K and only if the wire fits a narrow definition. Maricopa's contract specifies broader coverage. The current package does not deliver.
findings.recommendation: Resolved jointly by Findings 004 (Cyber) and 008 (stand-alone Crime). Target $1M+ social engineering / fraudulent instruction at full limit on either Crime or Cyber, plus $1M+ Computer Fraud / Funds Transfer Fraud. Avoid sublimits on these specifically.
discoveryQuestions: How many wire transfers does Run-Test send per month, and what's the typical amount?
What controls do you have around vendor-bank-account changes, and have they been tested?
Has anyone in finance ever reported a phishing or vendor-impersonation attempt that almost succeeded?

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through — Procedures Documentation
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: (Policy-level: subcontractor pass-through is a contractual / operational obligation, not a policy provision. Hanover GL allows for subcontracted work via standard CG 00 01 form; flow-down requires Run-Test to mirror requirements in subcontractor agreements.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.E requires Run-Test to (a) be responsible for sub acts/omissions and (b) ensure subs provide AI endorsements. Compliance is a vendor-management procedure, not a policy provision. Need to confirm Run-Test has a written subcontractor insurance flow-down protocol, COI tracking, and contractual indemnity language.
findings.plain_english: When you hire any subcontractor — print vendor, mailing partner, software developer — you're contractually responsible for their acts AND for making sure they list the County as Additional Insured on their policies. This is a vendor-management discipline that needs documentation.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Run-Test has: (1) written subcontractor insurance requirements that mirror or exceed county requirements; (2) COI collection and tracking before any sub starts work; (3) contractual indemnity from subs to Run-Test naming the County as third-party beneficiary; (4) annual subcontractor COI re-collection process.

findings.requirement_type: Course of Construction (Builders Risk) — Conditional / Likely N/A
findings.contract_quote: Course of Construction (COC) Waiver of Subrogation: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Course of Construction / Builders Risk policy in program. Run-Test's election services do not appear to involve construction projects per industry profile.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX is conditional on Run-Test maintaining a COC/Builders Risk policy. Run-Test (election services manufacturer) is unlikely to maintain Builders Risk unless physical construction is involved in scope. N/A unless construction work undertaken.
findings.plain_english: N/A — Sacramento's COC/Builders Risk requirement only triggers if you actually do construction work. You don't, so there's nothing to comply with here unless scope changes.
findings.recommendation: If at any point Run-Test takes on construction or facility-buildout scope, trigger Builders Risk procurement at that time and ensure WoS endorsement names the County.

findings.requirement_type: WC RMF — Maritime / DBA / USL&H / Foreign Voluntary
findings.contract_quote: (WC RMF Items 7, 9, 13, 14 — conditional N/A items.)
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — moot until WC bound. No maritime, vessel, harbor, or US-government-overseas-facility exposure indicated for an election services manufacturer based in AZ.)
findings.gap_description: Maritime / DBA / USL&H / Foreign Voluntary / Endemic Disease coverages are conditional. Run-Test profile (AZ manufacturing facility, domestic operations, no waterfront, no overseas US-government work) does not trigger any of these. UOCAVA mail handling is a possible foreign-touch but not a worker-overseas exposure. Confirm with operations.
findings.plain_english: N/A — you don't have maritime workers, dock workers, or employees at overseas US-government facilities, so these specialty WC extensions don't apply. (When WC is bound — Finding 002 — these can be skipped.)
findings.recommendation: Confirm with HR/operations there are no employees who travel internationally for work that would trigger Foreign Voluntary coverage. If yes, add Foreign Voluntary endorsement when WC is bound.

findings.requirement_type: Auto RMF — Lease Gap / Drive Other Car / No-Fault / Parked-Fleet
findings.contract_quote: (Auto RMF Items 4, 5, 11, 15 — conditional items requiring operational data.)
findings.policy_quote: (N/A by default until Auto bound — Finding 001. Lease Gap triggers if leased vehicles; Drive Other Car triggers if executive officers are Named Insureds; No-Fault analysis triggers if operations in NY/FL/MI/NJ/PA/KS/KY/ND/MN/MA/HI/UT; Parked Vehicles aggregate triggers if fleet parking exposure.)
findings.gap_description: Without an Auto policy in place these RMF items cannot be evaluated. When Auto is bound (Finding 001), evaluate based on operational profile: Run-Test serves 31 states + DC including several no-fault states (FL, MI, NJ, PA, KY, MN, MA — verify which); fleet parking exposure depends on size of owned/leased fleet at Phoenix HQ; Drive Other Car depends on executive structure.
findings.plain_english: These are Auto-specific items that we'll evaluate when the Auto policy is bound. Until then, they're parked. Some will likely be relevant given the multi-state footprint.
findings.recommendation: Address as part of Auto binding (Finding 001). Specifically: (a) confirm leased vs owned vehicles to determine Lease Gap need; (b) confirm executive officer Named Insured structure for Drive Other Car; (c) identify which no-fault states have actual ops; (d) determine if Phoenix HQ has a fleet parking concentration warranting aggregate deductible.

findings.requirement_type: ERISA Fiduciary Liability — Not in Program
findings.contract_quote: (RMF baseline — 50-200 employee company likely sponsors a 401(k) plan with ERISA fiduciary exposure.)
findings.policy_quote: EBL form CG 04 35 12 07 expressly excludes ERISA fiduciary liability. No stand-alone Fiduciary Liability policy in program submission.
findings.gap_description: ERISA imposes personal fiduciary liability on plan sponsors and committee members for breach of fiduciary duty in plan administration, investment selection, fee benchmarking, and disclosure. EBL covers benefits administration but expressly excludes ERISA fiduciary. No Fiduciary policy in program. Plan committee members and Run-Test as plan sponsor are personally exposed.
findings.plain_english: If you sponsor a 401(k), the people who serve on the plan committee — including officers — are personally exposed to ERISA fiduciary lawsuits over fees, investment selection, or disclosures. EBL doesn't cover this. There's no Fiduciary Liability policy.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Fiduciary Liability policy at $1M-$3M. Often combined with D&O / Management Liability program. Include settlor functions, voluntary compliance program coverage (HIPAA), and broad ERISA Section 502(l) penalties coverage where insurable.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test sponsor a 401(k) or other ERISA plan, and who serves on the plan committee?
Have plan fees and investment menu been independently benchmarked in the last three years?
If a former employee filed an ERISA fee or investment-selection lawsuit, who pays the personal defense for committee members?

findings.requirement_type: Deductible / SIR Disclosure to County
findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY. / The insurance policies may provide coverage that contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL deductible: not specifically stated in submission summary. Equipment Breakdown direct deductible: $100,000. Property deductibles by peril: not specified. Future Cyber and E&O policies will have SIRs typically $25K-$100K.
findings.gap_description: Counties require disclosure and approval of all deductibles and SIRs. Maricopa goes further: deductible/SIR cannot apply against the County's recovery, and the County reserves the right to require a surety bond or LOC. With future Cyber and E&O policies likely having SIRs at $25K-$250K, the LOC requirement could become a material collateral demand.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want to know every deductible and self-insured retention you carry, and Maricopa reserves the right to demand a letter of credit to secure them. As you bind Cyber, E&O, and other policies with meaningful SIRs, you may face collateral demands from counties.
findings.recommendation: (1) Document every deductible/SIR across the program in a single schedule for COI submission. (2) Disclose proactively to counties at contract execution. (3) Negotiate any LOC/bond demand against actual claims experience. (4) Consider deductible-buy-down endorsements where SIR is large.

findings.requirement_type: COI / Endorsement Copies Required Pre-Performance
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below. Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.
findings.policy_quote: (Operational — broker-managed COI/endorsement-copy delivery process required.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES (not just COI summary) attached to certificates, with County approval before performance commences. Many COIs only reference endorsements without including them. Need a documented broker process for delivering endorsement copies.
findings.plain_english: Counties want the actual endorsement documents — not just a COI saying 'AI: Yes.' If your broker isn't sending the endorsement PDFs themselves with every COI, you're not in compliance.
findings.recommendation: Establish broker-managed protocol: every county COI is accompanied by PDF copies of the relevant endorsements (AI form, P&NC form, WoS form, NOC schedule). Build a standard election-services COI package. Track approvals.

findings.requirement_type: Stop Gap (CGL) — N/A for AZ but Material Once WC and Multi-State Operations Confirmed
findings.contract_quote: Stop Gap - does the prospect have coverage under the CGL or WC?
findings.policy_quote: (AZ is not a monopolistic state. Monopolistic states are ND, OH, WA, WY. Run-Test profile shows AZ-based with multi-state service footprint — confirm whether any employees physically work in monopolistic states.)
findings.gap_description: Stop Gap is needed only if employees physically work in a monopolistic state (ND, OH, WA, WY). Run-Test is AZ-based; the 31-state service footprint may include employee travel into these states. If so, Stop Gap Employer's Liability endorsement on the GL is required because monopolistic-state WC funds do NOT include EL coverage. Currently moot because no WC policy exists (Finding 002).
findings.plain_english: Four states — North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, Wyoming — run their own state-fund WC programs that do NOT include Employer's Liability. If any Run-Test employees travel to or work in those states, you need Stop Gap on the GL. Currently moot because there's no WC policy yet.
findings.recommendation: When WC is bound (Finding 002), confirm employee travel/work in ND/OH/WA/WY. If yes, endorse Stop Gap Employer's Liability onto the GL with limits matching the EL on the WC policy ($1M/$1M/$1M).

findings.requirement_type: Property — Pollutant Cleanup Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — printing chemistry creates real cleanup exposure.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10 10 12: 'Pollutant clean-up at premises capped at $10,000 per 12-month period, AND only if discharge results from a Covered Cause of Loss AND reported within 180 days.' Hanover Gold Property Broadening adds Pollutant Cleanup of $100,000.
findings.gap_description: $100K Pollutant Clean-Up (boosted via Gold endorsement) is better than the $10K base but still inadequate for a printing/manufacturing operation with inks, toners, solvents. Real cleanup costs after a fire-driven chemical release routinely exceed $250K. Coordinates with Finding 013 (Total Pollution Exclusion + no CPL).
findings.plain_english: If a fire causes a chemical release, your cleanup coverage is $100K. A typical print-shop chemical-release cleanup runs higher.
findings.recommendation: (a) Increase Pollutant Cleanup sublimit on property if available. (b) Better: address via Premises/Contractors Pollution Liability policy (see Finding 013) with proper cleanup limits.
discoveryQuestions: What's the typical inventory of inks, solvents, and chemicals at the Phoenix facility?
Has there ever been a release event, however minor, in the company's history?
What are typical AZ DEQ remediation costs for a printing-shop incident?

findings.requirement_type: Vacancy Provision — 60-Day Trigger
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — election services has seasonal peaks; off-season facility utilization may vary.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10 10 12: 'If building vacant >60 consecutive days, NO coverage for vandalism, sprinkler leakage, glass breakage, water damage, theft. Other Covered Causes reduced by 15%.'
findings.gap_description: Vacancy provision deems a building 'vacant' if <31% rented or used for customary operations. Election services has seasonal cycles; facility may be at low utilization between major election cycles. Trigger may apply if extended low-use periods occur.
findings.plain_english: If your facility is empty or barely used for more than 60 days, your property coverage shrinks dramatically. Worth confirming your seasonal pattern keeps you out of the 'vacancy' definition.
findings.recommendation: Confirm facility utilization is continuous (production, storage, R&D) rather than seasonal-empty. If material vacancy windows exist, request a Vacancy Permit endorsement (CP 04 50) from the carrier.

findings.requirement_type: Utility Services Failure — BI/EE Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — utility-failure-driven BI is foreseeable for a power-intensive printing/processing operation.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 10 30 09 17 §B.1.e: 'Excludes failure of off-premises power, communication, water, or other utility services.' Hanover Gold endorsement provides $100,000 Utility Services BI/EE.
findings.gap_description: $100K Utility Services BI/EE limit is inadequate for a 24/7 production operation. AZ summer grid stress and microburst-driven outages are realistic. A multi-day power loss during election peak could exceed $1M in BI alone.
findings.plain_english: If the power, water, or communications fail off-premises and shut you down, you have $100K of BI/Extra Expense. During election peak that's not enough.
findings.recommendation: Increase Utility Services BI/EE sublimit to align with ADV (recommend $1M+, ideally tied to BI overall limit). Confirm coverage extends to overhead transmission lines (often excluded).
discoveryQuestions: What's a single-day BI loss for Run-Test during October peak?
Has the Phoenix facility had power events in the last 24 months?
Do you have backup generator capacity for full operations?

findings.requirement_type: Right to Adjust Coverage — County Open-Ended Modification Right
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection for COUNTY and for members of the public, COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level — not addressable by policy provision.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves unilateral right to demand additional or different coverage mid-term. This is a contract-management issue: be aware that limit/coverage demands can grow during the contract term. No policy fix available.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento can ask you to buy more or different insurance any time during the contract. It's an open-ended risk on the contract side, not on the policy side.
findings.recommendation: On contract negotiation, attempt to limit this clause to 'commercially reasonable' modifications and require X-day notice. Track all such demands across counties to ensure consistent broker response.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Indemnification (Maricopa) — Contractual Liability via Insured Contract
findings.contract_quote: the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County (as Owner)... but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor... The scope of this indemnification does not extend to the sole negligence of County.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 'Insured Contract' definition unmodified — provides blanket contractual liability for tort liability assumed under written contract. AZ comparative negligence framework recognized.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa indemnification is comparative-negligence-based with sole-negligence carve-out — squarely insurable under standard 'Insured Contract' definition. GL contractual liability responds.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification is the kind your insurance can actually back — limited to your share of fault. Your GL provides the blanket contractual liability needed to support it.
findings.recommendation: No action. Confirm same Insured Contract definition remains intact at every renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber/Data Breach — First-Party Only / Third-Party Liability Excluded
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence... defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties...
findings.policy_quote: 411-0669 01 15 §B.1.d excludes 'any fees, costs, settlements, judgments, or liability of any kind arising in the course of, or as a result of a claim for damages, lawsuit, administrative proceedings, or governmental investigation' EXCEPT regulatory investigation defense expenses. 'FIRST-PARTY-only form — third-party liability for data breach claims NOT covered.'
findings.gap_description: The Data Breach form is structured as first-party expense reimbursement only. Third-party liability claims (lawsuits by voters, vendors, counties, regulators) are expressly excluded. Maricopa's $5M cyber requirement explicitly contemplates 'defense, and claims expenses' — a third-party liability function that this form does not deliver. Subset of Finding 004 but called out separately because it is the most consequential single exclusion in the form.
findings.plain_english: The cyber endorsement only pays YOUR direct breach-response costs. It does not pay for lawsuits filed against you. So if 1 million voters sue after a breach, the policy pays nothing. This is the most important sentence in the form.
findings.recommendation: Resolved by Finding 004 (bind real Cyber). Real cyber forms grant third-party privacy liability and security liability as core coverages.
discoveryQuestions: If a class action of voters sued Run-Test after a breach, where in your insurance program does that defense come from?
Has anyone explained that the data breach endorsement only pays your costs, not lawsuits filed against you?
What's the largest plaintiff class size you could face if voter data from one county were exposed?

findings.requirement_type: WC — Sacramento California Other-States Coverage Trigger
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: No WC policy in program (Finding 002). California is not a state where 'Other States Coverage' (Item 3.C) typically extends to a non-California policy without explicit endorsement — California has unique statutory requirements that often require a CA-domiciled policy or specific state-fund participation.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento contractually requires California statutory WC. Run-Test is AZ-based with no WC at all. Even when WC is bound, simply listing CA as Item 3.C may not satisfy California's statutory requirements (CA generally requires a CA-rated policy or admission). This is both a Finding 002 dependency AND a CA-specific compliance issue worth separate flagging.
findings.plain_english: California has its own WC rules and won't accept just a casual 'Other States' note on an out-of-state policy. When you bind WC for Sacramento work, you may need a separate California WC placement or a WC policy specifically endorsed to comply with CA statutes.
findings.recommendation: When binding WC (Finding 002), specifically address CA exposure: either (a) endorse Item 3.A to include CA with a CA-rated policy, or (b) bind a separate CA WC monoline if any employees are CA-resident, or (c) confirm the Other States endorsement provides CA-statutory coverage. Validate with CA Department of Industrial Relations.
discoveryQuestions: Do any Run-Test employees physically reside in or travel to California for Sacramento work?
Has California EDD or Department of Industrial Relations ever inquired about WC coverage?
How will the CA exposure be priced — Item 3.C extension, or stand-alone CA monoline?

findings.requirement_type: Voluntary Parting Exclusion / Social Engineering Property Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — social engineering exposure for a manufacturer with vendor payments.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 10 30 09 17 §B.2.i Voluntary Parting Exclusion: 'Excludes property voluntarily surrendered due to fraudulent scheme/trick/false pretense.' 411-0793 02 23 Voluntary Parting sublimit $50,000.
findings.gap_description: Voluntary parting / social engineering exposure addressed only by a $50K Voluntary Parting Property sublimit. Inadequate against current BEC/vendor-impersonation loss severity. Coordinates with Finding 052 (Crime Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud).
findings.plain_english: When someone tricks an employee into handing over property or wiring money, the property policy gives you $50K. Real losses run vastly higher.
findings.recommendation: Resolved jointly by Findings 008 (Crime) and 004 (Cyber). Target $1M+ social engineering full-limit on Crime or Cyber.
discoveryQuestions: How are vendor payment instructions verified before AP processes wires?
Has Run-Test trained the team on BEC and vendor-impersonation indicators?

findings.requirement_type: Indemnification — Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level provision — not addressable directly by any policy.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa expressly states insurance limits do NOT cap the indemnification obligation. Any liability above the program's total liability tower is uninsured exposure to the Run-Test balance sheet. This makes the limits-shortfall findings (Findings 005, 009) more consequential because there is no contractual ceiling.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says: 'Just because your insurance has a limit, that doesn't cap what you owe us under indemnity.' So if a $25M loss happens and you have $11M of coverage, the other $14M comes from the company's checkbook. Worth understanding when sizing the umbrella.
findings.recommendation: Size the umbrella (Finding 005) to a level that protects the balance sheet — recommend $25M+ given the indemnity-uncapped-by-limits language and the operational profile. Document this as a board-level risk-tolerance decision.

findings.requirement_type: Notification of Claim / Lawsuit — Sacramento 30/10-Day Trigger
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level operational obligation — not addressable by policy. Independent of carrier notice obligations.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento creates a contractor-to-county notification obligation for any claim or lawsuit affecting the County: 30 days from claim receipt; 10 days from service of process. This runs in addition to carrier notice obligations. Need an internal claim-tracking protocol that flags Sacramento-related claims for both broker AND county notification.
findings.plain_english: Any claim or lawsuit that could touch Sacramento has to be reported to Sacramento — 30 days for claims, 10 days for lawsuits. Separate from telling your insurance company. Need a process to make sure both notifications happen.
findings.recommendation: Implement a claim-intake protocol: every incoming claim/lawsuit is screened for county-related impact; if affects Sacramento (or any other county with similar clauses), notification calendar tracks both broker/carrier notice AND county notice. Ideally embedded in legal/risk team workflow.

findings.requirement_type: Loss Payee — Property Loss Payee Schedule Comprehensive
findings.contract_quote: Property loss payees including ARC Airport 2800 LLC (1st Mortgagee), Banterra Bank (2nd Mortgagee), Wells Fargo Equipment Finance, Cisco Systems Capital, MailFinance, Canon Financial Services, Western Alliance Bank, Hewlett Packard Financial Services, Sunflower Bank, Black Mountain Investment Co LLC, Peoples Capital and Leasing, Contra Costa County, Runbeck Properties LLC, Lincoln Shields LLC.
findings.policy_quote: CP 12 18 10 12 Loss Payable Provisions (Page 184) — comprehensive schedule of property loss payees including all major lenders, equipment-finance partners, mortgagees, and a county loss payee (Contra Costa County).
findings.gap_description: Property Loss Payee schedule is well-populated, suggesting active broker management of lender and leasing relationships. Note that Property loss payees are NOT GL Additional Insureds — these structures address property/equipment financing relationships only.
findings.plain_english: Your property policy properly lists every lender, leasing company, and mortgagee. This is the right structure for protecting financing relationships.
findings.recommendation: No action — but verify any new equipment-financing or facility-financing arrangements get added by endorsement promptly. Note: Contra Costa County is on the Property loss payee schedule; verify whether any other counties should be added based on equipment leasing or other financial arrangements.

findings.requirement_type: Civil Authority / Extended Period of Indemnity
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — election services has fixed-date deadlines; civil authority disruptions during election windows are catastrophic.)
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 30 10 12 Business Income (and Extra Expense): 'Civil Authority (1-mile radius, 72-hr waiting, 4-week max), Alterations & New Buildings, Extended BI (60 days default).'
findings.gap_description: Civil Authority is limited to 1-mile radius and 4-week maximum — narrow. Election services is uniquely vulnerable to civil authority orders (security incidents, court orders, election-related government actions) potentially extending beyond 4 weeks. Extended Period of Indemnity at 60 days is also short for an election-services operation; recovery from a major loss during peak season may take months as election cycles re-baseline.
findings.plain_english: If a court order, security incident, or government action shut down access to your facility for more than 4 weeks, BI stops paying. After a major loss, customer recovery takes longer than 60 days during election cycles.
findings.recommendation: (a) Increase Civil Authority radius and time limits (target 5-mile / 8-12 weeks). (b) Increase Extended Period of Indemnity to 180 days minimum. (c) Add Dependent Property BI extension for key suppliers (paper, ink, equipment vendors).
discoveryQuestions: If a major incident on Election Day caused a court or government order to lock down your facility for 6 weeks, what would the BI loss be?
How long would it take to fully recover customer relationships and contracts after a 30-day operational outage during October peak?

findings.requirement_type: Punitive Damages, Right & Duty, Defense In/Out Limits — Umbrella RMF (N/A no Umbrella)
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Umbrella Items 5, 10, 11 — defense inside vs outside, punitive damages, right and duty when underlying exhausted.)
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — no Umbrella in program. See Finding 005.)
findings.gap_description: All Umbrella-specific RMF items (defense in/out limits, maintenance of underlying, punitive damages exclusion review, right and duty when underlying exhausted, follow-form scope, AI/WoS/Named Insured follow-form, professional liability follow-form, foreign liability) are unaddressed because no umbrella exists. Most consequential in election-services context: punitive damages exposure (politically charged litigation), defense-cost erosion in long-tail litigation.
findings.plain_english: Without an umbrella, none of the umbrella-specific protections — punitive damages where insurable, defense costs outside limits, drop-down when primary aggregate is exhausted — exist. These are critical for an election-services contractor where politically-charged litigation is foreseeable.
findings.recommendation: Resolved by Finding 005. When binding umbrella, negotiate: defense costs outside limits (where market allows), punitive damages 'most favorable jurisdiction' wording, right and duty to defend when underlying limits exhausted, follow-form across AI/WoS/Named Insured/Professional, and explicit drop-down for exhausted aggregates.
discoveryQuestions: In a politically-charged lawsuit, punitive damages can dwarf compensatory damages — how exposed are you today?
If a long-tail lawsuit erodes your $1M GL primary in defense costs alone, what's the next dollar of protection?
Have any past lawsuits hit punitive-damage theories?

findings.requirement_type: WC RMF — Experience Mod / Class Codes / Owner Exclusions / Credits / Claims Mgmt
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — no WC policy in program. When bound, full WC RMF walk required.)
findings.gap_description: All WC-specific RMF items (experience mod management, small claim back-to-work strategy, classification codes vs actual operations, owner inclusion/exclusion, premium credits, large claim management) are unaddressed because no WC exists. When WC is bound (Finding 002), full RMF walk required: confirm class codes for printing/manufacturing/election-tech/clerical match actual operations, evaluate owner inclusion/exclusion election, review experience mod calculation, audit claim history for back-to-work program savings.
findings.plain_english: When WC is bound, there's a whole checklist of optimization items — experience mod management, claim handling discipline, classification accuracy, premium credits — that need to be walked through. Skipping WC means skipping all that.
findings.recommendation: Address comprehensively as part of Finding 002. Before binding, request: (a) prior WC history if any; (b) NCCI experience rating worksheet; (c) classification code confirmation against actual job duties; (d) owner inclusion/exclusion analysis; (e) review of all available premium credits including drug-free workplace, safety program, deductible.

findings.requirement_type: Auto RMF — Symbols, Mobile Equipment, UM/UIM, Temp/Leased Workers
findings.contract_quote: (RMF Auto Items 12, 16, 17, 18.)
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — no Auto in program. When bound, all Auto-specific RMF items require walk: Symbols 1 vs 2 vs 7, Mobile Equipment vs Auto definition, UM/UIM, leased/temp worker carve-outs.)
findings.gap_description: Symbols (broadest is Symbol 1 for Any Auto), Mobile Equipment classification (forklifts, mailing-room vehicles), UM/UIM disclosure decisions, and leased/temp worker carve-outs are all unaddressed because no Auto exists. Critical when Auto is bound. Mobile Equipment exposure for printing/mailing operations may include forklifts, pallet jacks, golf carts — verify each is correctly classified.
findings.plain_english: When Auto is bound, several technical decisions matter: how broad the auto definition is (Symbol 1 vs 7), whether mobile equipment like forklifts is properly classified, what UM/UIM limits to choose, and whether temp workers are excluded from the 'employee' definition.
findings.recommendation: Address comprehensively as part of Finding 001. Specific items: (a) Symbol 1 (Any Auto) for owned + Symbols 8 & 9 for HNOA; (b) inventory of mobile equipment to determine Auto vs GL classification; (c) UM/UIM decision documented in writing with operations; (d) modify 'employee' definition to exclude temp/leased workers if staffing is used; (e) CA 9933 / CA 2054 for employee personal-vehicle use.
discoveryQuestions: Do you have forklifts, pallet jacks, or other mobile equipment at the Phoenix facility — and are any operated on public roads?
Do you use temp staffing for the printing/mail floor?
What's your stated UM/UIM strategy — match limits to liability, or minimum?

findings.requirement_type: Asbestos / Silica / Mold Exclusions — Standard, Operationally Low Concern
findings.contract_quote: (Standard market exclusions.)
findings.policy_quote: 421-0022 Asbestos Liability Exclusion (Page 188); CG 21 96 Silica Exclusion (Page 248); CG 21 67 Fungi Or Bacteria Exclusion (Page 244).
findings.gap_description: Standard market exclusions for asbestos, silica, and mold/fungi. Election services / printing operations are not high-risk for these categories. Operational concern is low. Disclosed for completeness.
findings.plain_english: Standard exclusions for asbestos, silica dust, and mold are on the policy — these are industry-standard and don't materially affect a printing/mailing operation.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Product Recall — Sublimited at $25K/$50K
findings.contract_quote: (Operational baseline — Run-Test produces ballots, mailings, and election technology. A defective production run could trigger costly recall obligations.)
findings.policy_quote: 421-2916 06 15 (9) Product Recall Expense '$25K/$50K with $500 ded'.
findings.gap_description: $25K each occurrence / $50K aggregate Product Recall Expense is token. A recall of mis-printed ballots across a county or state could cost millions in reprint, re-mail, and emergency replacement. Stand-alone Product Recall coverage available in market for manufacturing operations.
findings.plain_english: If a print error required recalling and re-issuing a county's ballots, your recall coverage is $25K. Reprinting and remailing 500K ballots would cost vastly more.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate stand-alone Product Recall / Product Withdrawal Expense policy with $1M-$5M limits. Coordinate with E&O (Finding 003) — many Tech E&O / Manufacturer's E&O forms include a recall expense extension.
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test ever had to recall, reprint, or re-issue ballots due to a production defect?
What does a typical re-mail / re-print event cost on a single county ballot run?
Who indemnifies whom in your county contracts when a print defect is discovered?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto Umbrella Attachment Ambiguity
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence... / If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — no Auto and no Umbrella in program. Question is academic until both are bound.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 has program-level umbrella permission but §8.2.11 Auto clause does not inline-mention umbrella attachment. Strict reading: Auto must independently meet $2M CSL; Permissive reading: Auto + Umbrella stacking permissible. When Auto is bound (Finding 001) and Umbrella is bound (Finding 005), confirm with Maricopa which interpretation they apply. Recommend conservative posture: Auto written at $1M-$2M CSL with umbrella stacking explicitly listed on COI.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's Auto requirement is $2M; the contract's general umbrella-permission clause may or may not let you bridge a $1M Auto with a $1M umbrella. It's safer to either write Auto at $2M outright or get Maricopa to confirm in writing that they accept Auto + umbrella stacking.
findings.recommendation: When binding Auto (Finding 001) and Umbrella (Finding 005): (a) preferable approach is $2M Auto CSL standalone + $10M+ umbrella; (b) if cost requires $1M Auto + umbrella attachment, get Maricopa Risk Management confirmation in writing that umbrella stacking satisfies §8.2.11.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber Umbrella Attachment Ambiguity
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence... / If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies...
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — no Cyber policy and no Umbrella in program. Cyber is not typically schedulable under standard commercial umbrellas — a separate Cyber Excess policy is the proper construct.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's general umbrella-permission clause does not specifically address cyber. Standard commercial umbrellas typically do NOT follow form over cyber — instead, cyber excess is structured as a stand-alone tower (e.g., $5M primary cyber + $5M cyber excess). When binding cyber (Finding 004), determine whether $5M is met by primary alone or primary + cyber excess.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $5M cyber. Most commercial umbrellas don't sit over cyber. So the $5M needs to come from a stand-alone cyber tower (primary plus cyber excess if needed) — not from a general umbrella.
findings.recommendation: When binding cyber (Finding 004): (a) bind $5M+ cyber primary directly (not relying on general umbrella); (b) consider $5M + $5M cyber excess for redundancy given client's voter-record exposure; (c) confirm with Maricopa Risk Management that a stand-alone cyber tower satisfies §8.2.13.

findings.requirement_type: Maintenance / Material Breach Trigger
findings.contract_quote: All insurance required herein shall be maintained in full force and effect until all work or service required to be performed under the terms of the contract is satisfactorily completed and formally accepted. Failure to do so may, at the sole discretion of County, constitute a material breach of this contract. / Failure to maintain required insurance in force shall be considered a material breach of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: (Operational — broker-managed continuous-coverage discipline required.)
findings.gap_description: Both contracts elevate any insurance lapse to material breach. With multiple gaps already present (no Auto, WC, E&O, Cyber, Umbrella, EPLI, D&O, Fiduciary, Inland Marine), Run-Test is technically in continuous breach today. Closing the gaps and instituting a continuous-renewal discipline is necessary not just for risk management but for contract maintenance.
findings.plain_english: Both Sacramento and Maricopa say a coverage gap = material breach of the contract — meaning they can terminate and pursue damages. Given the missing policies catalogued in this audit, you may technically be in breach today. Closing the gaps quickly is a contract-preservation issue.
findings.recommendation: (1) Prioritize binding all missing policies (Findings 001-008) in the next 30-60 days. (2) Establish broker-managed continuous-renewal calendar to prevent any future gap. (3) Document the remediation plan for legal/risk counsel and consider whether voluntary disclosure to counties is appropriate.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — General Liability Policy
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage... (Maricopa §8.2.10) // Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000 (Sacramento §III.A)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.10; Sacramento Pg 2 of 4 §III.A
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy submitted in this program review. Only Commercial Auto (Hanover AW4-H221414-05, eff 4/1/25–4/1/26) was provided.
findings.gap_description: No General Liability policy was provided as part of the program submission. Both Maricopa County (Arizona) and Sacramento County (California) require Commercial General Liability with specific limits ($2M/$4M/$4M and $1M/$2M respectively), additional insured status, primary & noncontributory wording, waiver of subrogation, contractual liability, and blanket/broad terms. Without a CGL, every premises, products/completed operations, and personal/advertising injury claim arising from Run-Test's operations is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy is the only liability policy I was given. If a county employee, a poll worker, or a member of the public is injured at one of your facilities, slipped on a misprinted ballot box, or was hurt by a defectively printed ballot, there is currently no policy in this program to respond. Both Maricopa and Sacramento County contracts treat absence of GL as a material breach — and absent any policy at all, claims for bodily injury, property damage, and personal/advertising injury have no carrier to pay them. This is the largest uninsured exposure in your program.
findings.recommendation: Place a Commercial General Liability policy immediately. Minimum: $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate / $4M products-completed operations to satisfy Maricopa's higher threshold (which automatically satisfies Sacramento). Insist on ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form, blanket additional insured (CG 20 33 + CG 20 37 for ongoing AND completed operations using 'arising out of' language), blanket waiver of subrogation (CG 24 04), primary & noncontributory (CG 20 01), per-project aggregate (CG 25 03), unintentional E&O giveback, and a Notice/Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement limiting imputation of knowledge to officers. No XCU exclusion. No third-party action-over limitation. Until bound, do not begin or continue contract performance — both contracts treat lapse as material breach.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens if a county Risk Manager asks for your COI tomorrow — what GL document do you currently provide them?
When was the last time someone independently confirmed your GL policy was actually issued, in force, and matches contract specs — the carrier, broker, or just the certificate-issuing system?
If a poll worker tripped over election equipment your team delivered and broke a hip, who would you call first — and which insurance carrier would they ultimately bill?
How are you currently funding the indemnification obligations you've signed in your county contracts? If GL isn't in place, indemnity flows straight to the balance sheet.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Workers' Compensation & Employers' Liability
findings.contract_quote: Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes... and Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. (Maricopa §8.2.12) // WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. (Sacramento §III.C–D)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.12; Sacramento Pg 1–2 of 4 §II.C, §III.C–D
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation policy submitted. Run-Test has 50–200 employees and operates in AZ and 30 other states.
findings.gap_description: No WC policy was provided. Arizona requires statutory workers' compensation for all employees. Sacramento requires CA-statutory WC plus EL $1M/accident/disease. Maricopa requires statutory WC plus EL $1M/$1M/$1M and waiver of subrogation. Without WC, the company faces uninsured employee injury claims, statutory penalties under A.R.S. §23-907, employer's liability tort exposure, and immediate breach of both contracts.
findings.plain_english: If a single employee is injured on the job today, the company pays out-of-pocket for medical, lost wages, and any tort claim — and Arizona can fine the company and pierce corporate protections for unpaid WC. With 50–200 employees, even one back injury or repetitive-stress claim can run into six figures. Both county contracts also flag WC as a strict-liability requirement; you can't begin work without it.
findings.recommendation: Place a Workers' Compensation policy with statutory coverage in AZ as the home state and Other States coverage (3.C) for every state where Run-Test has any employee presence — local, county, or state election work. Ensure California is on Item 3.A (not just 3.C) given the active Sacramento contract. EL limits at $1M/$1M/$1M to support umbrella attachment. Endorse Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (WC 04 03 for AZ; WC 04 03 06 for CA) and Notice of Cancellation to designated entities. Until bound, do not have any employee perform work in CA or under a Maricopa task order.
discoveryQuestions: When was your last Workers' Comp renewal, and who is the carrier? If you have one, why wasn't it included in this audit submission?
How are you currently handling claims when an employee gets hurt — you have 50 to 200 people, this happens?
When you send a print operator to a Sacramento County facility for installation, who's covering them under California WC — your AZ policy with Other States, or are you carrying a CA-specific policy?
Has anyone walked you through the personal-liability and corporate-veil exposure Arizona Industrial Commission can pursue if WC lapses? It's not just a fine.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Cyber / Network Security & Privacy Liability
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees... losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber Liability policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires a $5M Cyber/Network Security/Privacy Liability policy with one of the broadest enumerated coverage lists I've seen in a county contract: regulatory fines and penalties (not just defense), cyber extortion, network business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, and crisis management. No cyber policy was provided. Run-Test's core operations — election technology, ballot processing, voter data, election mail sorting — are exactly the operations cyber risk specialists target. The DHS designates election infrastructure as critical infrastructure (16th sector), and the Russian/Chinese threat actor activity around U.S. elections is well-documented. A breach affecting 90 million registered voters' data would be company-ending.
findings.plain_english: You handle data for 90+ million voters across 31 states. A ransomware event, a phishing-driven wire fraud, or a database breach would trigger 50 different state notification statutes, FBI involvement, regulatory investigations, and class-action litigation — all uninsured. Maricopa County contractually requires $5M of cyber coverage covering exactly this scenario, and the policy isn't there. This is the single most likely catastrophic exposure for an election services company, and there's currently no carrier to call.
findings.recommendation: Place standalone cyber liability coverage at $5M minimum (consider higher given voter-data exposure and critical-infrastructure designation). Insist on: 1st-party network business interruption with at least 8-hour waiting period, ransomware/extortion (preferably no sublimit or $2M+), social engineering (with reasonable sublimit), regulatory fines & penalties (where insurable by law), funds transfer fraud, computer fraud, system failure, dependent business interruption, breach response costs (notification, credit monitoring, forensics, crisis PR), retroactive date on or before Maricopa contract effective date, prior acts coverage, and reasonable retention. Use a specialty cyber market (Beazley, Coalition, Chubb, At-Bay, Resilience) — not a packaged sublimited cyber endorsement.
discoveryQuestions: Election infrastructure is federally designated critical infrastructure — when was your last tabletop exercise on what happens if your systems are encrypted on a Sunday night before a Tuesday election?
If your accounts payable team gets a spoofed email impersonating a county client and wires $200K, what policy responds today?
You serve over 90 million registered voters across 31 states — can you walk me through your incident response plan and where insurance would slot in?
Has Maricopa or any other county audited your COI for cyber compliance recently? They've been escalating cyber-spec scrutiny since 2024.

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Umbrella / Excess Liability
findings.contract_quote: If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements. (Maricopa §8.2.9) // UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) (Sacramento §II.E)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Pg 6 of 41 §8.2.9; Sacramento Pg 2 of 4 §II.E
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella or Excess Liability policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: No umbrella was provided. Both contracts contemplate umbrella stacking to reach minimum limits (Maricopa explicitly for CGL §8.2.10, Sacramento for GL/Auto/EL). Maricopa's $2M Auto CSL minimum cannot be reached on the current $1M Auto unless an umbrella sits over it. Beyond contract compliance, an election services company with PE backing, multi-state operations, fleet exposure, and high-stakes counterparties (counties, states, voter populations) carries catastrophic verdict potential — a single multi-vehicle accident, a ballot-error class action, or a defamation-style election claim can pierce primary limits.
findings.plain_english: Even if all your underlying policies were in place, you'd still be exposed for any claim that exceeds primary limits — and election services lawsuits are exactly the kind that go big. An umbrella is the cheapest insurance you can buy per dollar of limit, and Maricopa and Sacramento both expect one to be there. Without it, you're betting the company on every claim staying under $1M to $2M, which is not how plaintiff's lawyers operate.
findings.recommendation: Place a $5M–$10M Commercial Umbrella attaching over GL ($2M/$4M), Auto ($1M or $2M CSL), and EL ($1M/$1M/$1M). Confirm follow-form, no special exclusions broader than underlying, drop-down for reduced/exhausted aggregates, defense outside limits, blanket AI follow-form, blanket waiver of subrogation follow-form, per-project aggregate follow-form, no cyber exclusion, and that all underlying policies are correctly listed in the schedule. Confirm punitive damages NOT excluded (state law permitting). Consider $10M minimum given PE backing and $5M cyber underlying.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest jury verdict you've seen in your industry — and have you stress-tested that number against your current primary limits?
Your PE sponsor — are they aware that the program currently has no umbrella sitting above primary?
If a Run-Test van rear-ends a school bus, $1M Auto CSL is gone before the ambulances clear the scene. Walk me through what happens next.
Have you ever been pressured by a county to raise limits mid-contract? Both your Maricopa and Sacramento clauses reserve the right — what's your plan if that happens?

findings.requirement_type: Missing Coverage — Professional Liability / E&O
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... Umbrella expressly cannot be used to satisfy this minimum (Section II.E).
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions policy submitted in this program review.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County requires standalone Professional Liability at $1M/$1M, with retro on or before contract effective date and 1-year ERP if claims-made cancelled or non-renewed. Umbrella cannot satisfy. No E&O policy was provided. Run-Test's services — ballot design, printing, mailing, sorting, election emergency support technology — create classic professional/E&O exposures: errors in ballot layout, mailing wrong materials to wrong voters, missed certification deadlines, faulty election technology integration. GL won't respond to economic/financial loss without bodily injury or property damage; cyber won't respond to professional negligence in services; these claims live and die on E&O.
findings.plain_english: If you misprint ballots, mail to the wrong precinct, or your election support technology fails on Election Day and a county sues for damages, that's an E&O claim — not a slip-and-fall. There's no policy in your current program that responds to professional negligence in election services. With your client list (counties, states, 90 million voters), the political and reputational stakes amplify any error, and one missed certification can end multi-year contracts. Sacramento contractually requires this — a COI without it is a non-starter.
findings.recommendation: Place a Professional Liability / E&O policy specifically scoped for election services / printing / data processing. Ensure: definition of 'Professional Services' explicitly captures ballot printing, mailing, election mail sorting, election support technology, voter data processing, and any consulting work; retro date on or before earliest active contract; full prior acts; broad consent-to-settle (avoid 80/20 hammer); $1M minimum (consider $2M–$5M given PE-backed scale); duty-to-defend; reasonable retention.
