findings.plain_english: Your contract demands the broadest 'arising out of' trigger for additional insureds — meaning the county is covered any time a claim has anything to do with your work. The current AI endorsement uses narrower 'caused in whole or in part by' language, with a clause that caps it to whatever the contract requires. In theory that snaps back to the contract's 'arising out of.' In practice, an adjuster looking for a reason to deny will run with the narrower wording. Sacramento's 'no endorsed limitations' clause technically gives them grounds to reject the COI.
findings.recommendation: Confirm same review of Citizens primary CGL AI endorsement. Where possible, request a manuscript AI endorsement using 'arising out of' language. If carrier will not change, document the contract-controls language in writing with carrier so an adjuster cannot rely on the narrower language. Consider CG 20 33 (broader blanket AI) on renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county risk manager ever flagged the 'caused in whole or in part by' language on your AI endorsement?
If a county was sued for something only loosely tied to your work — say, a slip-and-fall on a county-owned sidewalk during ballot delivery — would your AI endorsement defend them?
When your COI is issued, does the certificate language describe AI coverage in 'arising out of' terms or 'caused by' terms?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa GL — $2M Each Occurrence vs Arch $1M
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: 'GENERAL AGGREGATE LIMIT $3,000,000; PRODUCTS/COMPLETED OPS AGGREGATE $3,000,000; PERSONAL & ADV INJURY $1,000,000; EACH OCCURRENCE $1,000,000.' Underlying Citizens primary (per Hanover Schedule): '$1,000,000 Each Occurrence / $1,000,000 PI&AI / $2,000,000 General Aggregate.' Hanover Umbrella: $10M each occurrence / $10M Gen Agg / $10M Products-Completed Ops Agg.
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Dec; Hanover Umbrella Pg 14; Hanover Umbrella Dec
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M each occurrence / $4M Gen Agg / $4M Prod-Comp Ops. Citizens primary CGL is $1M each occurrence / $2M Gen Agg. §8.2.10 expressly permits umbrella stacking ('and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance'). Hanover Umbrella at $10M follows form over Citizens, so $1M + $10M = $11M each occurrence (>$2M) and aggregates similarly. Compliance achieved via umbrella stack — ARCH security GL is not in this calculation. Per-occurrence/aggregate compliant via stacking; should confirm umbrella follows form on products-completed ops aggregate (Hanover umbrella shows $10M Products-Completed Ops Agg so OK).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M each occurrence on GL. Your primary is $1M, but Maricopa's contract specifically allows you to use the umbrella to get there, and you have a $10M umbrella sitting on top. Total tower: $11M. You meet the limit through stacking. We just need to confirm the COI clearly shows the umbrella sitting over the GL.
findings.recommendation: On COIs to Maricopa, ensure the umbrella line clearly references coverage over the underlying CGL (per §8.2.9 — 'Certificate of Insurance shall indicate which lines the Commercial Umbrella Insurance covers'). No coverage gap, but COI accuracy is the compliance risk.
discoveryQuestions: When you issue COIs to Maricopa, does the Umbrella row of the certificate explicitly note that it sits over the GL?
Has Maricopa's risk manager ever asked you to confirm umbrella attachment in writing?
If your primary GL had a $1M occurrence loss midyear, do you know how that affects your remaining tower for the rest of the policy term?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto — $2M CSL vs Underlying $1M
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence ...
findings.policy_quote: Underlying Auto (Allmerica AW4 H221414 05): $1,000,000 each accident. Hanover Umbrella Coverage A follows form over Auto for $10M xs $1M. Maricopa §8.2.9 (program-level umbrella permission) does NOT specifically reference auto in §8.2.11.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.11 (Auto) does NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment, unlike §8.2.10 (CGL) which expressly does. §8.2.9 grants program-level umbrella stacking. Two readings: (i) STRICT — Auto must independently meet $2M, umbrella permission applies only where stated; underlying $1M Auto fails; (ii) PERMISSIVE — §8.2.9 program-level permission flows through to Auto; $1M + $10M umbrella = $11M, complies. This is a classic ambiguous-attachment trigger.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires $2M auto liability. Your underlying auto is $1M; the umbrella sits over it for another $10M. The contract is ambiguous — one paragraph allows umbrella stacking generally; the auto paragraph doesn't repeat that permission. We don't know which way Maricopa will read this. Best practice: ask Maricopa Risk Management to confirm in writing OR raise underlying Auto to $2M to remove all doubt.
findings.recommendation: Two paths: (1) Confirm with Maricopa County Risk Management whether $1M Auto + $10M umbrella satisfies §8.2.11 (program-level permission interpretation). (2) Increase underlying Auto CSL to $2M at next renewal — minor premium impact, removes interpretive risk and improves position on every other county/contract. We recommend option 2.
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa ever sent a written acceptance or rejection of a COI showing $1M auto + umbrella, or has it been silent?
What's the cost difference between $1M auto and $2M auto at renewal — usually a small number relative to contract value?
Are there other county contracts that require $2M auto where you've already had to bump up the underlying?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — California Statutory WC for AZ-Based Employer
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: WC Policy (Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06) not provided in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is AZ-headquartered. CA statutory WC requires CA listed in Item 3.A of WC policy (preferred) — Item 3.C 'Other States' coverage is technically secondary and California has historically required 3.A listing for non-CA employers performing work in CA. Without seeing the WC policy, cannot verify. If CA is missing entirely, Run-Test has UNINSURED CA WC exposure — uncovered employer is liable for full benefits PLUS up to $100k penalties under Cal. Lab. Code §3700.
findings.plain_english: If you send AZ employees to Sacramento for ballot work and California isn't properly listed on your work comp policy, an injury would be uninsured — and California penalizes uninsured employers aggressively. Best practice for an out-of-state contractor doing work in CA is to have CA listed on Item 3.A of the work comp policy, not just 3.C. We need to see the WC policy to confirm.
findings.recommendation: Produce Mass Bay WC policy. Verify CA is listed in Item 3.A; if only in 3.C or absent, immediately request endorsement to add CA to 3.A before any Sacramento work occurs. Confirm CA WC waiver of subrogation (form WC 04 03 06) is endorsed for Sacramento.
discoveryQuestions: How many AZ employees physically work in California in a typical election cycle, and for how many days?
Does your WC policy show CA in Item 3.A or only Item 3.C? Do you know the difference?
If a Run-Test employee was injured loading ballots at a Sacramento County facility next month, what's the first thing your HR director would do?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Carrier Rating — A-VII Minimum
findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.
findings.policy_quote: Arch Insurance Company (Arch GL): A.M. Best A+ XV. Hanover Insurance Company / Citizens Insurance Company of America / Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company / Allmerica Financial Benefit Insurance — all Hanover Group subsidiaries: A.M. Best A (Excellent) XV.
findings.policy_page: Verify against current A.M. Best ratings
findings.gap_description: Both visible carriers (Arch and Hanover Group) historically meet A-VII. Best practice: re-verify ratings at every renewal and at COI issuance — ratings can change.
findings.plain_english: Your two visible carriers — Arch and Hanover/Citizens — both comfortably exceed Sacramento's A-VII minimum. Standard prudent broker practice: re-pull A.M. Best ratings at each renewal and at every major COI issuance.
findings.recommendation: Maintain current carrier set; verify A.M. Best at each renewal. When auditing the unviewed primary CGL, Auto, WC, and any Cyber/E&O, confirm same rating posture.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Carrier Rating — B++ Minimum
findings.contract_quote: ... AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.
findings.policy_quote: Arch (A+), Hanover Group (A) — both well above B++.
findings.gap_description: All visible carriers far exceed Maricopa's relatively low B++ floor.
findings.plain_english: Both Arch and the Hanover Group carriers exceed Maricopa's minimum carrier rating with significant margin.
findings.recommendation: No action — ensure the unviewed Cyber/E&O carriers also meet B++ when those policies are produced.

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa 30-Day / Broker 90-Day Target
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason, has expired, or will be expiring.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: 10 days nonpayment / 45 days other (per AZ amendment IL 02 58 04 21, Pg 14–16). No Designated Entity NOC endorsement (e.g., CG 02 24 / CG 20 12 / 401-1235) located. Hanover Umbrella: 10 days nonpayment / 45 days other (475-0176 AZ Changes, Pg 58). No Designated Entity NOC endorsement located.
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Pg 14–16; Hanover Umbrella Pg 58
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 requires 30-day notice 'to Maricopa County' — read literally, this requires the carrier to notice Maricopa directly (Designated Entity NOC). Maricopa also reads §8.2.15 as imposing an additional notification duty on Contractor (2-business-day pass-through). Standard ACORD COI cancellation disclaimer is not adequate. Neither viewed policy has a Designated Entity NOC endorsement scheduling Maricopa County (or any other entity). Sacramento §VI.A.2 takes a slightly different approach — notification obligation is on Contractor, not carrier — but still requires 'immediate' notice on receipt. Bogdan's broker target is 90 days for designated entities. Current AZ-amended 45-day non-pay-cancel and the absence of any Designated Entity NOC schedule mean: (a) policy NOC does not run directly to Maricopa County; (b) 45 days is below 90-day broker target.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30 days' written notice to them directly if any of your policies is canceled or materially changed. Your carriers send notice to YOU, not to Maricopa. The standard ACORD certificate disclaimer about notice doesn't bridge this. We need a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement that schedules Maricopa as a noticed party — and ideally other major county clients too. Best practice: 90 days. Your current Arizona-amended provisions cap at 45.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add Designated Entity NOC endorsement on Arch GL, Hanover Umbrella, and the unviewed Citizens CGL/Allmerica Auto/Mass Bay WC — schedule Maricopa County and any other contractually noticed entities. Hanover offers 401-1235 (Designated Entity NOC) for 30 or 60 days. (2) Negotiate 90-day notice where carrier permits — Hanover and similar standard markets often allow 60–90 day endorsements. (3) Maintain Contractor's internal 2-business-day pass-through workflow per §8.2.15.
discoveryQuestions: If your carrier sent a non-renewal notice tomorrow, who internally would catch it within 2 business days and forward to Maricopa County?
Has any county ever asked for a Designated Entity NOC endorsement as a condition of contract award?
On a 30-day notice window during election season, would you have time to source and bind replacement coverage if a carrier non-renewed?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Waiver of Subrogation (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County ...
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.8, Page 6 of 41 / Sacramento §VIII (WC) and inferred for liability lines
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL Schedule of Forms (Pg 8) and forms list (Pgs 11–68) does not include a Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (e.g., CG 24 04 or CG 20 24) in favor of additional insureds or contractually-required parties.
findings.gap_description: Per the policy analysis 'checklist.waiver_of_subrogation: false' — no Blanket Waiver of Subrogation form is on the Arch GL. Maricopa and Sacramento both require WoS on liability lines (excluding E&O / WC differently in each). If Arch is somehow the responding GL, lack of WoS is contract non-compliance.
findings.plain_english: On the security-guards GL, there's no blanket waiver of subrogation endorsement. If your carrier paid a claim and then chased the county for reimbursement, the county would argue you breached the contract. Counties generally require this waiver. Most likely the Citizens primary GL (which we haven't seen) has it — but the Arch security policy doesn't.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm Citizens primary CGL has Blanket Waiver of Subrogation (CG 24 04). (2) On Arch renewal, add CG 24 04 Blanket WoS to align with program standard, even though Arch responds to security ops only.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county ever pulled the Waiver of Subrogation endorsement and audited it form-by-form?
Does your Citizens primary GL have a CG 24 04 Blanket Waiver — and is the language 'in your favor' (correct) or 'in our favor' (wrong)?
If your insurer paid a $500k claim on county property and then tried to subrogate against the county, what does that do to next year's renewal of the contract?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Primary & Noncontributory (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: CG 20 01 12 19 'Primary And Noncontributory – Other Insurance Condition' (Pg 59). Triggered when (1) AI is named insured under such other insurance AND (2) written contract requires P&NC.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO P&NC endorsement is in place. Both county requirements are satisfied if/when the contract triggers (Sacramento and Maricopa contracts both expressly require primary & noncontributory).
findings.plain_english: On the security-guards GL, the primary & noncontributory endorsement is properly in place. Your coverage will pay first, and the county's coverage won't have to contribute. Confirm the same is true on the Citizens primary CGL.
findings.recommendation: Verify CG 20 01 (or equivalent) is on the Citizens primary CGL, Allmerica Auto, and Hanover Umbrella (umbrella P&NC by 'other insurance' clause).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Contractual Liability / 'Insured Contract' Definition
findings.contract_quote: The policy shall include coverage for ... blanket contractual coverage ...
findings.policy_quote: Standard CG 00 01 04 13 contractual liability via 'insured contract' (§V.9, Pg 53). 00 GL1058 (Contractual Liability Limitation, Pg 32) excludes only the part of any contract that indemnifies a person/organization for THEIR SOLE negligence — consistent with Cal. Civ. Code §2782(b).
findings.gap_description: Blanket contractual liability via base CG 00 01 is intact. Sole-negligence carve-out aligns with both Sacramento §VII.B (CA Civil Code §2782 acknowledgement) and broad-form expectations. No amended-insured-contract endorsement that would gut contractual liability is present.
findings.plain_english: Your contractual liability coverage is intact and broad — when you sign a hold-harmless with a county, your insurance backs that promise. The only carve-out is when you'd be indemnifying the county for their OWN sole negligence, which California law prohibits anyway.
findings.recommendation: Mirror review on Citizens primary CGL — confirm no Amendment of Insured Contract Definition endorsement is present that would limit blanket contractual.

findings.requirement_type: Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1058 'insured contract' definition excludes that part of any contract that indemnifies any person/organization for liability arising out of their SOLE negligence (Pg 32).
findings.gap_description: Standard carve-out aligns with §VII.B. No special endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's California public-policy carve-out is automatically satisfied — your policy already won't insure the county for their own active negligence, which is exactly what California law requires.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: GL — XCU (Explosion/Collapse/Underground) — No Exclusion (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: There shall be no endorsement or modifications of the CGL limiting the scope of coverage for liability arising from explosion, collapse, or underground property damage.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: No XCU exclusion located in Schedule of Forms or endorsements list. Citizens primary CGL not in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Arch GL doesn't appear to have an XCU exclusion (typical for security-guard ops which have no XCU exposure). Citizens primary CGL must be checked for any XCU exclusion (CG 21 42 or CG 21 43). For an election services manufacturer/printer, XCU is generally low exposure but the contract requirement is absolute.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says no XCU (explosion, collapse, underground) exclusions allowed on your GL. The security policy doesn't have one. We can't verify Citizens primary GL until we see it — most standard primary CGLs don't have XCU exclusions for non-construction risks, but it's worth a 30-second check.
findings.recommendation: Verify Citizens primary CGL has no CG 21 42 (XCU) or CG 21 43 (Underground only) exclusion when produced.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Action-Over Limits (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: [The CGL] shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: No specific action-over limitation endorsement located. Citizens primary CGL not in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Some carriers add an Employer's Liability / Action-Over exclusion (e.g., CG 21 39 or Cross-Liability exclusion) to the GL, particularly for construction or staffing risks. Cannot verify Citizens primary CGL — must produce.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says you can't have endorsements on your GL that limit 'action over' claims (the path where an injured worker sues a third party who then claims indemnity from the employer). Need to confirm Citizens GL doesn't have CG 21 39 or similar.
findings.recommendation: Verify Citizens primary CGL has no Action Over / EL exclusion endorsement when produced.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Per-Project Aggregate (Sacramento §III.A.3 — Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 ...
findings.policy_quote: Run-Test scope is election services (printing, mailing, processing) — not construction. Per-project aggregate trigger does not apply.
findings.gap_description: Per Sacramento contract notes, this requirement applies only to construction. Run-Test does not perform construction work. Requirement does not apply.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's per-project aggregate clause is for construction contractors. You're an election services manufacturer, not a builder — this requirement doesn't apply to you.
findings.recommendation: No action. Document non-applicability if Sacramento ever raises the question.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Damage to Premises Rented to You
findings.contract_quote: Fire Damage: $100,000.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: 'DAMAGE TO PREMISES RENTED TO YOU $1,000,000.' (Dec page)
findings.gap_description: $1M Damage to Premises sublimit far exceeds Sacramento's $100k 'Fire Damage' floor. Compliant with margin.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento wants $100k for fire damage to rented premises; you have $1M. Easy compliance.
findings.recommendation: Verify same on Citizens primary CGL (typical is $100k–$300k; $500k+ is preferred).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Mental Anguish in BI Definition
findings.contract_quote: Per RMF CGL-23: Bodily Injury definition should include mental anguish standalone — not connected to bodily injury.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 (Pg 53) standard definition: '"Bodily injury" means bodily injury, sickness or disease sustained by a person, including death resulting from any of these at any time.' No standalone Mental Anguish endorsement located.
findings.gap_description: Standard CG 00 01 BI definition does NOT include mental anguish standalone. Some carriers offer an 'Amendment of Definition – Bodily Injury' endorsement adding mental anguish. The Arch security GL does not have one. Citizens primary CGL must be checked for similar endorsement.
findings.plain_english: The standard insurance definition of 'bodily injury' typically requires actual physical injury before mental-anguish claims are paid. Some carriers offer an upgrade endorsement that covers mental-anguish-only claims (no physical injury required). Worth checking on the Citizens primary GL — particularly relevant for an election-services company where employees and the public can be subject to threats and harassment without physical contact.
findings.recommendation: Request Mental Anguish broadening endorsement on next renewal of Citizens primary CGL. Election-services workers regularly face hostile interactions; standalone mental anguish coverage is meaningful.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Care, Custody and Control (RMF CGL-2)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL-2: Could the Insured have property of others in their care, custody and/or control?
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.A.2.j 'Damage To Property' (Pg 43): excludes property in your care, custody or control. 00 GL1051 'Coverage Extensions' (Pg 28) restores items (4)–(6) of the exclusion for declared services on the security GL only.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles enormous volumes of county-owned property — ballots, voter records, election equipment, cure cards, signed signatures. CCC exposure is MASSIVE: a fire in Run-Test's facility could destroy entire counties' ballot inventories. CG 00 01 default CCC exclusion would deny GL coverage. Bailee's Customer's Goods coverage on a Property/IM policy is the right answer, not a CCC giveback on GL.
findings.plain_english: When ballots from Sacramento or Maricopa County are sitting in your warehouse, that's their property in YOUR care, custody, and control. If your sprinkler system soaked them or a fire destroyed them, your general liability policy generally excludes that. The right coverage is Bailee's Goods on a property/inland marine policy. We need to verify that's in place.
findings.recommendation: Verify Property and/or Inland Marine policy has Customers'/Bailee's Goods coverage with limits sufficient to cover the maximum amount of county property in Run-Test's possession at any one time during election season. This is a 7-figure-plus exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Property / Inland Marine (to be produced and audited)
discoveryQuestions: What's the peak dollar value of county-owned property — ballots, signed envelopes, election equipment — in your facility at any one moment during election season?
If a sprinkler discharge destroyed 200,000 Sacramento County ballots two days before an election, who pays to reprint, and where does that flow on your insurance?
Does your Property or Inland Marine policy have a Bailee's / Customers' Goods coverage line — and what's the limit?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Fellow Employee Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL-20: Is the Fellow Employee Exclusion deleted?
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 §II.2.a(1) (Pg 48): 'Each of the following is also an insured: Your "volunteer workers" only ...; or Your "employees" ... However, none of these "employees" or "volunteer workers" are insureds for: ... "Bodily injury" or "personal and advertising injury" ... To a co-"employee" while in the course of his or her employment ...' No Fellow Employee Coverage endorsement located.
findings.gap_description: Standard CG 00 01 fellow-employee exclusion in place. Standard carrier endorsement (often manuscript) deletes this so a supervisor sued by an injured employee has GL defense. Not present on Arch monoline; verify on Citizens primary CGL.
findings.plain_english: If a Run-Test supervisor is sued personally by an injured employee — say, for negligent training — the standard GL won't cover the supervisor as an additional insured because the fellow-employee exclusion blocks it. Many carriers offer a giveback that flips this. Worth checking on the Citizens GL.
findings.recommendation: Request Fellow Employee Coverage endorsement on Citizens primary CGL renewal.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Notice & Knowledge of Occurrence (Officer-Limited)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL-25 / Gen-4: Is the policy wording endorsed so notice of an occurrence is only considered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, and/or the risk manager is notified?
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 §IV.2.a (Duties In The Event Of Occurrence): 'You must see to it that we are notified as soon as practicable of an "occurrence" ...' No Notice of Occurrence/Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement located on either Arch GL or Hanover Umbrella.
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Pg 51 (Conditions); Hanover Umbrella main form 475-0001 (Pg 36 Conditions)
findings.gap_description: Without a Notice of Occurrence/Knowledge endorsement, knowledge by ANY employee can be imputed to the entity for notice purposes. For a company with 50–200 employees and dispersed election-mail processing operations, a low-level employee's awareness of an incident that goes unreported can be argued to constitute 'knowledge' that triggers the reporting clock, allowing carrier to deny for late notice. Industry-best practice is to limit notice trigger to executive officer / risk manager / insurance contact.
findings.plain_english: Without a special endorsement, any employee's awareness of a problem can technically be 'knowledge' the company had — and if it's not reported on time, the carrier can deny coverage. Best practice is to endorse the policy so notice only counts when an officer or your risk manager actually knows. Worth getting on every liability policy in the program.
findings.recommendation: Add Notice of Occurrence / Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement (carrier-specific form) to Citizens primary CGL, Arch GL, Allmerica Auto, Mass Bay WC, any Cyber/E&O. Umbrella follows form on this — endorsement on each underlying suffices.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Unintentional Errors and Omissions (Failure to Disclose)
findings.contract_quote: RMF Gen-2: Does the policy include an Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback?
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1050 'Unintentional Errors or Omissions' (Pg 27): 'Insured's failure to disclose hazards at inception not prejudicial unless intentional.'
findings.gap_description: Arch GL has unintentional E&O giveback. Need to verify same on Citizens primary CGL.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test accidentally fails to disclose something at policy inception (a new location, a new operation), the carrier can't deny coverage as long as the omission was unintentional. Good clause on the security GL — confirm same on the Citizens primary GL.
findings.recommendation: Verify Citizens primary CGL has equivalent Unintentional E&O giveback when produced.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Total Pollution Exclusion (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: Per RMF CGL-31: Total Pollution Exclusion endorsed?
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1047 'Total Pollution Exclusion with Hostile Fire and Self-Defense Spray Exception' (Pg 21).
findings.gap_description: Arch GL has Total Pollution Exclusion. Run-Test's election operations likely have low pollution exposure (no hazardous chemicals in printing/mailing typical), but ink/toner/cleaning solvent storage at the manufacturing facility creates some exposure. No Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL) policy in audit set. The Hanover Umbrella also has Total Pollution Exclusion (475-0027 + §VII.3.j).
findings.plain_english: Both your GL and umbrella have absolute pollution exclusions. If a printer-ink spill, cleaning-chemical leak, or HVAC refrigerant release caused a third-party claim, you'd have ZERO coverage anywhere. Probably low-frequency, but for a manufacturer with chemical/ink storage, a standalone Pollution policy is worth pricing.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory Run-Test's chemical/ink/solvent storage at manufacturing facility. (2) If any meaningful storage, evaluate Premises Pollution Liability or CPL placement — limits typically $1M–$5M, premium often modest for non-environmental industries.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Terrorism / TRIA
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL-32: Does the insured buy terrorism and has it been explained thoroughly.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: CG 21 73 01 15 'Exclusion of Certified Acts of Terrorism' (Pg 66). Hanover Umbrella: 475-0433 'Exclusion - Certified Acts of Terrorism' (Pg 64) — DESPITE TRIA disclosure on Pg 6 showing $75 terrorism premium charged and not rejected.
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Pg 66; Hanover Umbrella Pg 6, 64
findings.gap_description: Election services is a recognized HIGH-PROFILE TARGET for terrorism per DHS/CISA. Both visible policies exclude certified acts of terrorism. The Hanover Umbrella creates an internal contradiction — TRIA premium charged but exclusion endorsed. This is more than an academic issue: a coordinated act against an election vendor during an election cycle is a foreseeable scenario, and TRIA-certified status would mean ZERO coverage on the responding policies.
findings.plain_english: Election infrastructure is on every federal agency's terrorism-target list — DHS designates election systems as critical infrastructure. Your GL and umbrella both EXCLUDE certified acts of terrorism, even though the umbrella appears to have charged $75 of terrorism premium that wasn't rejected. A TRIA-certified attack would leave you uninsured on these lines. There's also a paperwork question — TRIA premium plus terrorism exclusion is unusual and warrants carrier confirmation.
findings.recommendation: (1) IMMEDIATE: Contact Hanover to clarify the TRIA-premium-charged-but-exclusion-endorsed inconsistency on the umbrella; obtain written confirmation of coverage posture. (2) Evaluate standalone Terrorism policy — markets like Pool Re, Lloyd's syndicates, Beazley specialize in this; election vendor profile justifies. (3) Discuss with Run-Test board given the heightened exposure profile.
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test had any threat assessments done by DHS, FBI, or state/local law enforcement in connection with election work?
If a Boston-Marathon-style incident occurred at your Phoenix facility two weeks before an election, where would your insurance respond?
Has anyone explained TRIA's certification process and what the $75 premium on the umbrella is actually buying?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Data Privacy / Cyber Stack of Exclusions (Sacramento Compliance Conflict)
findings.contract_quote: Form must be ISO CG 0001 occurrence ... No added exclusions/limitations without Risk Manager approval.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 69 12 23 'Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy' (Pg 56) — names BIPA, CCPA, GDPR. CG 21 06 12 23 'Access Or Disclosure Of Confidential Or Personal Material Or Information' (Pg 64). CG 40 35 12 23 'Cyber Incident' (Pg 68).
findings.gap_description: Triple-stack of privacy/cyber exclusions on the GL. Each one technically violates Sacramento §III.A's 'no added exclusions' requirement. More importantly: any coverage for voter-PII regulatory exposure must come from a standalone cyber policy — none verified in audit set. Sacramento contract requires GL to NOT 'limit third party action over claims' (Maricopa) — these endorsements limit data-privacy-related action-over.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards GL has THREE separate exclusions that strip out any cyber, data-breach, or privacy-violation coverage — including specifically calling out California's CCPA. If Sacramento ever audited the GL form-by-form, this would generate compliance pushback. The bigger issue is the underlying coverage gap: with these exclusions on the primary AND the umbrella, your only privacy/cyber response has to come from a standalone cyber policy — which isn't verified yet.
findings.recommendation: (1) Verify Citizens primary CGL exclusion stack (likely similar — most modern CGL forms have at least CG 21 06). (2) Sacramento Risk Manager approval should be sought OR the cyber policy must be presented as the standalone privacy/cyber response with $5M+ limits affirmatively covering CCPA, BIPA, and similar. (3) On COIs to Sacramento, consider attaching a brief cover letter noting cyber/privacy is on a standalone policy.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county risk manager ever asked you to identify which policy responds to a CCPA or BIPA claim?
When was the last cyber-policy audit done at the form level — checking that 'unauthorized acquisition of personal information' affirmatively triggers coverage?
Run-Test handles voter PII across 31 states. Have you mapped which state privacy laws apply, and does your cyber policy affirmatively cover regulatory defense AND penalties in each?

findings.requirement_type: GL — PFAS Exclusion (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: n/a — emerging exposure for printers/manufacturers
findings.policy_quote: 00 MLL0008 00 05 24 'Exclusion - Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)' (Pg 3).
findings.gap_description: Absolute PFAS exclusion now industry-standard on most GL forms. Run-Test is a printer/manufacturer; some inks, papers, and printer components historically contain PFAS. This is an emerging mass-tort exposure (3M, Chemours, DuPont). Verify Citizens primary CGL exclusion language and ink/paper supply chain.
findings.plain_english: PFAS — 'forever chemicals' — are showing up in mass-tort litigation against printers, paper-makers, and packagers because they're used in inks, coatings, and water-resistant papers. Your GL has an absolute exclusion. Worth a 30-minute call with your top ink and paper suppliers to confirm what's in your supply chain — and worth the same exclusion check on the Citizens primary GL.
findings.recommendation: (1) Audit ink, paper, and packaging supply chain for PFAS use. (2) Confirm Citizens primary CGL has PFAS exclusion (it almost certainly does at 2025/2026 renewals). (3) If supply chain reveals PFAS exposure, evaluate standalone Environmental Liability with PFAS coverage (sparse market but exists).

findings.requirement_type: GL — Phthalates Exclusion (Hanover Umbrella) — Manufacturing/Printing
findings.contract_quote: n/a — emerging exposure
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella 475-0639 07 23 'Exclusion - Phthalates Coverage' (Pg 70). Lists DBP, DIBP, BBP, DEHP, DINP, DIDP and many others. Applies to both Coverage A and B.
findings.gap_description: Phthalates are commonly found in printing inks, plastics, and packaging — emerging tort exposure. Umbrella absolute exclusion on both Coverage A (follow-form excess) and B (true umbrella). If Citizens primary CGL covers a phthalates claim, the umbrella will NOT extend over it. For an election services printer, phthalates-in-ink claims (especially as products end up in voters' hands) is a non-trivial possibility.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella has an absolute phthalates exclusion. Phthalates are in some printing inks and plastic ballot envelope coatings. If a class action ever links election materials to phthalate exposure, your primary CGL might respond up to $1M, but the $10M umbrella would not extend. Worth checking Citizens primary GL for the same exclusion and worth a supply-chain audit of inks.
findings.recommendation: (1) Audit ink/packaging supply chain for phthalates. (2) Verify Citizens primary CGL phthalates posture. (3) If exposure is real, push back on Hanover umbrella exclusion at renewal (sometimes negotiable for non-toy/non-medical-device manufacturers).
discoveryQuestions: Do your ink suppliers' SDS sheets show any phthalates — DEHP, DINP, BBP, DBP?
Have any of your county clients ever asked for chemical-content disclosure on ballot materials?
If an election ballot was alleged to leach phthalates onto voters' hands during early voting, where would that claim land in your insurance program?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Canine Liability Exclusion (Arch Security)
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1048 00 01 25 'Canine Liability Exclusion' (Pg 22): absolute exclusion for any BI/PD arising out of ownership, rental, maintenance or use of any dog or canine.
findings.gap_description: If Run-Test's security operations use K-9 units (common at high-value election facilities, especially during ballot warehousing), this exclusion strips coverage for any K-9 related incidents. Direct exposure point.
findings.plain_english: If your in-house security uses any K-9 dogs — for facility patrol or ballot detection — there is ZERO GL coverage for any incident involving the dog. Most security operations don't use K-9, but it's worth a 30-second confirmation.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Run-Test security operations do not use canines. If they do, urgent need to remove this exclusion or place dedicated canine-handler liability coverage.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Assault & Battery Coverage (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: n/a — Arch security GL specific
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1063 00 01 25 'Assault and Battery Coverage Endorsement' (Pg 37): Modifies Expected/Intended exclusion to NOT exclude (1) BI from use of physical force to protect persons or property; or (2) claims arising out of assault/battery by an employee.
findings.gap_description: Critical for security operations — restores coverage that would otherwise be excluded by the standard CG 00 01 expected/intended exclusion.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards GL specifically gives back coverage for use-of-force incidents and employee assault/battery claims — exactly what a security operation needs.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: GL — Errors & Omissions Coverage D (Arch Security GL — Limits Sharing Risk)
findings.contract_quote: n/a — Arch security GL specific
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1049 00 01 25 'Errors & Omissions Coverage Extension (Coverage D)' (Pg 23): 'Subject to General Aggregate AND Each Occurrence limits — shared with A/B/C, NOT a separate aggregate.'
findings.gap_description: Coverage D E&O exists for security operations errors but shares the $1M each occurrence and $3M general aggregate with Coverage A (BI/PD), Coverage B (PI/AI), and Coverage C (Med Pay). A single severe BI claim could exhaust limits before E&O ever responds. Plus numerous exclusions: contractual liability (except insured contracts), employment law, electronic data damage, fraud, intra-insured. Punitive damages and fines also excluded.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards policy includes a small E&O extension for errors in security work, but it shares the same limits as the BI/PD coverage. A serious injury claim could eat the entire policy before any E&O claim can attach. For real Tech E&O exposure, you need a standalone policy.
findings.recommendation: Treat Coverage D as a thin add-on to security ops only. Maintain standalone Tech E&O / Misc Professional Liability for real election-services exposure with separate aggregate.
discoveryQuestions: If a security-guard incident triggered an E&O claim and a BI claim in the same year, do you know that they'd share the same $3M aggregate?
How is the security-guards E&O on Coverage D different from your standalone Tech E&O?
Is the Arch security GL meant to be your primary security-ops policy, or is it stacked behind something else?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Independent Contractor Requirements Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1053 'Independent Contractor Requirements Endorsement' (Pg 30): 'Insured must obtain COIs from independent contractors with limits ≥ insured's CGL limits. Failure does not eliminate coverage but converts contractor's costs to premium basis at contractor classifications.'
findings.gap_description: Endorsement requires Run-Test to obtain matching-limit COIs from any subcontractor. Failure doesn't eliminate coverage but adds the sub's costs to Run-Test's premium audit base. Two implications: (1) Sacramento §VII.E flow-down obligation aligns with this — Run-Test must enforce its own subcontractor insurance program, and (2) loose enforcement creates premium audit exposure at year-end.
findings.plain_english: Your security-guards GL makes you responsible for getting certificates of insurance from any subcontractor you use, AND for making sure their limits match yours. If you don't, you'll get stuck with their payroll added to your premium at audit. Sacramento's contract also makes you responsible for sub flow-downs. So this is a discipline issue with both insurance and contract consequences.
findings.recommendation: (1) Implement (or audit) a subcontractor insurance verification program: matching-limit COI requirement, AI flow-down requirement, blanket waiver of subrogation in sub agreements. (2) Same discipline for the Citizens primary CGL operations. (3) Consider Patriot's COI tracking/monitoring services.
discoveryQuestions: How does Run-Test currently track subcontractor insurance — manual spreadsheet, third-party platform, or 'we'll deal with it at audit'?
If a county sub-mailer caused a delivery error two months from now, does your contract with them require AI flow-up to your client counties?
What does your last GL premium audit look like — were there sub payrolls added to your basis you didn't expect?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Coverage Extensions Narrowing (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1051 00 01 25 'Coverage Extensions — Section I, Coverages A and B' (Pg 28): '... Coverage A and B extended to BI/PD/PI&AI caused by negligent acts/errors/omissions in coverage territory but ONLY in connection with work/services listed on Dec.'
findings.gap_description: Reinforces Classification Limitation — Coverages A AND B are narrowed to declared classifications. This is a non-issue if Arch is responding to security ops only, but it's a structural reminder that this policy cannot be used as a fallback for any non-security operations.
findings.plain_english: This endorsement on the security GL confirms that the only operations covered are the declared security classifications. Reinforces the prior finding — this policy is NOT a backup GL for election services.
findings.recommendation: No action — informational. Document segregation in COI workflow.
discoveryQuestions: Does your COI vendor have logic to issue the Citizens GL for election work and the Arch GL for security work, or do they default to one for everything?
Has any county ever questioned whether your security operations are covered separately from your core election services?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — Indemnification & Hold Harmless Scope
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §VII.A AI requirement is the indemnity proxy; see also Civil Code §2782 carve-out.]
findings.policy_quote: Citizens primary CGL not in audit set; Arch GL contractual liability via standard CG 00 01.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento contract assumes broad indemnity but caps via Civil Code §2782(b). Without the underlying contract's full indemnity clause, can't fully verify whether contractor is assuming defense before liability determination. Comparison to Maricopa §8.1.1 (which is comparative-negligence-limited under AZ law) shows Sacramento may be broader.
findings.plain_english: We can see the AI section but the full indemnification clause from Sacramento and how it interacts with §2782 needs another pass. The Maricopa indemnity is comparative — only what you actually caused. The Sacramento language relies on the AI endorsement to do the heavy lifting. This is a contract-level question more than an insurance one.
findings.recommendation: Review Sacramento contract Indemnification clause in full when available. Confirm contractor's contractual liability picks up only what's permitted under §2782(b) — sole-negligence carve-out is already in place.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella $10M aggregate. Total liability tower: $1M Citizens GL + $10M Hanover Umbrella = $11M.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa indemnity is uncapped by insurance limits. Run-Test's balance sheet is exposed for any verdict above $11M. PE-backed manufacturer with $5–25M revenue and election-vendor reputational exposure → catastrophic verdict scenario is asymmetric (election-day disruption, voter-data class action, state attorney general action).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract makes clear: your indemnity to them is not capped at your insurance limits. If something goes really wrong and a verdict comes in at $20M, your insurance pays $11M and your balance sheet eats the rest. For a PE-backed company with election-day visibility, this isn't theoretical — class actions over voter records are filed regularly. Your tower may be undersized for the worst-case scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Run a limits-adequacy analysis: compare current $11M tower against (a) PE peer benchmarks (typically $25M–$50M GL/Umbrella), (b) cyber sublimits per voter records held, (c) historic verdict data on election-related litigation. Recommend exploring $25M total tower at next renewal cycle.
discoveryQuestions: Has your PE sponsor stated minimum insurance limit requirements in the investment documents?
If Maricopa lost an election due to a vendor error tied to Run-Test and a class of 500,000 voters sued, what's the floor on damages exposure?
When did you last benchmark your liability tower against other election-services peers — Tenex, Konnech, Hart, Election Systems & Software?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Deductible/SIR Allocation & Bond/LOC
findings.contract_quote: Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: $1,000 BI/PD combined deductible per claim (CG 03 00 01 96, Pg 57). Cyber and umbrella SIRs not visible/reviewed.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves the right to demand a surety bond or letter of credit backing any deductible/SIR. For most well-rated programs this is theoretical — but for cyber policies (often $25k–$100k SIRs) and umbrella SIRs, the County has a contractual leverage point. Sacramento §IV requires deductible/SIR disclosure and approval BEFORE performance — same point.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa technically has the right to make you put up a bond or letter of credit to back your insurance deductibles or self-insured retentions. They've never asked Run-Test (we presume), but if they do, that's a real cash demand. Higher deductibles and SIRs make this risk bigger. Sacramento separately requires you to disclose all deductibles/SIRs before starting work.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory every policy's deductible and SIR. (2) Confirm Sacramento has been provided full disclosure of all SIRs/deductibles BEFORE performance. (3) Maintain awareness — keep SIRs as low as economically feasible to minimize bond/LOC demand risk.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Cancellation Lapse = Material Breach
findings.contract_quote: All insurance required herein shall be maintained in full force and effect until all work or service required to be performed under the terms of the contract is satisfactorily completed and formally accepted. Failure to do so may, at the sole discretion of County, constitute a material breach of this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL & Hanover Umbrella both have AZ-amended 10-day nonpayment / 45-day other cancellation. No Designated Entity NOC scheduling Maricopa.
findings.gap_description: Lapse triggers material breach. Without Designated Entity NOC, Maricopa might not learn of a cancellation until COI expiration, and Contractor's 2-business-day pass-through (§8.2.15) becomes the sole notification path. Process discipline is critical.
findings.plain_english: If your insurance lapses for any reason — even briefly — Maricopa can declare the contract breached. Without a designated-entity notice endorsement, the carrier won't tell Maricopa. You will, but only if you have a process to catch carrier notices and forward them within 2 business days.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish (or audit) Run-Test's internal carrier-notice intake workflow with 2-business-day Maricopa pass-through. (2) Add Designated Entity NOC endorsement (see finding #019). (3) Build a renewal calendar with 60-day pre-renewal flag.
discoveryQuestions: Who at Run-Test opens the mail or e-mail notifications from carriers? What happens if they're on vacation when a non-renewal notice arrives?
Has any of your county clients ever flagged a coverage lapse — even an administrative one between renewals?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Right to Adjust Coverage Mid-Term
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection ... COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient ...
findings.policy_quote: n/a — contract right
findings.gap_description: County reserves unilateral right to require additional coverage mid-term. Open-ended cost risk.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento (and most county contracts) reserves the right to demand additional insurance at any time mid-contract if their risk manager decides current coverage is inadequate. You can't predict it, but you should price-protect by maintaining a strong baseline tower.
findings.recommendation: Maintain robust tower as baseline; budget for mid-term endorsement requests as part of contract administration.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento — COI With Endorsement Copies, Pre-Performance Approval
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below. Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.
findings.policy_quote: n/a — process requirement
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES — not just COI references. Many brokers issue COIs without attaching endorsement schedules. Sacramento also reserves the right to request certified policies. Audit Run-Test's current COI delivery practice.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento isn't satisfied with a regular insurance certificate — they want copies of the actual additional insured endorsement, the primary & noncontributory endorsement, and so on. If you've been sending plain ACORD certificates, you're not technically in compliance, and they could refuse to let work commence.
findings.recommendation: (1) Audit Run-Test's COI workflow — confirm endorsement copies ATTACHED for every Sacramento submission. (2) Standard package should include: CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (AI ongoing + completed ops), CG 20 01 (P&NC), CG 24 04 (Blanket WoS), CA AI/WoS/P&NC for auto, WC 04 03 06 (CA Waiver), Schedule of Underlying for Umbrella. (3) Consider Patriot-issued enhanced COIs for repeat county clients.
discoveryQuestions: When you ship a COI to Sacramento, are you attaching the actual additional insured endorsement copy, or relying on the certificate language alone?
What's your turnaround time when a county requests certified policy copies?
Have you ever had a county delay contract execution due to a missing endorsement attachment?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — COI Renewal 15 Days Before Expiration
findings.contract_quote: If a policy does expire during the life of the Contract, a renewal certificate must be sent to County 15 calendar days prior to the expiration date.
findings.policy_quote: n/a — process requirement
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires COIs delivered to them 15 days BEFORE renewal date. Process discipline issue. Hanover Umbrella renewal is 04/01/26; Citizens primary CGL renewal date unknown but presumed similar; Arch GL is 10/22/26. Each requires renewal COI to Maricopa 15 days prior.
findings.plain_english: Every time a policy renews, Maricopa wants a renewal COI 15 days before the old one expires. Easy to mess up if you're juggling multiple policies with different renewal dates.
findings.recommendation: Create a master renewal calendar with all policy renewal dates and 15-day pre-renewal Maricopa COI delivery flags. Same process for Sacramento §VI.A.2 (10-day pre-anniversary evidence).

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber — Claims-Made Retro on/before 11/01/2021
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: n/a — Cyber policy not provided
findings.gap_description: Cyber and any other claims-made policies must have retro on or before Maricopa contract effective date (11/01/2021 per the requirement notes). 2-year ERP required if non-replaced. Cannot verify without Cyber policy.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy (and any other claims-made policy) needs a retroactive date that goes back to at least November 1, 2021 — when the Maricopa contract started. If Run-Test has only had cyber for, say, 2 years, you're missing pre-existing claim coverage. Same for Sacramento — retro must be on or before that contract date.
findings.recommendation: Once Cyber policy is produced, verify retro date on/before 11/01/2021 (Maricopa) and on/before each Sacramento contract date. If retro is later, evaluate retro-date amendment, prior acts coverage purchase, or tail/ERP at non-renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Pro Liab — Retro & 1-Year ERP
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown ... B. Insurance must be maintained ... for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. C. If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed ... CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: n/a — Professional Liability policy not provided
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires Pro Liab retro on/before contract effective date, plus 1-year tail if not replaced.
findings.plain_english: When Sacramento contracts ended, you'd be obligated to keep professional liability in force for at least one more year — or buy a one-year tail. Worth confirming on the standalone E&O when produced.
findings.recommendation: Verify Pro Liab retro and ERP availability on E&O policy when produced.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Schedule of Underlying Includes All Required Lines
findings.contract_quote: Underlying Policies - Are they all listed, including the foreign liability?
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella Schedule of Underlying (Pg 14): CGL (Citizens), Auto (Allmerica), WC/EL (Mass Bay), Employee Benefits Liability (Citizens). NO listings for: Cyber, Professional Liability/E&O, Foreign Liability, USL&H, or any other line.
findings.gap_description: Schedule of Underlying lists only GL, Auto, WC/EL, EBL. The umbrella will NOT follow form over Cyber (excluded anyway) or Professional Liability (excluded anyway), so this is consistent. However: if Run-Test has Foreign Voluntary, USL&H, or any other liability line, those are NOT scheduled — claims hitting those lines would not benefit from umbrella attachment. Also: 475-0613 (Pg 66) clarifies that sublimits within underlying policies that are not separately listed on Schedule are NOT considered underlying — meaning umbrella will NOT drop down over sublimited coverages within the underlying policies.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella sits over your GL, auto, work comp/employer liability, and EBL — and those are the only ones. If you have any other liability coverage (foreign liability for international travel, longshore for waterfront, etc.), the umbrella ignores it. Also, any sublimited coverage inside your existing policies is invisible to the umbrella unless separately scheduled.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory all liability lines and confirm umbrella schedule completeness. (2) If Foreign Voluntary or USL&H is present (even if just 'if any'), schedule on umbrella. (3) For any meaningful sublimits in underlying policies, evaluate whether to schedule them.
discoveryQuestions: Do any Run-Test employees travel internationally for election conferences, training, or work?
Are there any liability lines you carry that you don't see listed on the umbrella schedule — Cyber, Pro Liab, Foreign Voluntary?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Defense Inside vs Outside Limits
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 5: Limits - Is Defense inside the limit versus outside the limit?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 main form §III.B and §IV: Defense costs in addition to limits for follow-form excess (Coverage A) when underlying provides defense outside limits; Coverage B umbrella defense provided as supplementary payment.
findings.gap_description: Standard-market umbrella with defense outside limits — preferred posture. E&S umbrellas often have defense INSIDE limits, which would erode coverage. This Hanover form is the right structure.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's defense costs are paid OUTSIDE the policy limits — meaning your $10M limit goes entirely toward indemnity, and legal fees are separate. That's the better structure (E&S umbrellas often have defense inside limits, which can chew up your coverage).
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal — confirm no carrier change to inside-limits structure.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Maintenance of Underlying Insurance
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 6: Maintenance of underlying insurance. Must the insured notify the carrier of any underlying changes?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VIII Conditions Maintenance of Underlying Insurance (Pg 36): Insured must maintain underlying in full force; reduction/exhaustion does not increase umbrella obligations; if underlying limits are reduced, umbrella applies as if underlying limits were maintained.
findings.gap_description: Standard maintenance-of-underlying provision. If Run-Test reduces a primary limit (e.g., shifts to lower auto from $1M to $500k), the umbrella attaches as if $1M were still in place — meaning Run-Test self-insures the gap. This isn't a defect, but it's a process risk: any change to underlying limits without telling Hanover (or in ignorance of the umbrella scheduling) creates an uninsured gap.
findings.plain_english: If you ever change anything on your primary policies — limits, retentions, additional insureds — without telling Hanover, your umbrella may not respond properly. The umbrella treats your primary as if it's at the limits originally scheduled, even if you've quietly downgraded. Process discipline matters here.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish broker workflow: any change to underlying limits/coverage triggers an umbrella re-cert + Schedule of Underlying update. (2) Annual pre-renewal review of Schedule of Underlying against actual underlying policies.
discoveryQuestions: Has any underlying policy limit been reduced in the past 12 months — even temporarily?
Who at Run-Test would update the umbrella schedule if a primary policy changed mid-term?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Punitive Damages Excluded
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 10: Punitive damages, are they excluded?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VII.3.l Coverage B (Pg 35): 'No coverage for punitive, exemplary, multiplied damages, taxes, fines, or penalties.'
findings.gap_description: Coverage B (true umbrella) excludes punitive damages, multipliers, fines, and penalties. Coverage A follows form on what underlying covers — so if Citizens primary CGL covers punitive (depends on state law and form), Coverage A might too; but Coverage B is silent. AZ does not insure punitives by statute. CA permits insurance of punitives but it's policy-specific. Election-services litigation often involves potential punitive exposure (intentional voter suppression theories, civil rights violations), so this gap matters.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's true-umbrella layer (Coverage B) excludes punitive damages outright. Election-services lawsuits sometimes seek punitive damages — a $10M underlying verdict could become $30M with punitives, and the umbrella wouldn't respond to the multiplier. State law also limits insurability (Arizona doesn't insure punitives at all). Worth a discussion about offshore wrap-arounds or specific-state policies if punitives become a real exposure profile.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm Citizens primary CGL position on punitives. (2) For high-exposure scenarios (voting rights litigation, civil rights claims), evaluate punitive damage wrap-around (Bermuda or offshore captive structures). (3) Document the exclusion in board reporting on uninsured exposures.
discoveryQuestions: Have any prior election-related lawsuits against Run-Test or peers sought punitive damages?
Does Run-Test's PE sponsor have a wrap-around or captive structure that backstops punitives?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Right and Duty to Defend When Underlying Exhausted
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 11: Does the policy state that the carrier has the right and duty to defend when the limits are exhausted in the underlying policy?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §I.B Coverage B Umbrella Liability — Right and duty to defend when no underlying applies; Coverage A follows form on defense.
findings.gap_description: Standard-market right-and-duty-to-defend posture once underlying is exhausted. Confirms expected behavior.
findings.plain_english: When your primary policies are exhausted, the umbrella takes over the defense. Standard for a standard-market umbrella; this is what you want.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Total Pollution Exclusion (Both Coverages)
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 12: Total Pollution Exclusion - is it endorsed or part of the policy?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0027 12 14 Total Pollution Exclusion (Coverage A, Pg 44). 475-0001 §VII.3.j Pollution Exclusion (Coverage B, Pg 35).
findings.gap_description: Absolute pollution exclusion on BOTH coverages — no givebacks, no exceptions. Combined with GL Total Pollution Exclusion, Run-Test has ZERO pollution coverage anywhere in the program (pending verification of Citizens primary CGL).
findings.plain_english: The umbrella's pollution exclusion is absolute on both coverages, with no exception — even for hostile fire or contractual indemnity. Combined with the GL pollution exclusion, you have no pollution coverage anywhere. For a manufacturer with ink/solvent storage, this should be on the upgrade list.
findings.recommendation: Cross-reference with finding #033 — evaluate Premises Pollution Liability or CPL placement.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Professional Liability Exclusion (Both Coverages)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.E: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... (other than Professional Liability) ...
findings.policy_quote: 475-0031 12 14 Exclusion - Professional Liability (Coverage A, Pg 46). 475-0001 §VII.3.k Professional Liability Exclusion (Coverage B, Pg 35).
findings.gap_description: Umbrella excludes Professional Liability on BOTH coverages. Sacramento expressly does not allow umbrella to satisfy Pro Liab minimum — so umbrella exclusion is consistent with that contract. But for Run-Test's actual exposure: a single E&O claim ($10M+ ballot mishandling, signature verification error class action) could exhaust the underlying $1M Tech E&O with ZERO excess. The umbrella structurally cannot extend over E&O.
findings.plain_english: Your $10M umbrella does NOT extend over your professional liability. If a class action over a ballot processing error costs $5M, your standalone Tech E&O burns through and the umbrella does nothing. Election-services E&O often needs $5M–$10M standalone; your $1M underlying (assumed) is light, with no umbrella backstop possible.
findings.recommendation: (1) Once standalone Tech E&O is verified, evaluate increasing limits to $5M minimum. (2) Sacramento expressly bars umbrella from satisfying its $1M E&O minimum — current structure aligns. (3) For Maricopa (which doesn't address E&O explicitly), confirm Tech E&O limits are sufficient on their own. (4) Discuss dedicated Excess E&O placement for Run-Test's election-services exposure.
discoveryQuestions: If a class action over election results affecting 250,000 voters arose from a Run-Test mail-sorting error, do you have an honest sense of total cost — defense plus settlement?
Is your standalone Tech E&O at $1M, or higher? Is there any excess E&O above it?
Would your PE sponsor accept $1M of Tech E&O as the entire response to a major election-day claim?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Abuse and Molestation Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 475-0050 12 14 Exclusion - Abuse and Molestation (Coverage A and B, Pg 48): including negligent employment, supervision, retention, or failure to report.
findings.gap_description: Standard exclusion. Low frequency for Run-Test (no children/youth/protected populations regularly served), but the negligent-supervision angle could catch Run-Test in employment-related abuse claims (between employees).
findings.plain_english: Abuse/molestation exclusion is standard and probably non-issue for an election-services manufacturer. The only edge case: an employee abuse claim against Run-Test for negligent supervision — that's excluded too. Best handled through HR controls and EPLI.
findings.recommendation: Document non-applicability; rely on EPLI for employee-related claims (verify standalone EPLI in finding #008).

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Discrimination Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 475-0215 12 14 Exclusion - Discrimination (Coverage A and B, Pg 60): age, gender, sexual orientation, marital status, race, nationality, religion, disability.
findings.gap_description: No umbrella excess for discrimination. Election services uniquely exposed to civil rights / Voting Rights Act / disparate-impact theories that may overlap with discrimination definitions. A successful disparate-impact claim against an election vendor is increasingly plausible — the umbrella will not respond.
findings.plain_english: If a voting-rights lawsuit claims your services had a disparate impact on protected classes — say, signature-verification rejecting more minority ballots — the umbrella has a discrimination exclusion. Combined with the privacy/data-law exclusions, the umbrella structurally avoids most modern election-litigation theories.
findings.recommendation: (1) Verify Tech E&O / Cyber have affirmative civil rights / disparate impact coverage (often a buyback). (2) Discuss with Run-Test board and PE sponsor: does the program need civil-rights-specific coverage given election-services exposure?
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test or any peer ever been named in a Voting Rights Act, Section 2, or disparate-impact lawsuit?
Does your standalone Tech E&O affirmatively cover civil rights claims or carve them out?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Recording & Distribution / TCPA / CAN-SPAM Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VII.1.h (Pg 31): No umbrella excess for TCPA, CAN-SPAM, FCRA/FACTA, or similar statutory privacy/communication claims.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's election-mail business has direct TCPA exposure (any voter contact via auto-dial/text), and CAN-SPAM exposure (voter email outreach). $1,500-per-violation TCPA statutory damages can quickly exceed primary GL limits. Umbrella will not respond.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test (or a county on Run-Test's behalf) ever sends robocalls, auto-texts, or bulk election-related emails, TCPA class actions are routine. $1,500 per violation × millions of voters = potentially huge. Your umbrella excludes all of this. Coverage has to come from cyber or a specialty TCPA policy.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm Run-Test's actual voter-outreach footprint: any robocalls, auto-texts, or mass emails? (2) Verify cyber policy affirmatively covers TCPA/CAN-SPAM (many forms exclude or sublimit). (3) For high-volume outreach, evaluate dedicated TCPA insurance.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test ever send robocalls, automated text messages, or bulk election emails — for any client county?
Have you reviewed your contracts with the counties: who's responsible for TCPA compliance — them, you, or both?
What's the volume of voter contact in a typical election cycle?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Multiple Named Insured Endorsement (LLC Friendly)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General All Policies — Named Insureds: Inc vs LLC entity-type mismatches; Broad Form Named Insured endorsements that may exclude LLCs.
findings.policy_quote: 475-0174 'Multiple Named Insured Endorsement' (Pg 56): Adds Runbeck Properties LLC, Runbeck Investments LLC, Runbeck Graphics Inc as Named Insureds.
findings.gap_description: Affiliates added by name on an LLC-friendly endorsement (no LLC carve-out). Reliable inclusion. Confirm same scheduling on Citizens primary CGL, Allmerica Auto, Mass Bay WC.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella correctly names the related Runbeck entities (Properties LLC, Investments LLC, Graphics Inc). The endorsement explicitly schedules them — there's no LLC carve-out trap. Now we need to verify the same scheduling exists on your primary GL, auto, and work comp.
findings.recommendation: Verify identical Named Insured scheduling on Citizens primary CGL, Allmerica Auto, Mass Bay WC, and any Cyber/E&O policies. ASYMMETRIC NAMED INSURED across the program is a frequent and damaging audit finding.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Named Insured: Runbeck vs Run-Test (Entity Discrepancy)
findings.contract_quote: Client identified as 'Run-Test Election Services' in audit context; Sacramento and Maricopa contracts reference the contracting entity.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services Inc.' (Inc). Arch GL Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services LLC.' (LLC).
findings.policy_page: Hanover Umbrella Dec; Arch GL Dec Pg 7
findings.gap_description: ENTITY-TYPE MISMATCH: Hanover names 'Runbeck Election Services Inc.' (corporation); Arch names 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' (limited liability company). These are separate legal entities. Client profile says 'Run-Test Election Services.' Three different entity references suggest one of: (a) typo/redaction artifact from the audit document, (b) entity restructuring not yet reflected on all policies, (c) entirely separate legal entities. This is a significant compliance issue — the contracting entity may not match the named insured on either policy.
findings.plain_english: We have an entity-name mismatch: the umbrella names 'Runbeck Election Services Inc.' (corporation), but the security GL names 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' (limited liability company). The audit context refers to the client as 'Run-Test Election Services.' If your contracts with the counties are signed under one entity but your insurance is in another, an adjuster could deny coverage on grounds the named insured isn't the contracting party. This needs immediate cleanup.
findings.recommendation: (1) URGENT: Confirm legal entity structure of Run-Test/Runbeck Election Services. (2) Verify which entity signs contracts with Sacramento, Maricopa, and other counties. (3) Update Named Insured on all policies to reflect contracting entity. (4) Reconcile Inc vs LLC mismatch — these cannot both be the operating entity. (5) Use a Broad Form Named Insured or specifically scheduled NI to ensure all relevant entities are insured on every line.
discoveryQuestions: Can you walk me through the Run-Test / Runbeck legal entity tree — which entity signs Sacramento and Maricopa contracts, which entity employs the staff, which entity owns the equipment?
When was the last entity restructuring, and were all policies updated?
Are there contracts with counties currently in force that name an entity not listed as a Named Insured on your policies?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Broad Form Named Insured Status
findings.contract_quote: RMF Gen-3: Broad Form Named Insured endorsements that may exclude LLCs/partnerships from automatic extension.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella: NO Broad Form Named Insured endorsement. NIs added by named-schedule via 475-0174 (Pg 56). Arch GL: NO Broad Form Named Insured endorsement.
findings.gap_description: Neither viewed policy has a Broad Form Named Insured endorsement that automatically extends coverage to newly-acquired or formed subsidiaries. Any new Runbeck affiliate would not be automatically insured — manual endorsement required. PE-backed companies often acquire/form new entities; this is an active risk.
findings.plain_english: Neither policy has a 'Broad Form Named Insured' endorsement that would automatically extend coverage to any newly-formed or acquired subsidiary. As a PE-backed company that may grow by acquisition, this means every new entity has to be manually added to every policy — easy to miss, and any gap leaves the new entity uninsured.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add Broad Form Named Insured endorsement on Citizens primary CGL, Allmerica Auto, Mass Bay WC, and Hanover Umbrella at next renewal. (2) Establish broker-side notification protocol for any Runbeck acquisition or new subsidiary formation.
discoveryQuestions: Has the PE sponsor signaled any planned acquisitions or new entity formations?
When the last new affiliate was formed, who was responsible for adding it to every policy?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Underlying Claims-Made ERP
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella supplemental ERP options
findings.policy_quote: 475-0618 06 22 'Underlying Claims-Made Coverage — Extended Reporting Periods' (Pg 68): 60-day Automatic ERP if cancelled/non-renewed; Optional ERP available with additional premium: 1 year = 100% / 2 years = 150% / 3 years = 200%.
findings.gap_description: Reasonable ERP availability. 1-year ERP at 100% of annual premium meets Sacramento §V.C tail requirement.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella has reasonable extended-reporting-period options if you ever non-renew — 60 days automatic, plus 1/2/3 year buybacks at 100/150/200% of annual premium. That covers Sacramento's 1-year tail requirement.
findings.recommendation: Document ERP availability for renewal planning.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Additional Insured Follow-Form
findings.contract_quote: Insureds: 1) Is the Additional Insured - follow form, or are conditional exceptions taken? ... Maricopa §8.2.7 requires AI status on umbrella; Sacramento §VII.A also implicit.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella has NO Additional Insured endorsement. Per analysis: 'additional_insured_blanket: false; additional_insured_scheduled: false; additional_insured_completed_ops: false.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.7 requires County named as additional insured on umbrella. Sacramento implicitly requires same (umbrella stacks on AI lines). The Hanover Umbrella does NOT have an explicit AI endorsement — it relies on follow-form mechanics. Most umbrellas auto-AI via follow-form, but there are technical concerns: (i) the Hanover form may not pick up AIs that the underlying CGL adds via blanket endorsement unless the umbrella's own AI definition tracks; (ii) Maricopa explicitly demands AI status per §8.2.7 — silent follow-form may not satisfy strict reading.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants the County named as an additional insured on your umbrella. Your umbrella doesn't have an explicit additional-insured endorsement — it relies on 'follow-form' from your primary GL's AI endorsement. Most carriers say that's sufficient, but Maricopa's contract reads strictly: AI on umbrella means AI on umbrella. We should request a Hanover endorsement that confirms AI status follows form, or schedule County directly.
