Combined with the missing GL/Cyber/E&O/Umbrella policies, Run-Test's net exposure on a Maricopa claim above limits is the entire balance sheet. Even when policies are bound, the company should evaluate worst-case exposure scenarios (multi-fatality, mass-tort, statewide election disruption) where damages could exceed any reasonable tower.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's indemnification clause says: whatever insurance you buy, the indemnification obligation isn't limited by it. So if a $25M claim hits and you have $10M of insurance, Run-Test owes the remaining $15M. With several required policies missing today, the gap is much wider. This drives the case for an aggressive umbrella tower and broad primaries.
findings.recommendation: Once primaries are bound, structure umbrella/excess to at least 2x-3x Maricopa's contract minimums. Discuss with PE sponsor whether captive / SIR strategy makes sense long-term given annual exposure profile.
discoveryQuestions: Has the PE sponsor ever stress-tested what a $20M claim against Runbeck would do to the balance sheet, and how much of it would land on equity?
Maricopa's indemnification isn't capped at your insurance — has anyone modeled the gap between policy limits and worst-case exposure?
Have you considered a captive structure for the higher-frequency / lower-severity exposures to free up capacity in the commercial program?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa & Sacramento
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. ... Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed for any reason, has expired, or will be expiring.
findings.policy_quote: designated_entity_noc_endorsements: [] (none on file)
findings.gap_description: No Designated Entity NOC endorsement is on file. Compliance is being achieved through the contractor's manual notice obligation under Maricopa §8.2.15. Best practice is direct carrier-to-county notice via Designated Entity NOC endorsement (Hartford's HSB-equivalent or CG 20 12). Adds no premium, removes operational risk of missing the 2-business-day pass-through window.
findings.plain_english: Hartford should notify Maricopa and Sacramento DIRECTLY when something changes — not rely on Runbeck to forward the email within 2 business days. One missed email is a contract breach. Adding a Designated Entity NOC endorsement is a no-cost fix.
findings.recommendation: Endorse Maricopa County and Sacramento County (and any other county with similar requirements) onto a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation form. Replicate on every other policy in the program (GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, E&O once bound).
discoveryQuestions: Today, if Hartford sent a cancellation notice, does anyone at Maricopa or Sacramento receive a copy directly, or only through Runbeck?
What's your internal SOP if a cancellation notice arrives during a county election cycle?
Has anyone added the counties to a Designated Entity NOC endorsement on each policy in the program?

findings.requirement_type: Property / Course of Construction (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — COC requirement is conditional. Election services manufacturer does not perform construction work.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's COC requirement is conditional — it only triggers if Run-Test maintains a Course of Construction / Builders Risk policy. Run-Test as an election services manufacturer is not engaged in construction. N/A pending confirmation that Run-Test does not perform any construction work for Sacramento County.
findings.plain_english: This requirement only applies if Runbeck does construction work. As an election-services manufacturer, you don't — so this section doesn't bite. Worth confirming there are no facility build-outs or improvements being done for the County under the contract.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Sacramento that no construction-type scope is included. If any tenant improvements, equipment installation, or facility build-outs are involved, evaluate Builders Risk requirement.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no Inland Marine policy provided in the program submission. Election services typically carries IM for mobile equipment, ballots in transit, and computer/election technology equipment.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's IM Waiver requirement is conditional — only triggers if Run-Test carries Inland Marine. For an election services company moving ballots and election technology between facilities and county sites, IM coverage on transit/property-of-others/EDP equipment is industry standard. We received no IM policy. Need to confirm whether IM exists outside this submission.
findings.plain_english: Runbeck moves ballots, mail, and election equipment around the country. That's textbook Inland Marine. We don't have any IM documentation. If IM exists, it needs a Waiver of Subrogation in favor of Sacramento. If it doesn't, that's a meaningful uninsured property exposure on equipment in transit.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Inland Marine status. If exists, confirm Waiver of Subrogation endorsement — preferably blanket. If not, evaluate need given Runbeck's equipment in transit, voter-mail in process, and high-value election technology assets. Common limit structures: $250K-$5M depending on TIV.
discoveryQuestions: How is ballots-in-transit and equipment-in-transit insured today — IM policy, on the auto, or uninsured?
What's the total value of election technology equipment, computers, and printing presses sitting at Runbeck and at county sites at any given time?
If a truck full of printed ballots was destroyed in transit, what insurance would replace them, and would Runbeck miss the election deadline?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Per-Project Aggregate (CG 25 03)
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).
findings.policy_quote: N/A — only triggered by construction projects.
findings.gap_description: Per-project aggregate requirement is construction-specific. Run-Test as election services manufacturer is not implicated unless physical construction work is involved.
findings.plain_english: This only applies if you're doing construction. You're not. So this requirement doesn't trigger.
findings.recommendation: Confirm scope. If GL is eventually bound and any construction-adjacent work emerges (facility improvements, equipment installation), revisit.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Claims-Made Retro Date — Cyber
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no Cyber policy in program. Cannot verify retro date predating 11/01/2021 contract effective date.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's claims-made requirement (retro date predating contract effective date AND 2-year ERP) is a known specification for Cyber. Without a Cyber policy in the program, this can't be evaluated. Once Cyber is bound, retro date MUST predate the Maricopa contract effective date (per the contract: 11/01/2021). If retro is set to 'inception' on a new policy, it WILL be in breach.
findings.plain_english: When Cyber is bound, the retro date has to go back to before November 2021 (Maricopa's contract effective date). Cyber carriers often default to the policy inception date. That would breach Maricopa from day one. This is the kind of detail that gets missed at binding and bites later.
findings.recommendation: When binding Cyber, request a retro date of 11/01/2021 OR 'full prior acts' (preferred). Document this in writing to the carrier. Same for E&O. If continuous coverage is later interrupted, exercise ERP for 2 years per Maricopa. Same scrutiny applies to E&O for Sacramento contract effective date.
discoveryQuestions: When you bind Cyber and E&O, the retro date controls whether old incidents are covered. Has anyone discussed setting retro back to your earliest county contract effective date?
If a voter-data breach surfaces six months from now but the underlying intrusion was three years ago, does your retro date allow coverage?
Have you ever had a claim denied because of a retro-date issue on a claims-made policy?

findings.requirement_type: RMF General — Waiver of Subrogation Cross-Program
findings.contract_quote: (General All Policies RMF #5 + Sacramento §VIII WC waiver + Maricopa §8.2.8 program-level WoS)
findings.policy_quote: Management Liability checklist: waiver_of_subrogation: false. WoS not relevant to D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary in standard structure (these aren't lines where WoS is contractually required by Maricopa or Sacramento — both contracts EXCLUDE E&O from WoS requirement). Cross-program WoS cannot be verified for GL/Auto/WC/Cyber — those policies are missing.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require WoS on GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/Umbrella (Maricopa explicitly carves out WC waiver in §8.2.12). E&O / Professional is excluded by both. Management Liability isn't typically subject to WoS. Cannot evaluate program-wide compliance with policies missing. When primaries are bound, Blanket WoS is the standard ask.
findings.plain_english: Once the missing policies are bound, every required line should have a Blanket Waiver of Subrogation in favor of any party where required by written contract. WoS isn't typically on D&O/EPLI/Fiduciary, so the Management Liability policy isn't the issue. The issue is verifying it's on each new line at bind.
findings.recommendation: When binding GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, and Umbrella: confirm Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement is in place on each. WC requires state-specific WoS form (e.g., CA WC 04 03 06 for CA work, AZ equivalent for AZ). Verify language is 'best practices' (any party where required by written contract — no narrow carve-outs).

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — subcontractor management is a contract-administration item, not a coverage item. However, Crime IA exclusion §V(B) and the D&O Manufacturing/Professional Services Exclusion both have implications if subs are involved.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento makes Run-Test responsible for subcontractor acts AND for ensuring subs provide AI endorsements to the County. Best practice: maintain a vendor insurance program with documented insurance requirements equal to or greater than what Sacramento demands. Need to confirm Run-Test has a subcontractor insurance compliance program.
findings.plain_english: When you use subcontractors on the Sacramento contract, Sacramento expects YOU to make sure those subs have proper insurance and have named the County as additional insured. If a sub creates a problem and the sub's insurance fails, Runbeck is on the hook. Need a documented vendor insurance compliance process.
findings.recommendation: Implement a vendor insurance compliance program: (a) standard insurance requirements language in every sub agreement matching county requirements; (b) sub COIs collected and tracked annually; (c) AI endorsement copies (not just COI references) collected; (d) annual audit. Common platforms: myCOI, Ebix, Riskonnect.

findings.requirement_type: General Liability — No GL Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento County: 'Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000.' Maricopa County: 'Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. ... There shall be no endorsement or modifications of the CGL limiting the scope of coverage for liability arising from explosion, collapse, or underground property damage.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.A, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.10, Page 6 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy is included in the program data provided for audit. Only the Hanover Workers Compensation policy (WD4-H218283-06) was made available.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento County and Maricopa County require Commercial General Liability with substantial limits ($1M/$2M Sac; $2M/$4M/$4M Maricopa), specific form requirements (ISO CG 00 01 occurrence for Sac, no XCU exclusion for Maricopa), Additional Insured status, Primary & Noncontributory wording, Waiver of Subrogation, and other conditions. Without a GL policy in the audit set, none of these requirements can be verified. If no GL exists, every premises, products, completed-operations, and bodily-injury liability claim from county work is uninsured. If GL exists but was not provided, the broker has not completed a defensible audit.
findings.plain_english: Your contracts with Sacramento and Maricopa Counties require a Commercial General Liability policy with specific limits and endorsements. We did not receive a GL policy to audit. Either (a) you don't have one — in which case any slip-and-fall, property damage, or product-related lawsuit from county work would come out of your bank account, not an insurer's, OR (b) you do have one but it wasn't shared with us. Either way, this needs to be resolved immediately. GL is the foundation of every commercial insurance program and the contract centerpiece for both counties.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a GL policy is in force and provide it for audit. If no GL is in place, bind one immediately — minimum $2M/$4M/$4M occurrence-form (ISO CG 00 01) with no XCU exclusion, blanket Additional Insured for ongoing AND completed operations (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37), Primary & Noncontributory (CG 20 01), Blanket Waiver of Subrogation, and Per-Project Aggregate. Until a GL is bound and audited, Run-Test is in material breach of both contracts.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your current general liability program — who is the carrier, what are the limits, and when does it renew?
When you bid on the Sacramento and Maricopa contracts, who reviewed your insurance against those county requirements? Did anyone compare your limits and endorsements line-by-line?
If a county facility staffer slipped on a pallet your team delivered tomorrow, what would happen — who pays the defense costs, who pays the settlement?
Has any county risk manager ever rejected one of your COIs or asked for additional endorsements? What was the issue?

findings.requirement_type: Commercial Auto — No Auto Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit.' Maricopa: 'Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.B, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.11, Page 6 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was included in the program data provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require Commercial Auto liability covering owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles, plus Additional Insured, Primary & Noncontributory, and Waiver of Subrogation endorsements. Run-Test's election-services operations include physical mailing, ballot delivery, on-site equipment installation, and field support across 31 states — vehicle exposure is high. Without an Auto policy in the audit set, the Run-Test BAP and the contract-required endorsements cannot be verified. If no Auto exists, every accident involving an owned/leased vehicle, employee using a personal vehicle on company errand, or rented vehicle is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your team almost certainly drives — to county elections offices, to printing facilities, to polling sites, to airports. Both counties require commercial auto coverage with specific endorsements naming them as additional insureds. We weren't given an auto policy to audit. If you don't have one, a single at-fault crash with a delivery truck on the way to a county facility could bankrupt the company and leave you in breach of every county contract you hold.
findings.recommendation: Provide the Commercial Auto policy for audit. Confirm symbol 1 (Any Auto) or symbols 7+8+9 (owned + hired + non-owned). Verify $2M CSL minimum to satisfy Maricopa, blanket AI and WoS, Primary & Noncontributory, Hired & Non-Owned coverage, and that all entities (Investments LLC, Properties LLC, Graphics Inc — listed on the WC) are also Named Insureds on the BAP. If no Auto is in force, bind immediately.
discoveryQuestions: How many vehicles does Run-Test own or lease, and do drivers ever use personal vehicles for company errands like courier runs to polling sites?
When ballots or election equipment are physically transported between facilities, who's behind the wheel — your employees, a contracted carrier, or both?
If a Run-Test driver caused a multi-vehicle accident en route to a Maricopa County facility tomorrow, what insurance would respond?
Has the auto policy ever been shared with Sacramento or Maricopa risk management for review against their requirements?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / E&O — No Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.' Section II.E expressly excludes umbrella from satisfying this minimum: 'Umbrella ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... (other than Professional Liability).'
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / E&O policy was provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County independently requires Professional Liability with a $1M/$1M minimum and expressly forbids using Umbrella to satisfy it. Run-Test provides election services — ballot printing accuracy, mail processing, election technology, voter data handling — these are quintessential professional services where a misprint, mis-sort, or system failure could cause significant economic loss to a county client and trigger a wrongful-act claim that GL would not cover (no bodily injury, no property damage). Without an E&O policy, every economic-damage claim from a county is uninsured. For an election-services company, this is the single most claim-likely line.
findings.plain_english: Election services is fundamentally a professional services business — accuracy of ballots, integrity of mail processing, reliability of election technology. A misprinted ballot, a mis-sorted mailing, or a software glitch could cost a county tens of millions and trigger a lawsuit. General Liability does NOT cover that — it covers bodily injury and property damage, not economic loss from a service failure. E&O / Professional Liability is the policy that responds. If you don't have it, you are uninsured for the most likely lawsuit your business will face. Sacramento expressly forbids using your umbrella to plug this hole.
findings.recommendation: Bind Technology / Miscellaneous Professional E&O immediately with a definition of 'Professional Services' that explicitly captures election technology, ballot printing/mailing, election mail processing, voter registration data services, and tabulation support. $1M/$1M minimum to satisfy Sacramento, but $5M+ should be considered given the scale ($5M-$25M revenue, 90M registered voters served). Verify retro date precedes the Sacramento contract effective date and any prior county contract dates. Negotiate consent-to-settle (hammer clause) with broker-friendly mechanics.
discoveryQuestions: If a county claimed your team mis-printed 50,000 ballots and they had to re-print and re-mail before election day, who pays for that — you, your insurer, or someone else?
Have you ever had a county or jurisdiction express concern about an error in ballot data, mailing accuracy, or technology performance? What happened?
Walk me through your professional liability policy — who's the carrier, what's the retro date, and how does the policy define 'professional services'?
When Sacramento County reviewed your insurance, were they satisfied with your E&O independently of your umbrella, since the contract specifically excludes umbrella from satisfying the E&O minimum?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — No Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa: 'Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses, network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.'
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber / Network Security / Privacy Liability policy was provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County mandates a $5M cyber policy with one of the broadest cyber specs we see — explicitly required components include regulatory FINES AND PENALTIES (not just defense), third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer fraud, business interruption, dependent BI, cyber extortion, breach response, credit monitoring, and crisis management, with specific carve-backs (no arrest-and-conviction requirement, off-premises losses included). Run-Test handles voter registration data, ballot delivery information, and election technology serving 90M registered voters across 31 states — this is among the highest-profile cyber/privacy risk profiles in the country given election-integrity threats and state attorney-general scrutiny. Without a cyber policy, any ransomware event, data breach, social engineering loss, or network failure is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: You handle voter data for 90 million registered Americans across 31 states. You serve county elections offices that are top-tier cyberattack targets — election infrastructure is on every nation-state actor's wish list. Maricopa demands a $5M cyber policy with one of the most comprehensive feature lists we see in any contract. Without cyber, a single ransomware event would cost Run-Test millions in forensics, restoration, breach notification, regulatory defense, business interruption, and downstream liability — all uninsured. The Maricopa requirement alone is a compliance imperative; the underlying business risk is existential.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Cyber Liability policy immediately with $5M minimum limit (both per-occurrence and aggregate), affirmative grants for: (1) regulatory fines and penalties to maximum allowed by law in every state, (2) third-party fidelity / social engineering with sublimit at or near full policy limit, (3) computer fraud / funds transfer fraud, (4) business interruption with 8-12 hour waiting period, (5) dependent business interruption, (6) cyber extortion / ransomware (verify no co-insurance), (7) breach response / forensics / notification, (8) credit monitoring, (9) crisis management. Verify retro date precedes Maricopa contract effective date (per §8.2.3, two-year ERP). Coalition, Beazley, At-Bay, or AIG are appropriate markets given operations scale. Carrier rating must satisfy Maricopa B++ minimum.
discoveryQuestions: If your systems were ransomware-encrypted three weeks before a major election, what's the response plan and who pays for the forensics, recovery, and lost productivity?
Has a county risk manager or state secretary of state's office ever asked specific questions about your cybersecurity posture or breach response?
How much voter PII does Run-Test currently process — names, addresses, signatures, registration data — and where is it stored?
If a state attorney general opened an investigation tomorrow over a privacy incident at a county you serve, who would defend that — your lawyers, or an insurer's panel?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — No Policy Available for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.E: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted ... and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) designated under the Minimum Scope of Insurance.' Maricopa §8.2.9: 'The insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.9, Page 6 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella / Excess Liability policy was provided for audit.
findings.policy_page: N/A — policy not in audit set
findings.gap_description: While neither contract independently mandates an umbrella, both contemplate one as the mechanism to reach high-limit requirements (Maricopa $2M Auto + $5M Cyber). For a $5M-$25M revenue PE-backed elections company serving 90M voters across 31 states, lack of umbrella is a critical capital structure risk — a single multi-vehicle auto accident or a class-action privacy claim could exceed primary limits. Maricopa's GL primary requirement is already $2M/$4M/$4M, which most companies layer with $5M-$25M umbrella. Without umbrella, every dollar above primary limits is uninsured exposure to balance sheet — and the indemnity-uncapped clause (Maricopa §8.1.3) means contractual liability above limits flows directly to Run-Test.
findings.plain_english: Even if all your underlying policies are perfect, a single bad day — a multi-vehicle accident, a class-action privacy lawsuit, an injury at a county facility — can blow through primary limits in hours. Umbrella is the safety net that catches that. Both counties expect you to have one, and Maricopa's contract specifically allows umbrella to stack on most lines to meet limit requirements. Without it, you're essentially betting the company on the assumption that no claim will ever exceed your underlying limits. That's not a bet a PE-backed business should be taking.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Umbrella with $10M-$25M limit minimum given operations scale. Verify follow-form for GL, Auto, Employers Liability — and explicitly confirm the umbrella DOES drop down for action-over claims, follows the underlying additional insured, primary/non-contributory, and waiver-of-subrogation status. Verify Per-Project / Per-Location aggregate follows form. Defense should be outside limits where possible. Schedule of underlying must list ALL primary policies. Confirm carrier meets Sacramento A-VII / Maricopa B++ minimums.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest loss your business could survive without insurance — and what's your current catastrophic-claim ceiling across all lines?
Your PE sponsor likely has expectations on tower limits — has anyone modeled what would happen to enterprise value if a claim exceeded your primary policies?
If a class-action privacy lawsuit named Run-Test as a co-defendant alongside a county, do you know what your total available limits would be?
When Maricopa accepted your insurance, did you stack umbrella to meet the $2M Auto and $5M Cyber requirements, or were those satisfied by primary alone?

findings.requirement_type: WC California Statutory Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.'
findings.policy_quote: States Covered Part 3.A includes: AZ, AR, CA, CO, FL, GA, IL, IN, MN, NY, NC, OR, PA, SD. CA-specific endorsements present: WC 99 03 04 California Broad Form, WC 04 03 01 D Policy Amendatory, WC 04 03 60 B EL Amendatory, WC 04 06 01 B Cancellation, WC 04 04 21 Optional Premium Increase, WC 04 04 22 Short-Rate Cancellation, WC 04 03 06 California Waiver of Subrogation.
findings.gap_description: California is properly listed as a 3.A statutory state on the WC policy with a complete suite of CA-specific amendatory endorsements. The CA Schedule Modification of 0.52 indicates favorable CA-specific loss experience. CA premium of $2,808 confirms exposure is being rated and reported. Run-Test can perform work in California and the WC policy will respond to a California injury under CA statutory benefits.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires you to carry California workers' comp before performing any work in California. Your Hanover WC policy properly includes California as a primary covered state with all the California-specific amendments and a favorable scheduled credit (you're paying about half what a similar California-rated employer would pay). This requirement is fully met.
findings.recommendation: Continue to confirm CA payroll is being properly reported in audits. Ensure any CA work travel is reported to confirm state remains in 3.A.

findings.requirement_type: WC Arizona Statutory Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa: 'Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes having jurisdiction of Contractor's employees engaged in the performance of the work or services under this contract.'
findings.policy_quote: Arizona is the primary state on the WC policy. AZ premium $23,179 represents the largest state allocation (~73% of total premium). AZ-specific endorsements: WC 02 06 01 C Cancellation/Nonrenewal Endorsement, WC 02 06 03 A Arizona Amendatory Endorsement, WC 8424d Notice to Employees. AZ Schedule Modification 0.75; AZ Experience Mod 0.69.
findings.gap_description: Arizona statutory WC properly in force for Run-Test's home-state operations. AZ is the primary state with the largest payroll exposure rated and full Arizona statutory amendatories applied. Policy will respond to an Arizona injury under AZ statutory benefits.
findings.plain_english: Arizona is your home state and the largest part of your workers' comp policy — about 73% of the premium. Arizona statutory coverage is in place with all required state-specific endorsements. Maricopa's requirement on this point is satisfied.
findings.recommendation: No action — Arizona statutory WC properly in place.

findings.requirement_type: WC Employer's Liability Limits — $1M/$1M/$1M
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease.' Maricopa: 'Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit.'
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: Employers Liability: $1,000,000 each accident; $1,000,000 disease each employee; $1,000,000 disease policy limit. (Oregon shows separate $500K floor per WC 36 03 06 — but $1M policy limits prevail.)
findings.policy_page: Limits page; Oregon-specific WC 36 03 06 at Page 190
findings.gap_description: EL limits are $1M/$1M/$1M, exceeding the standard $100K/$500K/$100K base limits and meeting both Sacramento ($1M) and Maricopa ($1M/$1M/$1M) contract minimums. New York receives effectively unlimited EL via WC 31 03 08 endorsement (Page 179). These limits are also adequate to support a typical $5M-$10M umbrella attachment without leveraging gap.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp policy includes Employer's Liability at $1M across all three categories — accident, disease per employee, disease policy limit. This satisfies both county requirements and is the standard floor needed to attach a commercial umbrella above it. Solid construction here.
findings.recommendation: Maintain $1M/$1M/$1M floor at every renewal. If umbrella is bound or increased, ensure EL remains the underlying for any action-over (employee suing third party, third party tendering to Run-Test) claim.

findings.requirement_type: WC Blanket Waiver of Subrogation — California-Specific Form
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VIII: 'The workers' compensation policy required hereunder shall be endorsed to state that the workers' compensation carrier waives its right of subrogation against the COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, agents or volunteers, which might arise by reason of payment under such policy in connection with performance under this Agreement by the CONTRACTOR.'
findings.policy_quote: WC 04 03 06 — Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others Endorsement — California. California-specific blanket waiver. AP = 2% of CA WC premium.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires WC waiver of subrogation in favor of the County. California requires a California-specific waiver form (WC 04 03 06) — and that exact form is endorsed on the policy as a blanket waiver applying to any party with whom the insured has a written contract requiring waiver. Sacramento's requirement is satisfied without needing a per-county schedule.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires your workers' comp carrier to give up its right to come after the county if a Run-Test employee gets hurt on county premises. California requires a specific endorsement form for this — and your policy has the exact right form, written as a blanket waiver. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: No action — confirm waiver continues at renewal and that CA payroll allocation supports the 2% surcharge tied to this endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: WC Blanket Waiver of Subrogation — Arizona & Other Scheduled States
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.12: '... waive all rights against this contract and its agents, officers, directors, and employees for recovery of damages to the extent these damages are covered by the workers' compensation and Employer's Liability ...' Maricopa §8.2.8 separately requires WoS on all required policies (with WC and E&O carve-outs in §8.2.8 but reaffirmed for WC in §8.2.12).
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 03 13 — Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others Endorsement (Blanket). Schedule lists: AZ, AR, CO, FL, IN, MN, NY, OR, PA. Premium charged each state.
findings.gap_description: Arizona is properly scheduled on the blanket WC waiver of subrogation endorsement. Maricopa County's WC waiver requirement (per §8.2.12) is satisfied for any AZ claim. Note that GA, IL, NC, SD are NOT on the schedule despite being 3.A states — if Run-Test has employees performing work in those states for a customer requiring waiver, the waiver would not apply there.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp blanket waiver of subrogation properly covers Arizona, satisfying Maricopa County's requirement. The same blanket also covers AR, CO, FL, IN, MN, NY, OR, and PA. Note: Georgia, Illinois, North Carolina, and South Dakota are not on the schedule — if you take on a contract there that requires a WC waiver, you'll need to add those states.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, request the broker add GA, IL, NC, SD to the WC 00 03 13 schedule for parity with the 3.A state list. Cost is typically nominal ($50-$250 per state per the schedule shown). Better still, request the carrier endorse a true blanket WoS that applies in any 3.A state without scheduling.

findings.requirement_type: WC Designated Entity NOC — Maricopa County Not Listed
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342 (09 11) — Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s). Schedule of designated entities: 'El Paso County Contracts & Procurement Division (200 South Cascade Avenue, Colorado Springs, CO 80903); Coconino County (219 East Cherry Ave, Flagstaff, AZ 86001); Amazon.com Services LLC (345 Boren Avenue North, Seattle, WA 98109).' Maricopa County is NOT listed.
findings.gap_description: The Hanover WC policy includes a designated-entity NOC mechanism (form 331-0342) that gives 30-day cancellation notice to scheduled entities. Maricopa County is conspicuously missing from the schedule — which lists Coconino County (a different AZ county), El Paso County (CO), and Amazon. The contract requires Maricopa receive 30-day notice of any cancellation, suspension, OR material change. Without Maricopa on the NOC schedule, the only mechanism for Maricopa to receive notice is the contractor's 2-business-day relay obligation under §8.2.15 — meaning Run-Test bears the full administrative burden and the consequences of any failure (which is a material breach per §8.2.2).
findings.plain_english: Your WC policy has a special endorsement that automatically tells specific government agencies if your insurance is being cancelled. Coconino County and El Paso County are on the list — but Maricopa County, the actual contract counterparty here, is NOT. That means if Hanover ever cancels or non-renews, Maricopa won't be notified by the carrier — only by you, manually, within 2 business days. If you miss that 2-day window, you're in material breach of the contract. The same form already covers Coconino and El Paso; adding Maricopa is a 5-minute fix that closes a real exposure.
findings.recommendation: Submit endorsement request to Hanover to add 'Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003' to the form 331-0342 schedule. Note: standard NOC endorsements typically cover cancellation/non-renewal but not 'material change' — verify the endorsement language and consider whether a custom endorsement is needed to satisfy Maricopa's broader 'material change' notice trigger. Also add Maricopa to all OTHER policies in the program once they are produced for audit (GL, Auto, Cyber, Umbrella).
discoveryQuestions: Do you know which counties are currently scheduled on your insurance cancellation-notice endorsements? Has anyone audited that list against your active contracts?
If your carrier non-renewed mid-contract, what's the operational process for notifying Maricopa within the 2-business-day window?
How many other county or government contracts do you hold where the contract requires 30-day carrier notice? Are all of them listed on the same endorsement?
Has any government client ever rejected your COI because the cancellation-notice provision wasn't on a designated-entity endorsement and was just stated on the certificate?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice Period vs. 90-Day Broker Benchmark
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.2 (10-day renewal evidence + immediate carrier-communication relay) and Maricopa §8.2.15 (30-day notice to County). Beyond contract minimums, Strategic Risk benchmark is 90-day notice for designated entities.
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342: '30 days written notice to designated entities for cancellation other than nonpayment.' AZ amendatory (WC 02 06 01 C): 30-day notice to insured and Industrial Commission of Arizona.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts are satisfied at 30-day notice. However, the broker benchmark for designated-entity NOC is 90 days, providing time to remarket and bind replacement coverage without lapse. At 30 days, Run-Test may have insufficient lead time to replace coverage and remain in compliance with all government contracts simultaneously. This is a program-design observation rather than a contract violation.
findings.plain_english: Your policy meets the contract minimum (30 days) but falls short of the Strategic Risk best-practice standard of 90-day notice to government clients. Why does this matter? If a carrier non-renews in May for a July expiration, 30 days isn't enough time to remarket and bind replacement coverage cleanly — especially with multiple counties to keep informed. 90 days gives you a real working window. This is a quality-of-program issue, not a compliance failure.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request Hanover endorse 90-day designated-entity notice on the WC, and replicate the 90-day standard across the GL, Auto, Cyber, and Umbrella once those policies are confirmed. Many standard markets will accommodate 60- or 90-day notice on request without premium impact.
discoveryQuestions: If your carrier non-renewed your WC tomorrow, how many days do you actually need to remarket and bind a replacement without a coverage lapse?
Have any of your county clients indicated they want longer notice than 30 days, or expressed concern about how late they'd find out about a coverage change?
Does your PE sponsor have any insurance covenant requiring specific notice periods that might exceed what counties demand?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier A.M. Best Rating — Sacramento A-VII Minimum
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.1: 'Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.' Maricopa §8.2.1: 'a company or companies duly licensed by the State of Arizona and possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.'
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (Hanover Insurance Group). A.M. Best rating not stated within the policy data provided.
findings.gap_description: Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company is part of the Hanover Insurance Group. Hanover Group is generally A.M. Best A (Excellent) rated with size category XV — substantially above both Sacramento's A-VII minimum and Maricopa's B++ minimum. However, the precise current A.M. Best rating for Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company specifically should be confirmed in writing before relying on it for compliance certification, especially given carrier ratings can change between renewals.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp is written by Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company, part of Hanover. Hanover is a strong A-rated carrier and almost certainly meets both county thresholds — Sacramento's A-VII minimum and Maricopa's B++ minimum. We just need to confirm the current rating in writing for the file so it's documented for the counties.
findings.recommendation: Pull current A.M. Best rating report for Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company and document in the audit file. Repeat annually at renewal for all carriers in the program. Apply the same check to GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro, and Umbrella carriers once those policies are produced.

findings.requirement_type: WC All States Endorsement — Item 3.A vs 3.C Coverage
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-3: 'All States Endorsement on WC / Additionally are any states omitted from 3.A that were picked up under 3.C in the previous year? If so, this can be very problematic.'
findings.policy_quote: Item 3.A states: AZ, AR, CA, CO, FL, GA, IL, IN, MN, NY, NC, OR, PA, SD. Item 3.C: 'All states except ND, OH, WA, WY (monopolistic) and the states named in 3.A.' Run-Test serves clients in 31 states + DC.
findings.gap_description: 14 states are scheduled in Item 3.A as primary covered states with full statutory coverage from day one. Item 3.C Other States Insurance covers all non-monopolistic remaining states. The Workers Compensation Broad Form Endorsement (990301B0316) extends Other States Insurance protection to a 60-day notification window for new states (vs 30 days standard). Stop Gap Coverage is provided for the four monopolistic states (ND/OH/WA/WY) — except in Indiana where the Broad Form is fully deleted. With Run-Test serving 31 states + DC, this construction is appropriately broad.
findings.plain_english: Workers' comp coverage rules differ by state, and a policy that doesn't list every state where you have employees can leave gaps. Your WC policy lists 14 'primary' states plus an 'all other states' clause covering everywhere except the four monopolistic states (where state-fund coverage is required and your policy provides Stop Gap protection). Combined with the Broad Form Endorsement, this gives you 60-day coverage in any new state you enter. Well-constructed for a 31-state operation.
findings.recommendation: Run a payroll-by-state report at each renewal and confirm any state with material payroll is in 3.A (not just 3.C). 3.A is preferred because rates are pre-filed and audited; 3.C can result in audit-time surprises. Also confirm coverage exists in any state where employees are temporarily working (election deployments).

findings.requirement_type: Indiana Voluntary Compensation & Other States Modification Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-3, WC-7: 'Endemic Disease, Foreign Voluntary and Repatriation costs.' RMF WC-3: 'All States Endorsement on WC / Additionally are any states omitted from 3.A that were picked up under 3.C in the previous year?'
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 99 03 08 03 16 — Indiana Exclusion - Other States Insurance & Voluntary Compensation. 'Material Indiana exclusion: deletes Broad Form's Other States Insurance modification, Transfer of Rights/Duties modification, and entire Voluntary Compensation/EL Coverage section for Indiana. IN reverts to standard NCCI WC 00 00 00.'
findings.gap_description: Indiana operations are explicitly carved out of the Workers Compensation Broad Form Endorsement. This means: (1) no Voluntary Compensation safety net for employees who are exempt or excluded from IN WC, (2) no extended Other States Insurance modification (only the standard NCCI 'as soon as possible' notice obligation), and (3) no Transfer of Rights/Duties enhancement. For a contracting employer with broader-state operations, this matters most if an Indiana-based employee performs work in a state not scheduled in 3.A — coverage could be denied under 3.C standard notice rules.
findings.plain_english: Indiana has its own state-mandated WC structure, and Hanover excluded Indiana from the broad-form enhancements that apply in every other state. This is an Indiana-specific quirk, not a general gap. Practically, it matters in two scenarios: (1) if you have an Indiana-based employee who travels to work in another state, the 60-day grace window doesn't apply — you have to notify the carrier 'as soon as possible'; (2) if you ever have a worker classified as exempt under IN law (sole proprietors, certain agricultural categories), there's no Voluntary Comp fallback. For an elections-services manufacturer, the exposure is probably modest, but it should be confirmed.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test has Indiana-based employees and the nature of their travel patterns. If employees travel from IN to other states for elections support, ensure 'as soon as possible' notification is being made systematically. If there are any exempt/excluded categories of IN workers, consider a separate Voluntary Comp endorsement. Note for renewal discussion with Hanover.

findings.requirement_type: Experience Modification Trend & Broker Management
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-8: 'Experience Modification - Is it being managed by the broker?'
findings.policy_quote: Experience Modifiers: AZ 0.69, AR 0.66, CO 0.69, FL 0.69, GA 0.69, IL 0.69, IN 0.69, MN 0.69, NC 0.69, OR 0.69, SD 0.69, NY 0.97, PA 0.95. Plus Schedule Modifications: CA 0.52, AZ 0.75. Effective date 4/1/2025.
findings.gap_description: Experience mods are favorable across the board — most states 0.69 (31% better than industry average), AR 0.66, with higher mods in NY 0.97 and PA 0.95 (both still under 1.0). California and Arizona benefit from additional underwriter-applied schedule modifications (0.52 and 0.75 respectively). This indicates: (1) favorable loss history relative to peer manufacturers, (2) underwriter is willing to apply discretionary credits, (3) program is being actively managed.
findings.plain_english: Your experience mod is the carrier's report card on your loss history — under 1.0 is good, over 1.0 is bad. You're at 0.66-0.97 across all states, with most at 0.69. That's roughly 30% better than the industry average — meaningful premium savings and an indicator your safety program is working. The carrier is also giving you discretionary schedule credits in California (50%) and Arizona (25%), which is unusual generosity and should be protected at renewal.
findings.recommendation: Maintain claims management discipline to preserve mod. Request mod worksheet from broker annually to verify accuracy and identify any claims that could be reclassified or settled to improve mod. Brief PE sponsor on the favorable mod as a measurable safety/risk-management win.

findings.requirement_type: WC Classification Codes — Verification Against Actual Operations
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-15: 'Are the classification codes correct?'
findings.policy_quote: Specific class code-by-state schedule of operations was not extracted in the available policy summary. Total Schedule of Operations Premium: $30,691; Total Estimated Annual Premium: $31,813.
findings.policy_page: Schedule of Operations (full schedule not in summary)
findings.gap_description: Run-Test operates as: (1) ballot printer (likely 4299 Printing — Books, Magazines NOC or similar printing class); (2) mail processing/sorting facility (4304 Newspaper Publishing Mailing Department or similar); (3) field services / elections support (potentially 8810 Clerical or 8742 Outside Sales depending on activity); (4) potentially light manufacturing of election technology hardware. The mix of operations creates classification complexity — a misclassification could result in either premium overcharge or audit-time reclassification with retroactive premium plus penalty. Without the schedule of operations code-by-code, classification accuracy cannot be confirmed.
findings.plain_english: Workers' comp premium is calculated by 'class code' — basically what kind of work each employee does. Run-Test has a complex mix: ballot printing, mail sorting, field installation, and possibly hardware manufacturing. Each has a different code with a different rate. If even one is wrong, you're either overpaying right now or the carrier will hit you with a back-charge at audit time. We need to validate the actual schedule of operations against what your team actually does.
findings.recommendation: Pull the full schedule of operations from the WC policy and compare each class code to actual job functions of the employees in each role. Specifically validate: (1) printing operations (likely 4299), (2) mail sorting (4304), (3) hardware assembly (likely 4470 or similar light manufacturing), (4) any field/installation activity (separately rated), (5) clerical/office (8810). Get the carrier's loss control rep to walk the operation and confirm before audit.

findings.requirement_type: Alternate Employer Endorsement / Staffing Arrangement
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-5: 'Alternate Employee Endorsement included on the leasing company's policy?'
findings.policy_quote: No Alternate Employer endorsement (WC 00 03 01 A) is identified in the endorsement schedule. No staffing/leasing arrangement is documented in the policy data.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has likely peak-season staffing demands tied to the elections cycle. If temporary or leased workers are used during peak periods (ballot printing rushes, mail processing, election-day support), the staffing arrangement matters: temps from a staffing firm are typically covered by the staffing firm's WC, but require an Alternate Employer Endorsement on the staffing firm's policy naming Run-Test as the alternate employer. Without this confirmation, an injured temp could file a tort suit against Run-Test that wouldn't be barred by WC exclusivity.
findings.plain_english: Election cycles create big seasonal staffing surges. If Run-Test brings in temps from a staffing company during peak periods, you need to be sure the staffing company's workers' comp covers them when they're at your facility — and that includes an 'alternate employer endorsement' naming you as a co-employer. If it doesn't, an injured temp can sue Run-Test directly in tort court (where damages are uncapped), bypassing the workers' comp 'exclusive remedy' shield that protects you from your own employees' lawsuits. This is one of the biggest hidden exposures in seasonal manufacturing.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test uses temporary or leased labor. If yes: (1) collect WC certificates from each staffing vendor showing Run-Test as alternate employer, (2) require the WC 00 03 01 A Alternate Employer endorsement on each staffing firm's policy, (3) verify the staffing firm has the right state coverage for any state Run-Test deploys to. Consider adding the Alternate Employer endorsement to Run-Test's own WC if Run-Test ever loans employees to other entities.

findings.requirement_type: Owners Excluded Review
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-12: 'Owners Excluded'
findings.policy_quote: Schedule of Owner/Officer inclusion or exclusion not extracted in the available policy summary. PE-backed structure may include working executives drawing a salary plus active operating roles.
findings.gap_description: PE-backed operating companies typically have a working CEO/President and active executive team drawing salaries. Whether they are included or excluded from the WC policy materially affects: (1) premium (including officers can be expensive at the executive comp level even when capped at state max payroll), (2) personal coverage if injured on the job, (3) Employer's Liability response. For PE structures, owners often elect exclusion because they have separate Executive Disability/Personal Accident coverage that is more responsive than statutory WC.
findings.plain_english: Your owners and officers are either included or excluded from workers' comp coverage. There's no 'right' answer — it depends on whether they have other personal coverage (disability, supplemental health, accident) that responds better than WC. For PE-backed companies, exclusion is common because the executive team has separate, richer disability protection. We need to confirm what's elected and that executives understand the trade-off.
findings.recommendation: Pull the WC schedule showing Officer/Owner inclusion/exclusion election. Confirm with each named officer that the election is intentional and that adequate personal disability/accident coverage exists for any officers who are excluded. Document for the file.

findings.requirement_type: Small Indemnity Claims & Back-to-Work Program
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-1: '# & amount of small indemnity claims in experience period - Can these be treated, in the future, with the utilization of a 'back to work' program, as medical only claims. Will this result in a 70% reduction for mod calculation purposes for those NCCI states that allow such an adjustment?'
findings.policy_quote: Loss runs and individual claim detail not provided in the policy summary.
findings.gap_description: NCCI rules (in most states) reduce the experience-mod impact of small indemnity claims by 70% if they can be reclassified as medical-only via an effective return-to-work / modified-duty program. Run-Test's mod is already favorable (0.69 in most states), but a single small indemnity claim avoiding RTW could swing the mod and cost real premium. Without loss run review, RTW program effectiveness can't be assessed.
findings.plain_english: Small workers' comp claims that involve any time-off-work get 'indemnity' status, which hurts your experience mod 3x harder than the same claim treated as 'medical only.' A real return-to-work / modified-duty program — where injured workers come back on light duty fast — converts indemnity claims into medical-only and saves you mod points. Your mod is already strong, but a back-to-work program is how you keep it that way.
findings.recommendation: Request Hanover loss runs covering the most recent 5 years. Identify any indemnity claims under $10K and assess whether RTW could have prevented or shortened time-off. Establish or formalize a written modified-duty program if one doesn't exist. Track success metrics annually.

findings.requirement_type: Small Medical Claims Management
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-2: '# & amount of small med claims in experience period, for states where #1 is not applicable - Can these small claims be paid resulting a mod savings?'
findings.policy_quote: Claims-by-claim detail not in policy summary.
findings.gap_description: Even small medical-only claims add to the experience mod calculation. In states without the 70% indemnity reduction, paying very small claims out-of-pocket (rather than through the carrier) can keep them off the mod entirely. This is most effective for sub-$1K medical-only claims.
findings.plain_english: Some workers' comp claims are so small that running them through the carrier costs you more in mod-impact than just paying them yourself out of pocket. For example, a $400 urgent-care visit reported and paid by the carrier hurts your mod for three years; paid directly, it doesn't appear at all. We should review your loss runs to identify any candidates.
findings.recommendation: Identify any sub-$1K medical-only claims in the last 3-5 years. Discuss with broker and CFO a policy for pay-direct on de minimis claims (compliant with state law — some states require all claims be reported). Coordinate with HR on injury reporting protocols.

findings.requirement_type: Large Claims Management & Reserves Review
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-10: 'Large claims by name and total incurred - Have these been managed correctly?'
findings.policy_quote: Loss runs not in policy summary. No large open or closed claims identified in available data.
findings.gap_description: The favorable experience mods (0.66-0.97) suggest no severe historical claims, but specific large-claim review (claims with reserves >$25K) is the standard audit step. Reserves are a major mod driver — over-reserved open claims inflate the mod even if they ultimately settle for less. Quarterly reserve review with claims adjuster is industry best practice.
findings.plain_english: When you have an open workers' comp claim, the carrier sets a 'reserve' — basically their estimate of what it'll cost. That reserve, not the actual eventual payment, drives your mod for 3 years. If the carrier over-reserves a claim that later settles small, you pay for a high mod for 3 years anyway. Quarterly reserve review with the adjuster — pushing back on inflated reserves — is how you protect the mod proactively.
findings.recommendation: Establish quarterly claims review meetings with Hanover claims adjuster. Identify any open claim with reserves >$25K and challenge or validate. Track reserve movements over time. For any closed claim with significant reserve > settlement variance, request retroactive mod adjustment.

findings.requirement_type: All Possible WC Premium Credits Applied
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-11: 'Does the comp policy contain all possible credits?'
findings.policy_quote: Premium Discount Endorsement WC 00 04 06 / 000406A0895 scheduled. Colorado Premium Credit for Certified Risk Management Programs disclosure shown (0%-12.5% available). Schedule modifications applied AZ (0.75) and CA (0.52). Pennsylvania merit credit applied (0.950).
findings.gap_description: Several credits are visibly applied (Premium Discount, AZ/CA schedule modifications, PA merit credit, CO disclosure), but state-specific credits available but unverified include: Colorado Risk Management Certified Program (up to 12.5% credit), Florida Drug-Free Workplace credit (5%), Florida Safety Committee credit, Illinois Industrial Commission programs, NY Safety Group, etc. Without state-by-state credit audit, leakage is likely.
findings.plain_english: Workers' comp has dozens of state-specific credits — drug-free workplace programs, safety committees, return-to-work programs, certified risk management programs. Some are worth 5-10% off premium. We see the carrier applied some discretionary credits but a thorough state-by-state credit audit can usually find another 2-5% in unclaimed credits.
findings.recommendation: Conduct state-by-state credit audit at next renewal. Specifically chase: CO Certified Risk Management credit (12.5% available), FL Drug-Free Workplace + Safety Committee credits, IL Industrial Commission programs, NY Safety Group eligibility. Document programs Run-Test runs internally that may qualify for credits not currently claimed.

findings.requirement_type: EL Limits Adequate to Support Umbrella Attachment
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-6: 'EL Limits - Are they adequate to support the Umbrella?'
findings.gap_description: $1M EL is the standard floor for umbrella attachment with most US umbrella markets. Run-Test's EL limits are sufficient to support a typical $5M-$25M commercial umbrella without leveraging gap on the WC side. (Note: umbrella itself is not in the program data — see separate finding.)
findings.plain_english: Most umbrella policies require your underlying employer's liability to be at least $1M before the umbrella will sit on top. Your $1M / $1M / $1M Hanover construction is the right floor. When your umbrella is bound or audited, this part won't be a problem.
findings.recommendation: Maintain $1M EL floor at every renewal. If umbrella is increased above $25M, consider increasing EL to $2M to maintain leverage ratio.

findings.requirement_type: Foreign Voluntary / Endemic Disease / Repatriation
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-7: 'Endemic Disease, Foreign Voluntary and Repatriation costs.'
findings.policy_quote: No Foreign Voluntary Compensation endorsement on policy. Run-Test serves clients in 31 US states + DC; no international operations identified.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Run-Test operates domestically (31 US states + DC). No Foreign Voluntary Comp, Endemic Disease, or Repatriation coverage required absent international employee travel.
findings.plain_english: N/A — Run-Test is a domestic-only operation, so foreign workers' comp coverage isn't needed. If international travel is ever contemplated (vendor visits, conferences abroad), revisit.
findings.recommendation: Reconfirm at each renewal that no employee international travel is occurring. If international business activity emerges, add Foreign Voluntary Comp endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: Maritime Coverage / USL&H / MEL
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-9 + WC-14: 'Maritime coverage endorsement included? / USH&L on an if any basis?'
findings.policy_quote: Standard EL exclusions WC 00 00 00 C §C.8-10 exclude USL&H, FELA, OCSLA, DBA, Jones Act, vessel crew. No giveback endorsements scheduled.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Run-Test is a printing / mail processing / elections technology company. No waterfront, vessel, dock-adjacent, or maritime exposure identified. USL&H, Jones Act, MEL not applicable.
findings.plain_english: N/A — Run-Test isn't a maritime employer. No maritime workers' comp endorsements needed.
findings.recommendation: Reconfirm at renewal — no action required.

findings.requirement_type: Defense Base Act (DBA) Coverage
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-13: 'Is Defense Base Act (DBA) included for workers working overseas at U.S. government facilities or for the benefit of the government?'
findings.policy_quote: Standard EL exclusion WC 00 00 00 C §C.8 excludes Defense Base Act. Run-Test's government work is domestic county/state elections — not overseas US government contracts.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Run-Test serves domestic state/county election officials. No overseas US government contracts identified. DBA not required.
findings.plain_english: N/A — DBA covers contractors working overseas on US government contracts (military bases, embassies). Run-Test does domestic county/state elections work, so DBA isn't applicable.
findings.recommendation: Reconfirm at renewal — no action required.

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Cross-Program Consistency
findings.contract_quote: RMF General-3: 'Named insureds — list for each policy and flag any missing.'
findings.policy_quote: WC Named Insured: Runbeck Election Services Inc. Additional Named Insureds via WCDECMISC: Investments LLC, Properties LLC, Graphics Inc — extended via Workers Compensation Broad Form Endorsement (990301B0316).
findings.gap_description: Four entities are recognized on the WC: Runbeck Election Services Inc + three affiliates (Investments LLC, Properties LLC, Graphics Inc). Without sight of the GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro, Umbrella policies, we cannot verify these same four entities are Named Insureds across the program — this is the single most common gap in PE-backed multi-entity programs. The two LLCs are particularly important: many GL forms (specifically the standard Broad Form Named Insured endorsement) limit automatic NI status to corporations, leaving LLCs uncovered unless specifically scheduled.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp policy correctly covers four entities — the operating company plus an Investments LLC, a Properties LLC, and a Graphics Inc. PE-structured businesses commonly have these holding/real-estate/affiliate entities, and they need to appear on EVERY policy in the program. The most common gap we see is when a parent or affiliate is on WC but not on GL, or on GL but not on Umbrella — leaving that entity uninsured for that line. We need to verify each of those four entities appears as a Named Insured on every policy. We can't do that until the other policies are produced.
findings.recommendation: Once GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro, and Umbrella policies are produced for audit, build a 4-entity x 6-policy matrix and confirm every cell is checked. Pay particular attention to LLC entities — verify Broad Form Named Insured endorsements DO extend automatic status to LLCs (some forms exclude LLCs/partnerships, which is the most-common PE gap).

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors and Omissions Across Program
findings.contract_quote: RMF General-2: 'Does the policy include an Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback ... Without it, an inadvertent failure to report a location, vehicle, or operation can result in coverage denial.'
findings.policy_quote: WC: Not a standard WC consideration (WC is statutory and reports payroll, not locations). For other policies in program: not verifiable without policies.
findings.gap_description: WC doesn't typically have an 'Unintentional E&O' giveback because the policy responds to statutory benefits regardless of policyholder reporting accuracy (subject to audit). However, on a multi-state employer like Run-Test with seasonal staffing, a Voluntary Comp endorsement giveback for unreported employees would be valuable. More importantly, GL, Auto, Cyber, Property, and Inland Marine policies should each have an Unintentional E&O giveback — we cannot verify this without those policies.
findings.plain_english: If you accidentally forget to tell the carrier about a new location, a new vehicle, or a new operation, an Unintentional Errors & Omissions giveback says the carrier can't deny coverage just because of the reporting failure. Workers' comp doesn't really need this — it just adjusts at audit. But every other line should have it, especially with Run-Test's multi-state, seasonal-deployment operating model where things change fast. We need to check this on the GL, Auto, Cyber, Property, and Inland Marine.
findings.recommendation: Once other program policies are produced, verify each has an Unintentional E&O / Inadvertent Reporting giveback endorsement. Most preferred carriers (Travelers, Hartford, CNA, Hanover) provide this at no additional cost for established commercial accounts.

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge Officer-Limited Endorsement (Cross-Program)
findings.contract_quote: RMF General-4: 'Is the policy endorsed so that a covered occurrence is only triggered when the company's officer, the person responsible for insurance, the risk manager, or equivalent is notified — rather than ANY employee's knowledge being imputed to the entity?'
findings.policy_quote: WC has standard reporting obligations under Part Two §B; not the type of policy where Notice & Knowledge officer-limitation endorsements typically apply. Other policies (GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro) should have the endorsement — not verifiable without policies.
findings.gap_description: Without GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro policies, Notice & Knowledge endorsements cannot be verified. This endorsement matters most on claims-made policies (E&O, Cyber) where any employee's knowledge of a circumstance prior to bind can void coverage if not reported. For an elections-services company with broad-based employee exposure to potential 'circumstances' (a misprint, a complaint, a system error noted by a tech), without officer-limited Notice & Knowledge wording, every front-line employee's awareness becomes a coverage trigger.
findings.plain_english: On claims-made policies (E&O, Cyber, D&O), a basic but critical endorsement says coverage isn't lost just because some random employee knew about a possible problem and didn't escalate it. Without this 'officer-limited Notice & Knowledge' endorsement, a complaint that a customer-service rep brushed off six months ago can cause a denial later. For an elections-services company with hundreds of touchpoints, this endorsement is high-value and we need to confirm it's on every applicable policy.
findings.recommendation: Once claims-made policies (E&O, Cyber, D&O if any) are produced, verify each has officer-limited Notice & Knowledge endorsement. Common form names: 'Notice Manager,' 'Knowledge of Occurrence,' 'Imputation of Knowledge.' Standard markets include this on request.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Civil Code §2782 Active-Negligence Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.B: 'Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — this is a contract-level acknowledgment of California public policy limitation, not a policy endorsement requirement.
findings.gap_description: California Civil Code §2782(b) prohibits a public agency from indemnification for its own active negligence in certain construction contracts. Sacramento's contract acknowledges this limit by carving back the AI grant — Run-Test's AI coverage to the County will not extend to defending or indemnifying the County for the County's OWN active negligence. This is automatic California public policy and does not require a policy endorsement; the contract's acknowledgment is sufficient. No action required.
findings.plain_english: California law has a public-policy rule that says you can't be forced to indemnify a public agency for the agency's own active negligence. Sacramento's contract acknowledges this — your AI coverage to the County applies, but not for the County's own active negligence. Nothing for you to fix; this is just the County recognizing California law.
findings.recommendation: No action required — contract-level acknowledgment of CA Civ. Code §2782(b) statutory limitation.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity Uncapped by Policy Limits
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.1.3: 'The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — uncapped contractual indemnity is a balance-sheet exposure, not a coverage form question.
findings.gap_description: Standard uncapped contractual indemnity clause — Run-Test's indemnity obligation to Maricopa is NOT capped at insurance limits. Any liability above primary + umbrella limits flows to Run-Test's balance sheet directly. Combined with absence of an umbrella in the audit set, this is a critical capital structure exposure that needs to be modeled and discussed with the PE sponsor.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract says: 'Just because you have insurance with limits, doesn't mean your indemnity to us is capped at those limits.' This is standard contract language but it has real teeth. If a $10M judgment lands, your insurance pays its limit and the rest is on your balance sheet. The fix is enough total insurance tower (primary + umbrella) to cover realistic worst-case scenarios. Right now, without an umbrella in the program, that tower is dangerously thin.
findings.recommendation: Model worst-case scenario for Run-Test (multi-vehicle accident, ballot misprinting class action, ransomware shutdown affecting elections cycle). Compare to total program limits (once GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella audited). Brief PE sponsor on the indemnity-vs-limits gap and recommend umbrella sized to cover the gap (likely $10M-$25M minimum).

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Deductible / SIR Disclosure & County Approval
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.6: 'Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.' Sacramento §IV: 'Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY.'
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County and Sacramento County contract requirements
findings.policy_quote: WC has no insured deductible elected (Illinois 'No' deductible per WC 34-IL form). For other policies — not in audit set.
findings.gap_description: WC has no insured-elected deductible — clean. But Cyber policies typically carry $25K-$250K SIRs, Professional/E&O $25K-$100K retentions, and umbrella may have a $10K-$25K SIR for non-underlying claims. Each must be (a) disclosed to both counties, (b) approved before performance, and (c) potentially backed by surety bond or LOC at Maricopa's option. This could become a material collateral demand.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa and Sacramento both want to know about every deductible and self-insured retention you have, and Maricopa specifically reserves the right to demand a surety bond or letter of credit backing those retentions. Cyber and Professional Liability typically carry meaningful retentions. Once those policies are produced, we need to disclose every deductible/SIR to both counties and be ready for Maricopa to potentially require collateral.
findings.recommendation: Once GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro, Umbrella policies are produced, build a deductible/SIR schedule by line and disclose to both counties before performance. Negotiate with PE sponsor on any meaningful retention to ensure Run-Test (not the sponsor) has the cash or LOC capacity. Consider buying down high SIRs if collateral demand becomes problematic.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Endorsement Copies Required With COI
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §I: 'Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — operational/COI process question, not a policy form question.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES — not just COI references — to be attached. Most brokers issue COIs without endorsement copies; Run-Test must specifically request endorsement attachments at COI issuance. Failure to provide compliant COI bundle = no work begins. This is also a renewal-cycle obligation.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento doesn't accept just a COI — they want actual copies of the additional insured endorsement, the primary/non-contributory endorsement, the waiver of subrogation, etc. Most brokers send a COI without those attached unless asked. We need to make sure your COI process for Sacramento (and any similar county) automatically attaches all relevant endorsement copies, every time.
findings.recommendation: Establish standard COI-issuance protocol that for any government client, endorsement copies are bundled with the COI. Annual renewal: refresh the bundle with current-edition endorsements. For initial Sacramento submission: confirm CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (or equivalent), CG 20 01, CA AI endorsement, CG 24 04 / WC 04 03 06 waiver, are all included as PDF attachments.

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project Aggregate (Construction Trigger)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.A: 'Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503.'
