findings.policy_quote: N/A — Sacramento per-project aggregate trigger is conditional on construction. Run-Test is an elections services manufacturer, not a construction contractor.
findings.gap_description: Conditional requirement — only applies if Run-Test performs physical construction work for the County. Election services / ballot processing operations do not trigger this requirement. If Run-Test does any installation work at county facilities (server racks, scanning equipment), that may be considered installation rather than construction; nonetheless, recommending a Per-Project Aggregate as a best-practice add-on to the GL once produced is prudent given multi-county/multi-project workflow.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires per-project aggregate only if you're doing construction work — pouring concrete, framing buildings, etc. Election services and ballot processing don't trigger it. However, if you ever do hardware installation at county sites, Sacramento could push back. Adding Per-Project Aggregate to your GL as a best-practice is cheap insurance against that interpretation question.
findings.recommendation: Confirm scope of work with Sacramento — clarify whether installation/setup work is considered 'construction.' Add CG 25 03 (or carrier equivalent) Per-Project Aggregate to GL at next renewal regardless of strict requirement, given multi-county simultaneous work pattern (mod cost typically nominal).

findings.requirement_type: Course of Construction (COC) Loss Payee & WoS
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — conditional requirement only triggered if Run-Test maintains COC/Builders Risk for construction work.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test does not appear to perform construction subject to COC/Builders Risk. N/A.
findings.plain_english: N/A — this only applies if you're running a construction project, which you're not.
findings.recommendation: Reconfirm scope of work with Sacramento — no action required absent construction.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — Inland Marine policy not in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test profile flags 'High-value equipment' as a special risk, and elections technology routinely involves high-value equipment in transit (scanners, tabulators, ballot-on-demand printers, signature verification systems) — classic Inland Marine exposure. If an Inland Marine / Equipment Floater policy is in force, it must include a waiver of subrogation in favor of the County. Cannot verify without the IM policy.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento expects that if you have Inland Marine coverage on your equipment (which moves between locations), the carrier waives the right to come after the County if equipment is damaged on county property. Given Run-Test's high-value election equipment that moves between facilities and counties, you almost certainly have an Inland Marine policy or equipment floater. We need to confirm it's in place, includes blanket WoS, and lists the high-value equipment by category.
findings.recommendation: Produce Inland Marine / Equipment Floater policy for audit. Verify (1) blanket WoS endorsement, (2) coverage limit adequate for total equipment value, (3) transit, off-premises, and county-premises locations all covered, (4) named insureds match WC entity list (4 entities).

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.E: 'CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTOR's subcontractor.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — sub-contract management process question.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is responsible for subcontractor acts/omissions and must ensure subs provide AI endorsements flowing through to the County. No subcontractor management process is documented in available data. Common gaps: subs with sub-limit policies, subs not listing County as AI, subs without WC, missing pass-through indemnity/insurance language in sub-contracts.
findings.plain_english: If you use subcontractors — printers, mail vendors, IT contractors, software providers — Sacramento holds you responsible for them. You need each one to (a) carry insurance matching what the County requires of you, (b) name the County as additional insured, and (c) have a written contract with you that flows down all the same insurance terms. We need to see your subcontractor agreement template and a sample COI from a recent sub to verify.
findings.recommendation: Request: (1) standard subcontractor agreement template Run-Test uses, (2) sample COI from a recent subcontractor. Verify pass-through insurance/indemnity language matches Sacramento and Maricopa county minimums. Build a sub-COI tracking system with calendar reminders for renewal cycles.

findings.requirement_type: WC TRIPRA Terrorism Coverage
findings.contract_quote: RMF General — TRIA / terrorism coverage for an elections-services contractor (high political-target profile).
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 00 04 22 C — Terrorism Risk Insurance Program Reauthorization Act Disclosure. 'TRIPRA disclosure; 80% federal reimbursement above insurer deductible; $100B annual cap. Premium charged $1,463.' Florida-specific TRIPRA endorsement WC 09 04 03 C also present.
findings.gap_description: Workers comp policies are required by law to cover certified acts of terrorism for workplace injuries. The TRIPRA disclosure is properly in place at $1,463 premium charge. Given Run-Test's elevated political-target profile (election infrastructure is a known nation-state target), this coverage is meaningful — a terrorism event at a Run-Test facility or election site would be covered for employee injuries.
findings.plain_english: Election infrastructure has been publicly designated 'critical infrastructure' and is a known target for nation-state cyber and physical threats. Your workers' comp properly includes federally-backed terrorism coverage so that if an act of terrorism injures employees at a Run-Test facility or election site, the carrier responds (with the federal government picking up 80% above the carrier's deductible). Solid construction.
findings.recommendation: Maintain TRIPRA election at every renewal. Verify GL, Auto, Cyber, Pro, and Umbrella policies similarly include terrorism coverage when produced — given critical-infrastructure designation, terrorism exclusion on any line is a serious gap.

findings.requirement_type: Oregon EL Limits — Statutory Floor
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-6 / Oregon-specific WC 36 03 06 EL minimum requirements.
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 36 03 06 — Oregon Limits of Liability Endorsement. 'OR EL minimum limits $500K/$500K/$500K (or higher amount in Item 3.B).' Policy carries $1M EL — exceeds OR floor.
findings.gap_description: Oregon mandates a $500K EL floor, and the $1M policy limit prevails. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Oregon has a unique $500K Employer's Liability minimum that some carriers default to (which would underwhelm umbrella attachment). Your policy keeps the $1M limit in Oregon — which is the right answer.
findings.recommendation: No action — Oregon construction is correct.

findings.requirement_type: New York Effectively Unlimited EL
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC-6 — NY-specific limit construction.
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 31 03 08 — New York Limit of Liability Endorsement. 'Insurer may not limit liability for damages payable due to BI to employees arising out of/in course of employment subject to and compensable under NY WC Law. Effectively unlimited EL for NY claims.'
findings.gap_description: New York statutory construction provides effectively unlimited EL for NY-jurisdiction injuries. This is uniquely NY and provides Run-Test with strong protection for any NY-based action-over claim.
findings.plain_english: New York is the only state where EL limits are essentially unlimited for NY-based employee injuries — that's good news for you on any New York claim. No action needed; this is just baked into NY law.
findings.recommendation: No action — recognize this as a beneficial state-specific construction.

findings.requirement_type: Audit Noncompliance Charge — California 3X Multiplier
findings.contract_quote: Standard premium-audit best practice and CA-specific exposure.
findings.policy_quote: Form WC 04 04 21 — Optional Premium Increase Endorsement (CA): 'If audit access not provided within 90 days post-expiration, insured liable for 3X current annual premium estimate plus audit attempt costs.' Florida WC 09 04 07 A: 'up to 3X most recent estimated annual premium for audit non-cooperation; $500 cost-defrayment for denied physical inspection; 10X penalty + attorney fees for understated/concealed payroll.' WC 00 04 24 audit non-compliance charge (general): up to 2X estimated annual premium.
findings.gap_description: Severe audit-noncompliance penalties exist in CA (3X), FL (3X / 10X for concealed payroll + attorney fees), and across the program (2X). For a multi-state employer with $30K+ premium, audit noncompliance could result in $60K-$100K+ in penalty premium. Run-Test must have a robust audit response process given multi-state, multi-class operations.
findings.plain_english: If you don't cooperate with the carrier's annual premium audit, the penalties are punitive — California can charge 3 times the premium, Florida can charge 3 times normally and 10 times if they find you under-reported payroll (plus attorney fees). For a $30K+ premium, that's a $60K-$300K downside risk. Build a calendar reminder and a clean audit-prep process.
findings.recommendation: Establish annual audit response process: (1) calendar reminder 30 days before audit window, (2) pre-prepared payroll-by-state, payroll-by-class breakdown, (3) classification documentation supporting any disputed codes, (4) named audit contact. Document Florida-specific quarterly earnings reports submitted to FL DOR with sworn officer attestation per WC 09 04 07 A.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cancellation 'Material Change' Notice — Broader Than Standard NOC
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: Form 331-0342 — Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): '30 days written notice to designated entities for cancellation other than nonpayment.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's notice requirement covers cancellation, expiration, suspension, AND 'material change.' Standard NOC endorsement form 331-0342 covers cancellation only — not 'material change' (e.g., limit reduction, coverage carve-out, named insured deletion). Even if Maricopa were on the schedule (which it isn't — see separate finding), the endorsement wouldn't satisfy the 'material change' notice trigger. Run-Test's 2-business-day relay obligation under §8.2.15 partially fills this — but only after Run-Test learns of the change.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30-day notice not just for outright cancellations but for 'material changes' — limit drops, coverage carve-outs, or anyone deleted from the policy. Standard cancellation-notice endorsements don't cover material changes. The contract puts that burden on you (the contractor) to relay any such notice within 2 business days. The exposure is procedural: a quiet mid-term limit reduction could happen without anyone noticing until a claim hits.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate with Hanover to expand 331-0342 (or replace with a custom endorsement) to include material-change notice for designated entities. As a backup process control, schedule quarterly review of all required policies for any mid-term endorsements that constitute 'material change' and report them to Maricopa (and Sacramento) within 2 business days as required.
discoveryQuestions: If Hanover endorsed a coverage reduction mid-term, what's the workflow that would surface that to Maricopa within 2 business days?
Has Run-Test ever had a mid-term policy change that should have been reported to a county client? What happened?
Who at Run-Test owns the insurance file day-to-day and reviews carrier endorsement issuances as they arrive?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Right to Adjust Coverage (Open-Ended Risk)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.B (preamble): 'COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection ... COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — open-ended contract risk, not a policy form question.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento has a unilateral right to demand additional coverage mid-term. Open-ended exposure: limits, lines, and endorsements could grow at the County's discretion. This is a contract-level concern, not a policy gap, but should be flagged for the CFO's awareness.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento reserved the right to come back later and say, 'We want more insurance from you.' They can change limits, demand new lines, or insist on new endorsements — and you have to comply. Most CFOs miss this clause. It's not a coverage gap, but it's a budget risk we should plan for.
findings.recommendation: Brief CFO and PE sponsor on this clause. Build a 10-15% contingency into the insurance budget for any contract Run-Test signs with this language. Any County demand for coverage adjustment goes through broker for negotiation before binding — Sacramento may accept alternatives.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Notification of Claim / Lawsuit (Sacramento parallel)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §X: 'CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice ... within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — operational obligation on contractor.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has direct contractual obligation to notify the County of any claim within 30 days of receipt and any lawsuit within 10 days of service. This is independent of carrier reporting obligations. Run-Test needs an internal claims-tracking workflow that triggers notice to the County, not just the carrier. Failure could create breach exposure beyond any insurance issue.
findings.plain_english: If anyone sues Run-Test or files a claim that could affect the County, Sacramento wants to know within 30 days (claim) or 10 days (lawsuit) — separately from telling your insurance carrier. Most companies have a process for the carrier; few have a parallel process for client notification. We need to build that.
findings.recommendation: Build internal claim/lawsuit tracking process with two-track notice obligation: (1) carrier notice per policy terms, (2) client notice per contract terms. Calendar reminders set for 30-day and 10-day clocks. Standard form letter to County drafted and reviewed by counsel. Apply same workflow to Maricopa and any other government client with similar provisions.

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering — No Standalone Policy in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa cyber spec §8.2.13 expressly requires: 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction.'
findings.policy_quote: No Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering policy in audit set. Maricopa explicitly requires these features inside the Cyber spec.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber spec mandates components that traditionally live in a Crime/Fidelity policy: third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, theft. Election services companies handle voter list payments, vendor payments, and county-flow funds — exposures to vendor impersonation, employee theft, and wire-transfer fraud are real. Even if cyber covers some of these (often sublimited), a standalone Crime policy is the proper home. PE-backed structures often discover this gap during a CFO-level treasury fraud event.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's cyber spec mixes features that usually live in TWO different policies — the cyber stuff (data breach, ransomware) and the crime stuff (employee theft, wire fraud, social engineering). Many cyber forms include the crime components only as low sublimits (often $100K-$250K against your $5M tower). A standalone Crime policy gives full limits for theft and funds transfer. Given how exposed election services is to vendor-impersonation and wire fraud, a Crime policy belongs in the program.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Crime / Commercial Crime policy with: $1M-$5M Employee Theft, $1M+ Computer Fraud, $1M+ Funds Transfer Fraud, $250K+ Social Engineering / Impersonation Fraud, Third-Party Fidelity. Treat as complement to Cyber, not substitute. Travelers, Hartford, Chubb are appropriate markets.
discoveryQuestions: What's your wire transfer authorization process — is it dual-control, and how often does it touch payments to county or vendor accounts?
Has Run-Test ever experienced a vendor-impersonation or 'CEO fraud' attempt where someone tried to redirect a payment? What happened?
If an employee in your AP department wired $250K to a fraudulent account based on a spoofed vendor email, is that covered by your current cyber policy — and if so, at what sublimit?
Has your treasury team ever evaluated a standalone Crime policy alongside Cyber, or is the assumption that Cyber covers all funds-transfer risk?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI / Employment Practices — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: WC EL exclusion §C.7 (Page 102): 'Excludes damages from coercion, criticism, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, termination, or any personnel practices/policies/acts/omissions. EPLI required to fill this gap.'
findings.policy_quote: WC EL excludes employment-practices claims; no EPLI policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Workers' comp EL expressly excludes employment-practices liability — the most common employee lawsuit category (wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation). With 50-200 employees in a multi-state operation, statistically Run-Test will face an EPLI claim. PE-backed companies frequently have heightened EPLI risk during integration / restructuring periods. Without a standalone EPLI policy, every employment lawsuit is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp will not cover the most common employee lawsuit you'll face — wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation, hostile work environment claims. Those need a standalone Employment Practices Liability (EPLI) policy. With 50-200 employees, multi-state, PE-backed (which often correlates with integration/turnover stress), this is one of the highest-likelihood gaps in the program. We didn't see EPLI in the audit set.
findings.recommendation: Bind standalone EPLI with $1M-$3M limit minimum, third-party coverage (harassment by/against non-employees), wage & hour defense costs sublimit, broad definition of 'employee' to include temps/contractors. Travelers, Hartford, AIG, Chubb appropriate. Often packaged with D&O as Management Liability — verify packaging with broker.
discoveryQuestions: What's your turnover rate, and have you had any employee complaints, EEOC charges, or wage/hour claims in the last 3 years?
If a terminated employee sued for wrongful termination next month, who would defend that claim and pay any settlement?
Has your PE sponsor surveyed portfolio companies on EPLI specifically? Many sponsors require it as a baseline policy.
How often do supervisors get harassment / discrimination training, and is that documented?

findings.requirement_type: D&O / Management Liability — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: PE-backed structure typically requires D&O for board protection. No contract requirement, but standard for risk-tier matching Run-Test profile.
findings.policy_quote: No Directors & Officers policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: PE-backed companies typically have D&O policies for: (1) board member personal indemnification, (2) entity coverage for securities-style claims (less common in private), (3) regulatory investigation coverage. Election services companies face heightened regulatory and political scrutiny — state secretaries of state, election integrity oversight, congressional inquiries, and potential litigation around election outcomes. Without D&O, individual directors and officers face personal exposure for any decisions challenged in litigation or investigation. PE sponsors typically require D&O as a baseline in portfolio companies; if not in place, the sponsor's expectations should be confirmed.
findings.plain_english: Election services puts directors and officers in the political crosshairs. Anytime an election outcome is challenged — whether legitimate or not — D&O is what protects board members and executives personally for the decisions they made. PE sponsors almost always require it for portfolio companies. We don't see D&O in the audit set. If it's not in place, every officer and director is personally exposed to any lawsuit or investigation about Run-Test's election services decisions.
findings.recommendation: Bind a D&O policy with $5M+ limit (consider $10M-$25M given regulatory/political profile), entity coverage Side A/B/C, regulatory investigation coverage including SOS and AG investigations, broad definition of 'Claim' to include written demands, and prior acts coverage extending back to the entity formation. Confirm bump-up exclusion is removed if PE sponsor anticipates exit. Travelers, Hartford, AIG, Beazley, Chubb appropriate markets. Consider Management Liability package combining D&O + EPLI + Crime + Fiduciary for cost efficiency.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's PE sponsor have an insurance covenant requiring D&O coverage at portfolio-company level, and what's the limit floor?
If a state secretary of state opened an investigation into a Run-Test election technology decision, who pays for the executives' personal legal defense?
Has the board or any officer ever been named in a complaint, demand letter, or subpoena related to election services? What happened?
Has your PE sponsor or transaction counsel reviewed the D&O coverage as part of the insurance covenant compliance?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Not in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX (COC conditional) and general property exposure for elections-services manufacturer with high-value equipment.
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Property policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is a manufacturer with high-value equipment (printing, mailing, scanning, tabulation hardware), facility-based operations, and significant business interruption exposure tied to election cycles. A facility fire 30 days before a major election could be existential. Without a Property policy in audit set, building values, contents, business interruption limits, extra expense, dependent BI, and high-value-equipment scheduling cannot be verified.
findings.plain_english: You're a manufacturer with high-value equipment in a facility-based operation. A fire, flood, or major equipment failure 30 days before an election cycle could cripple the business — not just the property loss, but the lost revenue and the contractual breaches with counties whose ballots couldn't ship. We didn't see your Property policy. We need to confirm building values, contents limits, business interruption (with adequate indemnity period for election cycles — likely 18-24 months not the standard 12), and a sublimit-free schedule of high-value equipment.
findings.recommendation: Produce Commercial Property / Building & Contents policy. Verify (1) full replacement cost on building and contents, (2) high-value equipment scheduled at agreed value, (3) Business Interruption with 18-24 month indemnity period, (4) Extra Expense, (5) Contingent BI for key vendors and supply chain (paper, envelope, mail processing), (6) Equipment Breakdown coverage for printing/mailing equipment, (7) Ordinance & Law if applicable.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Claims-Made Retro Date & ERP — Professional
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §V.A-C: 'The Retro Date must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance ... Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. ... If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed, and not replaced ... the CONTRACTOR must purchase extended reporting coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.'
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability policy in audit set; retro date and ERP construction cannot be verified.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento independently mandates retro-on-or-before contract effective date AND a 1-year minimum ERP if claims-made coverage is cancelled/non-renewed. Without the Professional Liability policy, neither can be verified. For elections services, retro-date alignment to contract date is critical because the most likely E&O claim would relate to ballot accuracy or processing performed at the start of the engagement.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a stricter standard than Maricopa on this — retro date must be on or before the contract effective date, AND if you ever cancel/non-renew the E&O without replacing it with continuous-retro coverage, you must buy a 1-year tail (ERP) at minimum. We don't have the E&O to verify any of this. This is one of the highest-likelihood claim sources for an elections-services company; getting it wrong is genuinely existential.
findings.recommendation: When Professional Liability/E&O is produced: (1) verify retro date precedes each Sacramento (and Maricopa) contract effective date, (2) calendar a 1-year ERP purchase trigger at any cancellation/non-renewal, (3) maintain retro continuity through any carrier change. Best practice: secure ERP quote at policy bind so cost is locked. Consider 3-year ERP rather than 1-year for additional buffer.
discoveryQuestions: When you bound your professional liability policy, was the retro date set to capture all prior elections work, or just the carrier-specific bind date?
Has anyone confirmed the E&O retro date is on or before each county contract effective date — Sacramento, Maricopa, and the other 29 states?
If you decided to switch E&O carriers next year, do you have a process to either get full prior acts on the new policy or buy ERP on the old one?
What's the worst-case dollar value of an E&O claim you could face — say, a misprinted ballot batch in a major county? Have you sized the policy limit to that?
